Independent U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn speaking durring his rally in La Vista on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)Two paid staffers of Dan Osborn’s 2024 campaign joined an effort to dissolve a rival political party last year, according to records obtained by the Flatwater Free Press. The records reveal the lengths Osborn’s allies have gone to clear the field for the nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate as he attempts to unseat Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts.
The two staffers, Christoph Marsh and Will Ramsey, joined Nebraska’s Legal Marijuana NOW Party’s executive board at a virtual party convention in April 2024, when they were among 10 people elected as vice presidents of the state’s smallest political party. That group also included at least two Osborn campaign volunteers and three others with ties to his campaign, its staffers or his political allies, according to documents Flatwater obtained from the Secretary of State’s Office and other public records.
The group gave no indication of their ties to Osborn when they joined the virtual convention. Marsh introduced them as friends who had newly joined the party and offered proof of their voter registrations. “I trust you Christoph,” the party’s chairman, Mark Elworth Jr., wrote later.
The reason for their presence in the party’s upper ranks would later become clear: They could help ensure an Osborn proxy could not be replaced if she won the party’s nomination and then withdrew.
That in turn could help narrow the field for Osborn, first against Sen. Deb Fischer in a close race Osborn lost and now in a matchup against Ricketts that could help determine control of the U.S. Senate. Both races were believed to be close enough that the existence of another non-Republican on the ballot could spoil Osborn’s chances.
The methods Osborn’s supporters pioneered in the Legal Marijuana NOW Party’s 2024 race have played out again this year. Republicans have accused candidates in two primaries of being Osborn plants running the same playbook: Win and then drop out to narrow the field for Osborn.
Their victories have prompted backlash from the Republican secretary of state and drawn a lawsuit from the Democratic primary’s runner-up, who himself has been accused of being a Ricketts plant. They have spurred the creation of two new suspect political parties and yet more lawsuits challenging their legitimacy.
Long before any alleged plant candidates filed to run for office this year, the Osborn supporters and staffers filed paperwork with Secretary of State Bob Evnen’s office seeking to dissolve the Legal Marijuana NOW Party altogether, according to the documents obtained by Flatwater.
LMNdissolutionPub
 
Chelsea Richardson, a volunteer for Osborn’s 2024 campaign, sent Evnen’s office a notice in April 2025 claiming that the party had decided to dissolve itself with the support of a majority of the party’s executive board. Richardson provided sworn affidavits supporting the move from nine supposed vice presidents of the party, including herself, the Osborn staffers Marsh and Ramsey and Delanie Ness, a paid employee of Kerry Eddy’s 2024 campaign for the Legal Marijuana NOW Party’s Senate nomination, which she won after campaigning as an Osborn proxy.
 
MarshAffidavit
 
Richardson’s husband, Ramsey’s father and Ness’s fiancé also signed sworn affidavits supporting the party’s dissolution.
In the end, the effort failed.
Elworth, then the party’s chairman, told Evnen’s office the party elected new officers two days before Richardson filed her notice, ousting all nine of the vice presidents who sought to dissolve the party. In a June 2025 letter to Richardson, Evnen concluded that the group of nine didn’t appear to have the authority to dissolve the party and rejected their attempt.
 
2025 06 03 LMN Dissolution Response
 
Geoff Lorenz, an associate professor of political science at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln who studies political parties, called the effort a “wild case” of what American political operatives from both major parties have long sought to do: use election laws to prevent third parties and third-party candidates from succeeding.
“If I was going to do what they were trying to … I would only do it if I really believed that actually, legally speaking, I counted as an officer of this party,” he said.
The attempt to end the political party drew criticism from rival political operatives who cast it as an early effort by Osborn and his allies to meddle in an election that has since been plagued by dueling allegations of deceit.
Elworth, who has since moved to Colorado, called the effort “fraudulent” and said it undermined Nebraska’s democracy.
Max Oberg, the deputy campaign manager for Ricketts, said in a statement that Flatwater’s findings marked “a new low – even for the Osborn campaign.”
“Osborn is so desperate to win he’ll dissolve parties, rig ballots, and plant fake candidates to trick voters,” Oberg said. “The steps Dan Osborn has taken to subvert democracy and undermine our elections should alarm every Nebraskan. The authorities should investigate accordingly.”
Xavier Royer, the spokesman for Osborn’s campaign, said Osborn “had nothing to do with the Legal Marijuana Now Party activities.”
“The reason Dan is an independent candidate is to avoid the gamesmanship that comes with party politics,” Royer said in a statement, noting that Osborn’s campaign and the Legal Marijuana NOW Party share some goals, including the protection of legal medical marijuana in the state and the federal rescheduling of cannabis. “It’s not surprising there might be individuals with connections to both.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The campaign did not make Ramsey, a paid staffer of Osborn’s 2026 campaign, available for an interview. Flatwater’s efforts to contact Marsh, who did not return to work for Osborn’s campaign staff in 2026 and who lived in Missouri when he signed his affidavit supporting the marijuana party’s dissolution last year, weren’t successful. Richardson declined to comment.
Osborn has long distanced himself from the partisan candidates who have campaigned promising to support him and the Democratic Party altogether. His independence has helped bring him some level of electoral success: Osborn lost to Fischer in 2024 by less than 7% while Ricketts beat his Democratic challenger by more than 25 points.
But in the last two election cycles, outside groups have spent big money backing Osborn while at the same time propping up the candidacies of alleged Osborn plants.
In 2024, when Eddy won the Legal Marijauna NOW Party’s Senate nomination that she pledged to reject in support of Osborn, a Nebraska-based Super PAC called Railroaders for Public Safety spent $34,658 boosting Eddy’s candidacy in a primary race, much more than her opponent spent in total.
The same PAC spent $1.34 million supporting Osborn and opposing Fischer, according to Federal Election Commission filings.
This year, Republicans labeled two primary candidates – Cindy Burbank in the Democratic primary and Mike Marvin in the Legal Marijauana NOW primary – as Osborn plants. Burbank sought the Democratic nomination only after a Trump-supporting pastor, Bill Forbes, filed to run. Nebraska Democratic Party leaders, who opted not to run a Senate candidate and endorsed Osborn, cast Forbes as a Ricketts plant meant to dilute Osborn’s chances.
Burbank joined the race and ran the Eddy playbook, winning her party’s primary but declining its Senate nomination in a move that the secretary of state called “a cynical manipulation of the ballot process.” Her withdrawal prompted a stalled legal challenge from Forbes that is unlikely to change the outcome: a narrowed field for Osborn.
Marvin, meanwhile, won his primary but did not withdraw from the Senate race. If he had, the Legal Marijuana NOW Party could have nominated a replacement candidate – which it sought to do when Eddy withdrew in 2024 in an effort that was voted down in part by Osborn supporters who had joined the party.
Marvin told the Nebraska Examiner earlier this month he never planned to leave the race but also has no plans to hold any campaign events before the general election. His campaign website promises to “work with other candidates in the race to make sure we have a united front against Pete Ricketts in November.”
Both Burbank and Marvin’s primary campaigns were boosted by the same donor: the Common Defense Action Fund, a PAC that spent $73,445 on print and digital ads supporting Marvin, $286,048 supporting Burbank’s campaign and another $63,331 opposing Forbes, her Democratic primary opponent, including on mailers depicting him with Ricketts.
Registered nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn leaveing a podium in Lincoln on June 11, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Common Defense Action Fund has in turn drawn much of its funding this year from two sources: Contours Inc., and Common Defense Civic Engagement.
Contours Inc., a Delaware-based nonprofit, has also donated $450,000 to the Working Class Heroes Fund, a PAC Osborn launched following his loss to Fischer in 2024. Common Defense Civic Engagement has also donated $10,000 to that same Osborn PAC.
The PAC money is not the only spending that ties Burbank’s and Marvin’s campaigns together.
When they filed to run for Senate in their respective primaries 15 minutes apart on the March 2 deadline day, Burbank wrote the check that paid for Marvin’s $1,740 filing fee, the Examiner reported in March.
Burbank told that news outlet she paid Marvin’s fee after Evnen’s office refused to accept his own check, which she said was for $10 too much. Marvin said he had never heard of Burbank. His campaign refunded Burbank for the check in May, according to FEC records.
Neither Burbank nor Marvin returned phone calls seeking comment for this story.
More than a month after both won their respective primaries, dueling campaigns launched to gather enough signatures to create two new political parties in Nebraska that could place yet more Senate candidates on the November’s ballot.
First came the Nebraska Working People Party, which Nebraska Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb has tied to Ricketts and said is meant to “divide the vote and create chaos.”
Then came the America First Party, sponsored by John Cartier, an attorney listed in FEC records as Marvin’s campaign treasurer this year and Eddy’s in 2024. Marvin’s campaign filed an amended statement of organization Monday naming a new treasurer.
Nebraska’s Republican Party called Cartier’s attempt to establish the America First Party a “fraudulent” one designed to “trick conservative voters into splitting their vote,” linking it to Osborn and the Democrats. Cartier did not return a phone call or email seeking comment.
The Nebraska Democratic Party and state GOP each sued to halt the new political party they claim is meant to deceive their own voters. A Lancaster County judge dismissed those suits Thursday, potentially clearing the way for both parties to place candidates on November’s ballot pending appeals.
The plant candidates and legal challenges have been a source of frustration for Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democrats, who said her party remains “the only one that’s been honest throughout this process.”
“We said from the beginning we are making a conscious decision as a party not to field somebody in the U.S. Senate race, because we think Dan Osborn has a great shot of beating Pete Ricketts,” she said. “And then all these other games happened.”
Elworth, the former Legal Marijuana NOW Party chairman, said he expects electoral reforms that could harm parties like his. He said he fears lawmakers, after watching this year’s primary fights and the legal battles that followed, could make it harder for third parties to maintain ballot access in Nebraska.
“I’m going to tell you what’s gonna happen next,” he said. “Now, the Unicameral, after this election – they are going to crack down.”
The Flatwater Free Press is Nebraska’s first independent, nonprofit newsroom focused on investigations and feature stories that matter.

description: Lawmakers are hauling the Missouri Children’s Division back to the Capitol on Wednesday. The hearing will cover some of the agency’s recurring trouble spots: relative foster placements, child fatalities, reunification rates and how the department has carried out laws passed since 2020. text:
(Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Lawmakers are hauling the Missouri Children’s Division back to the Capitol on Wednesday. The hearing will cover some of the agency’s recurring trouble spots: relative foster placements, child fatalities, reunification rates and how the department has carried out laws passed since 2020.
Steph Quinn published two stories this week that, read together, are an argument about what the last six years of fixes have actually produced.
The first showed child abuse investigations piling up again.
Missouri says investigators should carry no more than 15 open cases. At the end of July, workers in St. Louis County averaged 97.
The average investigation there had been open 144 days. State law generally gives the division 45.
This isn’t ancient history. Three years ago, Missouri had more than 10,000 backlogged abuse and neglect cases. Frontline turnover had hit 55%. Lawmakers put money into hiring more workers, and the division knocked down most of the backlog.
Now it’s coming back.
But this time workers are pointing to more than staffing. They describe a job increasingly consumed by mandatory consultations, checklists and supervisory reviews. The rules are supposed to prevent mistakes.
Workers say they also leave less time to interview families, visit children and close cases.
Then there is Steph’s second story this week, this one focused on Korbin Papadopoulos.
Korbin was 17, autistic and diabetic. In May, the Children’s Division needed to find him a foster home equipped for elevated medical needs.
They found one 300 miles away.
But there was a problem: The foster parent was licensed only to care for his own relatives. Korbin wasn’t one of them.
Workers figured that out six days later. The foster parent asked at least twice for Korbin to be moved.
He stayed another 18 days.
Korbin died June 6 from diabetic ketoacidosis, a build-up of toxins in the blood that happens when the body has too little insulin.
We don’t know that an overloaded system caused his death. Steph’s reporting doesn’t establish that.
But look at what happened next.
In August, Children’s Division Director Sara Smith sent workers a memo clarifying the rules for foster placements. It reminded them that they need approval from a foster family’s licensing worker before making a placement and spelled out what they must check when an emergency placement happens after hours.
The memo also made something else explicit. A relative foster home is licensed for particular children. Placing an unrelated child there is “a violation of law and a significant safety risk.”
Translation: Make sure the home is actually licensed for the kid you’re sending there. Move the kid when the foster parent says he can’t stay.
Missouri has spent years putting new safeguards around the Children’s Division. Usually, they come after something has gone wrong and are meant to keep it from happening again.
The problem is that every new safeguard becomes another thing somebody has to do. And the people doing this work say they are already drowning.
Ashley Allen left her job investigating abuse and neglect in Jasper County this spring with more than 30 open cases. She described days when she was racing to find a child in a three-hour emergency while emails piled up asking why other cases weren’t closed.
None of this means the answer is less oversight. A state agency that can remove children from their parents needs plenty of it. But there is a difference between writing a safeguard and having a system capable of carrying it out.
That distinction should be at the center of Wednesday’s hearing. Lawmakers will hear about policies, restructuring and implementation. All of that matters.
But I’d start somewhere simpler.
How did Missouri reach the point where “make sure the foster home is licensed to take the child” had to be spelled out again in an August memo?
And what good is the next new rule if the people responsible for carrying it out are already buried under the last ones?

text:
A sign stands outside a polling location at St. Luke's Methodist Church on an election day Aug. 27, 2024, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Voters go to the polls Tuesday to pick nominees for various partisan posts, including governor, state superintendent and U.S. Senate.
Voters will be asked to decide the fate of two state questions lawmakers put on the ballot.
The race generating the most attention is the Republican primary runoff for governor. 
Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond faces financial planner Mike Mazzei in the race that has already resulted in historic spending.
Drummond and Mazzei were the top vote getters in the June 16 primary, but neither secured enough votes to avoid a runoff.
Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt is finishing his final term and can’t seek reelection to the post.
Republicans will also select their nominees for state superintendent and Oklahoma’s next labor and insurance commissioners.
Robert Franklin faces James Taylor in the Republican runoff for state superintendent.
John Pfeiffer faces Kevin West in the Republican runoff for labor commissioner.
Marty Quinn and Bob Sullivan are vying for the Republican nomination for insurance commissioner.
Democrats have one statewide race on their partisan ballot.
Democrats Jim Priest and N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas are vying for the party nomination for Oklahoma’s U.S. Senate seat that was vacated earlier this year by Republican Markwayne Mullin, who now heads the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
Fifteen partisan legislative races are also on the ballot.
All registered voters are eligible to vote on two state questions that seek to change the state Constitution.
State Question 844 would give lawmakers the power to recalculate the amount paid under a manufacturing tax incentive program. Some school leaders say reducing payments could negatively impact districts. Supporters say it is necessary to deal with overly expensive reimbursements.
State Question 846 would enshrine voter identification in the state Constitution. Supporters say it will ensure the integrity of elections despite it already being state law. Critics say it would expand legislative power over election law and give lawmakers the power to determine what identification is acceptable.
In order to cast a ballot in Tuesday’s election, voters must provide proof of identity. The document can be issued by the state, federal government or tribe. It must include the name of the person to whom it issued, a photograph and expiration date that falls before the date of the election, unless it does not expire.
It can also include a voter identification card issued by a county election board.
Polls open at 7 a.m. and close at 7 p.m.
Results will be posted on the Oklahoma State Election Board website after polls close.
The winners of the GOP and Democratic statewide runoffs advance to the General Election on Nov. 3.

title: Oklahoma courts need to get with the 21st century and allow photos and video
description: Last month, I found myself scratching my head – and not for the first time – that no cameras were in the courtroom to allow Oklahomans to witness the sentencing of restaurant owner Brent Swadley. Public interest was high, as Swadley had recently been convicted by a jury of defrauding the Oklahoma Tourism and Recreation […]
text:
A photo taken from outside the courtroom of Epic Charter School co-founder Ben Harris arriving for a preliminary hearing Feb. 25, 2026, at the Oklahoma County Courthouse in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)Last month, I found myself scratching my head – and not for the first time – that no cameras were in the courtroom to allow Oklahomans to witness the sentencing of restaurant owner Brent Swadley.
Public interest was high, as Swadley had recently been convicted by a jury of defrauding the Oklahoma Tourism and Recreation Department by generating fake invoices. A jury recommended he be sentenced to 10 years in prison and pay tens of thousands in fines. But it would ultimately be up to an Oklahoma County judge to decide his fate.
While the courtroom was packed with spectators, one thing was noticeably missing — cameras and recording devices.
That’s because our state’s judicial system stubbornly refuses to adopt healthy processes that allow for increased public access, understanding and accountability by routinely allowing recording and photography.
During most criminal and civil proceedings in Oklahoma’s courtrooms, there is generally no recording or photography permitted despite it being the year 2026 and technology ruling the roost everywhere else. 
That’s why if you ever have the misfortune of being in the Oklahoma County Courthouse, you might witness photojournalists chasing people down hallways or see someone attempting to photograph a courtroom proceedings through a small window on the door of a courtroom. 
There has been some movement toward transparency. The Oklahoma Supreme Court now offers an audio and video feed of oral arguments, but no still photography. And rarely you might find a judge who agrees to open his or her courtroom to photography or recording.
Largely, however, access remains blocked and the onus remains on media outlets to describe what’s happening in courtrooms or on everyday Oklahomans to take time out of their busy lives to attend proceedings in person.
It shouldn’t be that way, and we shouldn’t have a critical part of our democracy that too often remains shrouded in mystery.
I’m not the only one who has been wondering why Oklahoma’s judicial system is operating like it’s 1972. 
Earlier this month, Scott Mitchell, while hosting his weekly political roundup for CBS affiliate News9, asked the two participants point blank if cameras should be in courtrooms. His question was prompted by a civil case playing out in Oklahoma County over how an insurance company is processing claims. 
Mitchell said the “public can’t see what’s happening” during court proceedings.
“These are important issues that are happening in courtrooms,” he said. “Is it time for us to join the 21st century and have cameras in the courtrooms, so we can see what’s going on?” 
The Democratic panelist, a lawmaker-turned-lobbyist, was disappointingly wishy-washy in his answer, but Sen. Paul Rosino, R-Oklahoma City, was blunt. It is absolutely time for cameras to be allowed in courtrooms to help with transparency, he said.
“We talk about transparency all the time,” he said. “The people of Oklahoma are educated. They understand what’s happening. They want to see it in real time.”
Oklahomans deserve to see court proceedings play out, and courts should not be immune from the same scrutiny that other public entities face.
Most law enforcement officers wear body cameras that allow the public to view the actions of the people they’re interacting with and their decisions. Oklahoma lawmakers also now stream all hearings and proceedings.
Courts should face a similar high bar of scrutiny because they’re also making decisions that change lives.
Unlike fictional television courtroom dramas that feature bombshells and loud arguments, civil and criminal courtroom proceedings in Oklahoma are often sedate and incremental. During civil and criminal cases that don’t require juries, oftentimes attorneys gather around a judge’s bench to argue in low-tones the merits of their cases.
It’s hard for spectators to hear. I know because as the plaintiff in an open records case against a state agency, I found myself sitting in the front row of a courtroom last month, struggling at times to hear the arguments for and against the release of the severance agreement we were fighting for. It’s so hard to hear that sometimes you’ll see older journalists sitting in the jury box next to the judge.
Before I moved to Oklahoma, I worked in Utah, whose judicial system has long had strong public transparency protections.
Like other states, it has a pool system in place for photography and recording. In journalism lingo, it means all media outlets are required to share broadcast feeds or still images of the proceedings.
Ahead of hearings, there’s a clear process in place for news outlets to apply for permission to shoot still photography or video of a proceeding. 
The judge selects an applicant and fills out a form indicating what can and cannot be pictured. Usually the defendant, judge, prosecutor and defense attorneys are fair game. The victims, witnesses and juries are generally off limits, except in very limited circumstances. 
A media liaison employed by the court system acts as the go-between and operates a private social media channel to communicate to media outlets which hearings will be covered and who will be the pool photographer. The judge determines where photographers should set up.
Anyone not selected can still attend, they just can’t record or photograph.
The process works seamlessly. The vast majority of cases receive no media coverage, but when someone needs access, it’s easily available.
That’s why you might have seen pictures of Tyler Robinson, who is accused of assassinating conservative activist Charlie Kirk, in court or seen clips of Robinson’s pretrial hearings on the news.
Utah is not the only state that has a formal process to help ensure public access. Many others do, too. Florida, for instance, allows cameras unless a judge finds a reason to bar them. The state also operates a channel to broadcast and stream newsworthy proceedings.
It’s puzzling why Oklahoma’s judicial leaders have not implemented a similar process. 
It’s past time that they do something because Oklahomans are noticing in an era of social media and instant access that our judicial system operates differently than others. And I would say in an inferior way.
If our judicial leaders can’t figure out a solution on their own, it will only be a matter of time before our lawmakers do it for them.

name: WyoFile
title: Locals concerned as Trump admin fast-tracks public process for Wyoming rare earth mine
description:
The 30-day deadline to submit comments on an open-pit mine in the Black Hills National Forest is Friday. Developers received millions in federal and state subsidies.
The post Locals concerned as Trump admin fast-tracks public process for Wyoming rare earth mine appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The U.S. Forest Service in July began a 30-day public comment period on its plan to review a rare-earth element mining project in northeast Wyoming — the only opportunity for the public to weigh in on the federal process that is being fast-tracked by the Trump administration.
Colorado-based Rare Earth Resources plans to construct an open-pit mine at Bull Hill in the Black Hills National Forest 12 miles northwest of Sundance and about 22 miles from Devils Tower. Raw materials from the mine will be trucked to its “demonstration” processing plant near Upton.
People with concerns about the mine’s implications for health, wildlife, exemptions to the Black Hills Forest management plan, air and water quality have until Friday to submit comments. 
Thirty days is precious little time to absorb a complex mining proposal and environmental review documents, Sundance resident Justin Johnson told WyoFile. He’s lived in the area for more than a decade, and the project’s fast-track nature came as a surprise.
“It was kind of hush-hush, in my opinion, as far as not much word about it around Sundance,” Johnson said. “All of a sudden, in July when it came to our attention, it’s like, ‘Holy cow. We got little time before the federal deadline to get our comments and concerns to the Forest Service.'”
Crook County Commissioner John Davis acknowledged that locals are caught off guard with the expedited process. 
This image shows contact between an iron-rich pod (left) and quartz monzonite dike (right), formations that could host rare earth elements, along Wildcat Road on the Union Pass. (Wyoming State Geological Survey)
“We’re in favor of the project, and we hope it goes forward,” Davis told WyoFile. “We’ve got a lot of questions and a few concerns ourselves that we’re hoping get squared away, too.”
The commission is hosting a special meeting at 4 p.m. at the courthouse in Sundance to pose questions to staff from the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality and the Wyoming State Geological Survey.
Rare Element Resources’ Bear Lodge Rare Earth Project is among more than 50 projects in queue for fast-track federal permitting under FAST-41 coverage — one tool the Trump administration is using to address what it describes as a national security priority to increase domestic production and curb U.S. reliance on China for rare-earth elements, or “critical minerals.” The metals are increasingly in demand as building blocks for everything from magnets to batteries in devices like cell phones and MRI machines. They’re also frequently used in military equipment such as radars and jet engines.
Last year, President Donald Trump issued the Immediate Measures to Increase American Mineral Production executive order while invoking the Defense Production Act to fast-track permitting and help finance mining and processing efforts.
Rare Element Resources touts “one of the highest-grade deposits for the critical magnet [rare earth elements] neodymium and praseodymium, as well as samarium and terbium,” according to the company’s website. “These elements are expected to see the largest demand growth and price support over the next 10 years due to their importance in permanent magnets used in defense systems, transportation, advanced energy and other high-tech applications.”
“You would think there’d be a lot more time for the actual owners of public land — the citizens of the U.S. — to have a response to what’s going on.”Justin Johnson, Sundance resident
Regardless of the demand for rare-earth elements, there’s no excuse to rush a mining project that involves public natural resources, said Rachael Hamby, policy director for the Colorado-based conservation and advocacy organization Center for Western Priorities. Especially for hard-rock mining in a national forest.
“They [federal officials] know that their actions on national public lands, and related to our natural resources, are deeply unpopular with the public,” Hamby told WyoFile. “That’s why we see them trying anything they can to avoid and minimize taking public comment, because they know it’s not going to go their way.” 
The company, meanwhile, says there will be additional opportunities for public participation — via other federal and state entities — later in the process.
Bear Lodge project
Rare Element Resources is headquartered in Firestone, Colo. General Atomics, a U.S. defense contractor, is a majority shareholder in the company, and its affiliates play a key role in the refining technologies that will be used to process critical minerals from the Bear Lodge mine.
The company has invested about $180 million in the project, it says, and could spend up to $250 million. The mine would support a combined 110 permanent jobs and contribute more than $75 million in state taxes over its 17-year operational life, it says. 

This map depicts the location of the Bear Lodge Rare Earth Project in Crook County. (U.S. Forest Service)

The jobs and economic benefits of the processing plant in nearby Upton are less clear. However, Rare Element Resources received a $4.4 million Energy Matching Funds grant from the Wyoming Energy Authority in 2022 and $24.2 million in federal funding — both to support the processing facility in Upton. The plant is essentially built, but the company and its affiliates are still working out kinks to conduct full operational testing. 
Rare Element Resources submitted its draft Bull Hill mine operations plan to federal officials in July as part of the federal permitting review. One of the key questions before the Forest Service is whether to “authorize deviation from existing visual standards and guidelines in the Black Hills Forest Plan,” according to the agency’s “notice of intent” published in the Federal Register.
In addition to the open-pit, the company proposes to build access roads, a power line and support infrastructure — some of which would be located on adjacent private land.
As with any proposed mining activity, locals have voiced concerns and posed questions about potential impacts to water and air quality, as well as what some feel is a rushed federal permitting process. The Bull Hill area is also a popular place for locals to hike before and after work, Johnson said.
“Where this mine is, the drainage basically goes through Cook Lake before it heads out of there,” Johnson said. “It’s at the headwaters of a lot of creeks that leave the Bear Lodge [area] and head somewhere.” 
Fast-tracked
The FAST-41, or Fixing America’s Surface Transportation Act, was established under the Obama administration in 2015. Originally intended to increase transparency and expedite permitting for transportation infrastructure projects among multiple federal agencies, the program was expanded under the Biden and Trump administrations. President Trump, in his second term, has directed federal agencies to use the program to expedite mining projects, including for rare-earth minerals.
Though the Forest Service will conduct an “environmental impact statement” review, it “will not publish a draft environmental impact statement or conduct an objections process,” according to the agency’s notice in the Federal Register. That’s a major departure from public engagement typically required under the National Environmental Policy Act.
“As originally intended, the FAST-41 program is supposed to be about transparency in permitting,” Hamby said. “What I think we have seen a little bit more of is the Trump administration trying to treat it as a fast-track [tool], and that is certainly how the general public perceives it, and they don’t like that.
“People don’t like when things are rushed through,” Hamby added, “when they don’t feel heard or listened to, and they don’t have an opportunity to weigh in.”
Johnson confirmed that assertion.
“You would think there’d be a lot more time for the actual owners of public land — the citizens of the U.S. — to have a response to what’s going on,” Johnson said.
Despite the short public comment period, local and state governments will have additional opportunities to weigh in on the federal permitting process, according to Rare Element Resources.
“State and local agencies (and other federal agencies) are all part of the NEPA process (as cooperators and participating agencies), and do have inputs to the process post Aug. 28, for sure, through the EIS progression,” Rare Element Resources Vice President and General Counsel Kelli Kast told WyoFile via email.
State agencies — primarily the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality — will also have a role in shaping the project’s regulatory parameters, she said. But, she added, the company “has not yet made applications for those permits and licenses, as we’re in the pre-application phase.”
Johnson said he and his neighbors are not against mining. “Mining for Wyoming is huge. I mean, a lot of towns in Crook County would not survive if the coal mines were not in operation.”
But, he said, hard-rock mining for rare-earth minerals in a national forest — that’s a new aspect that he and others have a lot of questions about, and they deserve to be more engaged in the process.
“We would actually like them to say, ‘Yeah, we would like to extend the period of review, so we make sure that everything’s looked at.”

text:
From left, Democrat Kaylee Peterson, independent Sarah Zabel, and incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher. (Photos courtesy of the candidates)Idaho Democrat and District 1 congressional candidate Kaylee Peterson announced Wednesday she has invited incumbent U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher and independent Sarah Zabel to a public debate in October. 
The debate is set for 6-8 p.m. Mountain Time on Oct. 17 with an option to attend in-person or virtually. Peterson’s campaign said in a press release that she is trying to work with all three campaigns to set a location. 
US District 1 candidates: Idahoans face high healthcare costs. Here’s how they want to fix it.

Constitution Party candidate in the race, Brendan Gomez, was not included in the press release about the debate; the Peterson campaign could not be reached for a comment as to whether he was invited. 
Peterson has run against Fulcher twice before in 2022 and 2024. She said in the press release he has declined her past invitations to debate. 
“Idahoans in this district haven’t had a real debate in years, so we built one ourselves,” Peterson said in the press release. “This (debate) series has always been about giving voters direct access to the people asking for their vote. Now that Sarah Zabel has entered the race, it’s only right she has a seat at the table too. My invitation to Congressman Fulcher stands, just as it has for four years. Idahoans deserve to hear from all of us, together, in the same room.”
Fulcher could not be reached for comment. 
The press release said that if Fulcher is unable or declines to attend, “the campaign will proceed using his public testimony and record, and his cardboard cutout, so Idaho voters get the direct comparison they deserve regardless of whether he shows up.” 
Zabel told the Idaho Capital Sun that she plans to attend the debate. 
“I want the people of this district to hire me to do a job, and so of course I will make my case to them in every forum I can find,” Zabel said in an email. 
The three candidates and Gomez will appear on ballots for the Nov. 3 general election

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Healthcare costs, Medicaid cuts draw increased scrutiny from NC Democrats ahead of midterms
description: In the waning days of summer, Stacy Staggs should be thinking about how to celebrate the birthday of her twin girls, who turn 13 in September. Instead, the Charlotte mother is anxiously waiting for Congress to return from their August recess to address a growing healthcare crisis. Staggs’ daughters were born prematurely and spent months […]
text:
North Carolina families are increasingly worried about rising healthcare costs. A recent national poll by KFF finds healthcare costs continue to top the public’s list of affordability worries. (Photo: Getty Images)In the waning days of summer, Stacy Staggs should be thinking about how to celebrate the birthday of her twin girls, who turn 13 in September. Instead, the Charlotte mother is anxiously waiting for Congress to return from their August recess to address a growing healthcare crisis.
Staggs’ daughters were born prematurely and spent months in the intensive care unit at the Levine Children’s Hospital.
Stacy Staggs becomes empotional as she thinks about what Medicaid cuts could mean for her daughter Emma. (Photo: Screengrab from Defend America Action press conference)
While Sara and Emma have complex medical needs, Emma’s condition and disabilities are so serious she qualifies for North Carolina‘s Medicaid CAP/C waiver. Staggs said Sara is able to be insured through coverage offered by her husband’s employer.
“Medicaid affects every single facet of Emma’s life. It is her ability to stay in the home she grew up with, with the family who loves her, in her school and community and in her bed with her toys that she likes to play with,” Staggs told reporters Friday during a press call hosted by Defend America Action, a political advocacy organization.
Staggs is worried cuts to Medicaid could also affect their ability to provide nourishment for Emma, who is fed by a gastrostomy tube.
“The formula that she’s able to take is medical, it is prescription, it is wildly expensive and it’s covered by Medicaid,” Staggs said. The loss of that one service would likely mean surrendering her daughter.
Sen. Jay Chaudhuri, D-Wake, is also anxious about what the coming months will mean for families like the Staggs. He represents a county with the second largest Medicaid enrollment in the state.
“We have watched that math break down for families across North Carolina, not in the abstract but in real time,” said Chaudhuri. “Nearly 165,000 North Carolinians have lost their Affordable Care Act coverage after premiums spiked by more than 150% a year, and 100,000 plus North Carolinians have lost Medicaid as part of the roughly $1 trillion in Republican cuts to the program.”
Sen. Jay Chaudhuri, D-Wake (File photo)
Chaudhuri said when the state finally expanded Medicaid in 2023, it provided a lifeline to hundreds of thousands of North Carolinians. But now under new federal changes, some immigrants granted humanitarian protections will no longer be eligible for Medicaid starting Oct. 1, 2026. Someone admitted to the U.S. as a refugee or granted asylum will lose their ability to receive Medicaid coverage. A veteran or active-duty service member who is not a citizen also stands to lose Medicaid coverage this fall.
Starting Jan. 1, 2027, Medicaid applicants will see new work requirements and the need to recertify for their coverage every six months.
Chaudhuri believes state officials may not have seen the worst of it yet.
“More than 225,000 more North Carolinians are projected to lose coverage, not because they stop qualifying, not because their lives are changed, but because they’ve gotten lost in the maze of new paperwork and red tape designed, it seems, to make people give up,” Chaudhuri said.
U.S. Rep. Deborah Ross, D-N.C., has spent the August recess listening to constituents about their struggles to afford healthcare. With looming cuts to Medicaid and rising healthcare premiums, she worries that more families will face medical debt.
“Medical debt is the largest debt that people have in this country. It knows no political party, and it knows no geographic limitation,” Ross said.
Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, North Carolina is expected to lose nearly $50 billion over the next 10 years, according to analysis by the NC Department of Health and Human Services.
Even as inflation eases slightly, North Carolina families still feel squeezed from all sides

“And what the $50 billion in cuts is going to do is it’s going to mean fewer hospital beds, longer drives for emergency care, and fewer jobs in communities that can’t afford to lose them,” Chaudhuri said.
It’s the impact of those projected cuts that prompted U.S. Sen. Thom Tillis, R-North Carolina, to break from his party and vote against the legislation last year.
“We can and must do better than this,” Tillis said in a June 2025 statement.
With 71 days until the November midterm elections, it’s unlikely the U.S. Senate or the House will find common ground to address the Medicaid cuts or the affordability crisis.
A recent national poll by KFF finds healthcare costs continue to top the public’s list of affordability worries. An April KFF Health Tracking Poll found nearly 9 in 10 voters say the issue will influence their decision to vote in this year’s midterm elections.
Staggs said for the first time ever, her family’s healthcare premiums are higher than their mortgage. And for families like hers that rely on North Carolina’s Medicaid CAP/C waiver, there is a very real worry about what will happen if a claim for coverage is denied because of shifting eligibility requirements.
“It’s just a bunch of paperwork and it’s meant for people to fall out of the process,” said Staggs. “That sucks because that’s not what it’s supposed to do. It’s not the spirit of the program. It’s not the spirit of America.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: How Tennessee would replace Marsha Blackburn in the U.S. Senate if she becomes governor
description: U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn plans to choose her replacement for the U.S. Senate if she’s elected governor in November.  Blackburn made this announcement to the Nashville Banner ahead of her primary victory in August.   But it has also raised state and federal constitutional questions because, by law, Tennessee’s governor makes the appointment and no public of[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett, Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs and former Core Civic CEO Damon Hininger are thought to be leading candidates to replace U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn in the Senate if she wins Tennessee's gubernatorial race in November. (Burchett and Jacobs photos by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout; Hininger photo from the office of Gov. Bill Lee) U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn plans to choose her replacement for the U.S. Senate if she’s elected governor in November. 
Blackburn made this announcement to the Nashville Banner ahead of her primary victory in August.  
But it has also raised state and federal constitutional questions because, by law, Tennessee’s governor makes the appointment and no public official has held both a U.S. Senate seat and gubernatorial office at the same time. 
Blackburn’s ability to legally choose her replacement may come down to the timing of her U.S. Senate resignation and swearing into office. Tennessee’s next governor will be inaugurated on Jan. 17, 2027. If she steps down anytime before January 17, the appointment power would fall to Gov. Bill Lee. 
John Vile, a constitutional expert at Middle Tennessee State University, said the mechanics of how she would choose her replacement have no precedent. 
“It’s a fascinating question,” Vile said. 
Lee told reporters Wednesday he didn’t want to discuss Blackburn’s statement that she would choose her replacement, and not him.  
“We’ll take governors one at a time, and I don’t give advice to the next governor,” Lee said. 
Blackburn won the Republican primary for Tennessee governor in August, setting up a matchup with Memphis city councilwoman Jerri Green, the Democratic nominee, and several independent candidates. Blackburn is heavily favored to win the race, as a Republican has not lost a statewide office since 2006. 
The last time Tennessee replaced a U.S. Senator mid-term was in 1993, after Al Gore became Vice President. At the time, Gov. Ned McWherter chose Gore’s replacement, tapping advisor Harlan Matthews. Following state law, Matthews served until the next November election, which in his case was 1994. 
Another factor that could shape Blackburn’s decision is the U.S. Senate organizing that occurs the first week in January. If Blackburn waits to resign until mid-January, her appointment choice could cause problems for Tennessee’s next U.S. Senator in securing certain committee appointments. 
Jim Hall, an advisor to McWherter in the 1990s during the replacement process, said it was important for Gore to resign the seat before that process. 
“From a seniority point, everything in Washington, D.C. depends on it,” Hall said. 
Blackburn’s ability to choose her replacement has been a talking point since she announced her candidacy, serving as a potential reward to several of her major backers. 
Damon Hininger, the former CEO of private prison giant CoreCivic, has expressed interest in the appointment and created a political organization called Believe in Tennessee to showcase it. Hininger and his wife were among the largest donors to Blackburn and to political action committees supporting her. 
Other contenders are thought to be Knoxville U.S. Rep Tim Burchett and Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, who serves as Blackburn’s gubernatorial campaign treasurer, and Commissioner of Economic and Community Development Stuart McWhorter. 
Blackburn’s ability to appoint her replacement could also backfire, Vile said. 
“She’ll make one person happy, but might make 10 people angry,” Vile said. “Appointments don’t always work out as you would think.”
John Partipilo contributed to this report.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: After attacks, Alabama-founded LGBTQ+ history non-profit moves to North Carolina
description: Before June 2023, Invisible Histories flew under the radar in Alabama.  The non-profit organization, which archives and researches southern LGBTQ+ history, began collecting items in 2018, just two years after President Donald Trump was elected for his first term. “People seemed just kind of quasi-interested, and then 2016 happened,” said Maigen Sullivan, co-[...]
text:
Maigen Sullivan, co-founder of Invisible Histories, speaks at the Department of Archives and History on Thursday, June 15, 2023. In March 2026, the organization moved from Birmingham to Charlotte, North Carolina. (Jemma Stephenson/Alabama Reflector) 



  Key Points 


Invisible Histories is a non-profit organization that researches and archives LGBTQ+ history.
In June 2023, Maigen Sullivan, one of the co-founders of Invisible Histories, gave a talk at the Alabama Department of Archives and History about LGBTQ+ history in the state which sparked attacks against Sullivan and the department.
The organization was previously based in Birmingham but recently moved to Charlotte, North Carolina this year for reasons including funding, space, and the hostility within the state. 

 



Before June 2023, Invisible Histories flew under the radar in Alabama. 
The non-profit organization, which archives and researches southern LGBTQ+ history, began collecting items in 2018, just two years after President Donald Trump was elected for his first term.
“People seemed just kind of quasi-interested, and then 2016 happened,” said Maigen Sullivan, co-founder of the nonprofit, in a recent interview. “People were all of a sudden very interested in the urgent need to preserve at-risk history, and we see that was too much foreshadowing, I think.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
But now Invisible Histories is no longer in Alabama. In March, Sullivan and Joshua Burford, the other co-founder of the organization, decided to relocate from Birmingham to Charlotte, North Carolina. The new facility is set to open to the public in November. 
There were several reasons for the move, including funding and a need for space. 
“The biggest push was the humanities cuts (to) funding. Running an archive is not sexy and is incredibly expensive. The standards for keeping old things in a box are actually really high and very costly, and so we could not be in one of the poorest states.” Sullivan said.
But another reason for moving, Sullivan said, was a mounting political hostility to Alabama’s LGBTQ+ communities, which Sullivan experienced firsthand after delivering a talk about Alabama’s LGBTQ+ history at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in June 2023. 
“(Charlotte) is in a state that also has a lot of problems, but is not quite as actively hostile to LGBTQ things as Alabama particularly is,” she said.
 An Archives presentation 
Sullivan’s 2023 talk was a part of the department’s Food for Thought series, a year-long series of presentations with a different speaker each month. During the lecture, Sullivan discussed the history of LGBTQ+ people and organizations in Alabama. 
Figures mentioned during the speech include singer Gertrude “Ma” Rainey and actress Nell Carter, who would be considered bisexual by today’s standards, and the organization Lambda Inc., which Sullivan described as the state’s first LGBTQ+ resource center.
Following the presentation, Sullivan and Archives and History became the targets of conservative media in the state, which sparked attacks from Republicans in the Alabama Legislature. Legislators made several attempts to defund Archives and filed bills that would overhaul the department’s governing board.
“Intentionally erased:” Invisible Histories Project cofounder speaks on Alabama’s LGBTQ+ history

Sen. Chris Elliott, R-Josephine, who sponsored the defunding bill and several other bills looking to reappoint members of the department’s board, said in a recent interview that Sullivan’s talk made him realize the board was “self-perpetuating” and not being confirmed by the Senate.
“We really just need to update the board’s appointing process. And again, I think as this continues to go on, you have board members that for multiple years now, three plus years, have not been confirmed by the Alabama Senate, and yet they continue to serve,” Elliott said.
None of the bills Elliott have proposed have gone into effect. He said during the interview he will bring another piece of legislation related to the Archives board during the next legislative session.
Sullivan’s speech was not the first time Sullivan or Burford had worked with the Department of Archives and History. Steve Murray, the executive director of the Alabama Department of Archives and History, said Burford in 2022 “gave a talk about (the) Invisible Histories Project and that organization and what they were doing to preserve historical materials related to LGBTQ topics.” 
Burford wrote in an email Thursday that he was surprised by the backlash.
“We give talks all the time, and we have never had a Senator ever give any feedback at all,” Burford said. “Some of it was scary, especially being doxxed by a ‘news’ organization but in a lot of ways it wasn’t really that shocking considering this elected official was trying to ride some wave or (anti-LGBTQ+) sentiment for his own reasons. Since the talk was about folks from Alabama who were part of the queer community, there was very little to react to, honestly.”
Murray said when Burford gave his speech in June 2022, there was no pushback from lawmakers on the topic of LGBTQ+ history preservation, nor was there any pushback in the months leading up to Sullivan’s speech.
“Usually, like right after Christmas, we’re sending out the (Food for Thought speaker) list for the next year, and so that’s how that happens every year, and including those two years,” Murray said. “Those were schedules that had been set for about nine months, before the program happened, and we had been promoting it since January, but we didn’t hear any criticisms or questions about any of that until literally the day before the program was supposed to take place.”
One main question Murray said he got from lawmakers was regarding the audience the program was created for. He said when lawmakers called him, he assured them that Sullivan’s lecture wasn’t aimed at children. But because of the backlash, the department has not had a public program centered on LGBTQ+ topics since 2023.
Patricia Todd, a former state representative who chairs Alabama Equality, an organization that advocates for LGBTQ+ rights, called the attacks “disrespectful” and said Republican lawmakers should focus on other issues in an interview Friday.
“It’s ridiculous. I mean, we are not the problem, okay? But they need to pay attention to issues that affect average (people) the price of gas, groceries, lack of healthcare, access to healthcare. That’s what they need to be focusing on,” she said.
 Prior work 
Murray said Invisible Histories began working with the department years before either co-founder participated in the Food for Thought programs. 
“So they had approached us years earlier about what they were trying to do in building those connections, and so we welcomed that as an opportunity to meet potential prospective donors, and so over those several years, they helped us. They introduced people to us as an institution, and facilitated some conversations about is your repository an appropriate place for this person’s collections,” he said.
LGBTQ history program part of recommitment effort, says Archives and History

Some of the items collected by the non-profit had ties to Mardi Gras, the AIDS crisis and marriage equality.
“What started out as the Montgomery AIDS outreach back in the 80s in response to the AIDS crisis, it changed names over time, but still exists and and and serves a broader community today” Murray said. “But so there’s Mardi Gras, marriage equality, and various organizations that were kind of advocating for LGBTQ rights in Alabama, so all of those kind of fit within our larger umbrella of collecting emphases on things that affect public policy or documenting change in Alabama.”
Burford said the decision to not platform LGBTQ+ history is because “institutions will always look out for the interest of their own organizations” and are “risk averse and often back away for fear of reprisal.”
Sullivan said she saw the backlash to her lecture coming.
“I think that people are so afraid of history,” she said. “I mean, the literacy crisis that we’re in did not just happen, right? It is not just about tech. It is about an attack on knowledge and intellect and expertise. There are concentrated efforts to make us the way that we are right now, and I think one of the reasons why history is such a threat to this very alt-right conservative movement that we’re having right now is because it happened, and it is a weapon to show people how you can fight back.”
Sullivan also believes the emphasis being put on science, technology, engineering and math (STEM) careers has taken away from the humanities.
“Now we’re seeing not just the defunding of humanities, but also diversity, LGBTQ work, generally speaking, with some places having prohibitions on funding that,” she said. “Now what we’re starting to see, and again, this has been kind of subtly happening, is a direct erasure. We’re seeing websites being pulled down. We’re seeing things being censored.”
Sullivan mentioned a July hearing from the Subcommittee on Delivering on Government Efficiency involving the committee sharply attacking the Smithsonian Institute for promoting “divisive, inappropriate, and factually inaccurate programming on U.S. history” as an instance of censorship happening in America.
 A new start in Charlotte 
Prior to the move, Invisible Histories was being lent space from AIDS Alabama, an organization that provides services to those affected by HIV, and were cycling donations they received to universities and libraries.
Todd said Invisible Histories relocating was sad, but due to the lack of public access, she wasn’t sure if it’d make a difference in Alabama.
“I’m sad to see them go, but you know you don’t have access to the archives they have, so it doesn’t matter where they are,” Todd said. “When I gave them the material, the boxes of information, I thought they were going to be for public view, and so they really need to think about that, or people won’t give.”
At the non-profit’s new location in Charlotte, Sullivan said there is far more space for them to maintain their donations and will also be more accessible to the public.
“It (the old space) was down a flight of stairs. It was harder for people with mobility issues or older folks to get up and down (and) the way we were operating then it made it a little bit harder for us to show things,” Sullivan said. “So it was more about preservation. The new space is prioritizing accessibility, getting people in the door, come on in, sit down, feel comfortable. So it is more accessible, more inviting.”
Despite Invisible Histories moving to Charlotte, the organization could still face attacks. Sullivan said she’s not fearful of any potential backlash.
“I do think it will happen. I’m definitely not fearful. I’m a very froggy person, and you will pull this history out of my cold, dead hands,” Sullivan said. “I don’t think this is the time to be afraid. I feel very resilient.” 
She said looking at LGBTQ+ activists of the past makes her want to fight to maintain the history more.
“What would it be for me to shrink into the shadows now, when socio-politically it is incredibly terrifying, purely for trans people. But culturally, things have shifted. Culturally, things have changed,” Sullivan said. “And while there is some backsliding, it just feels like if I’m going to be a bearer of this history, then I have to live in the shadow of those people, and I owe it to them to fight back.”
The Key Points box was written by Reporter Andrea Tinker.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: As temperatures get hotter, pesticides are more dangerous to farmworkers
description: This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here. For the nation’s 2.4 million farmworkers, climate change is poised to exacerbate the harms of pesticides, a growing body of research shows. Heat stresses the body, making it m[...]
text:
A farmer on a tractor sprays soybean crops. (Photo by Westend61/Getty Images)This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.
For the nation’s 2.4 million farmworkers, climate change is poised to exacerbate the harms of pesticides, a growing body of research shows.
Heat stresses the body, making it more vulnerable to pesticides and other toxicants, and protective clothing worn in the heat only adds to this stress. Hotter temperatures can also lead to higher evaporation rates, increasing farmworkers’ exposure as more pesticides are applied to crops. And heat can boost rates of chemical transformation of pesticides into more toxic compounds.
“When it’s in the air, you are inhaling it through your nose. You are exposed to it through your other organs like skin. Your skin can absorb some of the pesticides [that are] in the air, and also when you’re sweating as part of doing your work you are increasing the pore size of your skin,” said Omanjana Goswami, a scientist in the food and environmental program at the Union for Concerned Scientists, an advocacy group. “It is awful. There is no other word for it.”
In addition to threatening workers, rising temperatures likely will expand pesticide use, as pests and pathogens enlarge their ranges and more weeds spring up in crops, according to a report by the Union for Concerned Scientists.
Thousands of U.S. farmworkers suffer annually from acute pesticide poisoning, although data is limited, according to the Union for Concerned Scientists report, citing the Environmental Protection Agency. Many cases go unreported, and states also have different reporting practices.
The problem affects a population that is particularly vulnerable. A majority of U.S. farmworkers were born in other nations and are people of color. Jeannie Economos, pesticide safety and environmental health project coordinator at the Farmworker Association of Florida, characterized farmworkers as “landless farmers.”
“This is definitely a case of environmental injustice,” she said. “If they had access to capital, to land, to nondiscriminatory regulations and practices, to financial assistance, they might be able to be farmers themselves. But they’re not.
“And if they had legal status and they weren’t being demeaned because of their immigration status, if they weren’t experiencing horrible conditions in their home countries, they might be farmers themselves. But they are relegated to being farmworkers because they are at the behest of government and the system.”
Farmworkers are at risk whether or not they work directly with pesticides, and field workers who do not directly handle the chemicals account for the majority of reported poisonings, the Union for Concerned Scientists said in its report. Many employers do not post adequate warnings about fields that recently were sprayed and fail to provide protective gear or trainings on how to use it, the report said. Other research shows that protective PVC gloves actually can break down as temperatures increase and become less impervious to the chemicals. Family members or other close contacts can be exposed when they encounter residue on farmworkers’ skin and clothing.
Chronic pesticide exposure is associated with cancer, depression, diabetes, neurodegenerative diseases and reproductive issues, according to the Union for Concerned Scientists report.
“We tell people, don’t pick up your children when you get home until you take your clothes off and take a shower, because you’re going to contaminate your kids,” Economos said.
Heat is the leading weather-related killer in the United States. Every year, thousands of U.S. workers suffer heat-related illnesses and injuries. A total of 1,042 worker deaths related to heat were documented between 1992 and 2022, an average of 34 annually, according to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), citing the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Excess heat affects the body’s ability to regulate its internal temperature, which can lead to heat cramps, heat exhaustion and heatstroke. Hotter temperatures can also exacerbate nervous system, respiratory, cardiovascular and diabetes-related conditions and even affect children’s ability to learn. For outdoor laborers, symptoms such as fatigue and dizziness especially can be hazardous when the work involves dangerous conditions or equipment.
There are few federal or state regulatory protections for farmworkers from heat. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration in 2024 proposed a new standard that would more clearly define employer obligations and require employers to evaluate and control heat hazards in their workplaces. Two years later, the proposal is moving forward, but slowly.
In the absence of a specific federal regulation, OSHA has relied on the general duty clause of the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970. The clause requires employers to provide a workplace free of “recognized hazards” that can cause “death or serious physical harm.”
California, Colorado, Maryland, Minnesota, Nevada, Oregon and Washington have implemented state-level heat protections. But some states, including Florida and Texas, have prohibited the protections at the local level. In 2024, Florida lawmakers banned local governments from establishing any such protections for outdoor workers. The legislation came after commissioners in Miami-Dade County considered a proposal that would have required construction and agricultural companies to provide water and rest breaks when the heat index hit at least 95 degrees. The proposal also would have required training in heat illness and first aid.
“Farmwork is dignified, important work,” Economos said. “I’m not trying to get people out of farmwork. We’re trying to elevate farmwork because it is a skilled profession. Unlike what (people say), that it is unskilled work—try it.”

text:
States Newsroom graphic illustration New Developments
Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers on Thursday said he now backed a statewide moratorium on new data centers. While Rogers said the pause would allow the state to develop a comprehensive strategy before approving additional projects, his altered stance followed disclosures by The Lever that he holds millions of dollars in AI-related investments. Rogers had previously supported policies to speed data center development.
The American Prospect reported that U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) was positioning himself as an opponent of data centers despite voting for 2025’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which provided tax incentives benefiting companies building data centers. In a campaign ad, Barrett is now emphasizing local control, while Democratic challenger Will Lawrence has made opposition to data centers a central issue in the 7th Congressional District race.
WXYZ Channel 7 reports that Ypsilanti Township has approved a six-month moratorium on large electric utility structures as officials assess the potential impact of the University of Michigan’s planned supercomputing facility. Although U-M has described the facility as a research computing center rather than a traditional data center, the moratorium addresses the substantial electrical infrastructure needed to support a project of its size. Township leaders say the pause will give them time to review regulations and prepare for the potential power needs of the facility.
 
Updates
Mason City Council unanimously approved a new communications plan aimed at keeping residents informed about the potential development of data centers. WILX News 10 reports the “Mason Connect” initiative will include a Sept. 14 town hall and neighborhood meetings where residents can receive updates and raise questions or concerns. City officials said the effort is intended to provide greater transparency and improve communication with the community.
Genoa Township has extended its moratorium on new data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities for another six months as officials work to finalize zoning regulations. WHMI’s Jessica Mathews reports that the extension will give the township time to complete a noise study and determine how proposed restrictions can be enforced. Township officials said the pause is intended to ensure new regulations adequately protect residents before additional projects move forward.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Federal childcare subsidy for working North Dakota families to expire in September
description: A pilot program designed to attract and retain workers in North Dakota by assisting with childcare costs will stop in September, ending financial support for hundreds of families. The ND Working Parents Child Care Relief Program began in 2023 using federal COVID-19 relief funds. The goal of the program, which is administered by the state […]
text:
Jennifer and Travis Klath, pictured Aug. 16, 2026, in Moorhead, Minnesota, benefit from the ND Working Parents Child Care Relief Program. The program, which uses matching dollars from participating employers and the federal government to subsidize childcare, ends in September. (Photo by Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)A pilot program designed to attract and retain workers in North Dakota by assisting with childcare costs will stop in September, ending financial support for hundreds of families.
The ND Working Parents Child Care Relief Program began in 2023 using federal COVID-19 relief funds. The goal of the program, which is administered by the state Department of Health and Human Services, was to make it easier for parents to join or rejoin the workforce after the pandemic.
“We knew that quality, affordable childcare was a key infrastructure needed for parents to return to work after COVID,” said Jennifer Prince, early childcare workforce administrator at North Dakota’s HHS. “This was one way we could meet that need.”
The program requires participating employers to contribute up to $300 a month per child for eligible families. Then the childcare relief program matches those employer contributions.
Those subsidies have made a difference for some families. 
North Dakota families, childcare providers frustrated by growing waitlist for assistance

Jennifer Klath started looking for a new job when her oldest turned 3 but hesitated because her family received discounted childcare through her former employer.
In 2024, she accepted a position with Tellwell, a creative agency in Fargo. She accepted the position largely because of the benefits the company offered, including participation in the Working Parents Child Care Relief Program. 
Since then, Klath’s husband has accepted a different job. The family also switched daycares and added a second child. All of these adjustments were easier because of childcare assistance, Klath said.
“It helped us stay afloat through all of the changes we’ve had to and wanted to make in the past few years,” she said.
Overall, there are 524 working parents representing 61 employers enrolled in the program, according to HHS. Seventy-two of those parents work in the private sector. The others work for the state of North Dakota or the state university system, which were granted matching funds by the Legislature.
Bismarck State College is one of the public colleges that participates in the program. The college has six parents who receive assistance, according to a written statement from Juanita Lee, the college’s spokeswoman.
Matching funds have been available to working parents with qualifying household incomes less than 150% of the state median and whose children are younger than 5 years old. Those children must attend licensed childcare in North Dakota. 
Health and Human Services allocated $5 million to the program for the 2023-25 biennium, according to data from Donna Aukland, chief financial officer for HHS. Unused funds were carried over to cover costs for 2026. All funding will be used by September. 
Prince said parents have told the department the benefit has made a difference in their ability to succeed at work. She has also heard from businesses that successfully recruited workers because of the benefit. Over the program’s three years, the number of private employers has increased slightly by about 1.5%, she said.  
State lawmakers of both parties say it’s time to rethink America’s fragile childcare system

Still, HHS doesn’t have funding to extend the program beyond its deadline, said Tim Eissinger, executive director of HHS.
He said the department recognizes the impact of reducing or ending assistance on families but must prioritize new budget realities. 
“If we had the ability to continue programs like this, we would,” he said.
In April, Gov. Kelly Armstrong shared guidelines that included a 10% budget cut for the state’s largest agencies, which includes HHS. That means the agency needs to evaluate programming, Eissinger said. 
“We’re committed to honoring his guidelines to make sure we don’t have governmental creep,” he said. “We need to look at creative ways to realign programs.”
That said, the pilot program served a valuable purpose, he said, and suggested the department can be a resource for businesses that want to start their own childcare assistance programs.
“We’d like to see this balance out, so it’s as much a private initiative as a public initiative,” he said.
For some businesses, however, the program not only relieved financial stress among employees, but also provided a benefit that might otherwise be difficult to afford.
Max Kringen, founder of Tellwell, said the program allowed his company to better compete with larger companies that offer higher wages and extensive benefits.
It also gave employees opportunities to be more selective about childcare rather than simply choosing the least expensive care option, he said.
“We would love the state to continue something along these lines,” Kringen said.
Prince said HHS has been transparent about the deadline for the pilot program and has directed families toward other state-supported childcare assistance programs.
One of these is the Child Care Assistance Program, which faced an unexpected $35.5 million funding deficit in December 2025 because of increased enrollments. Nearly 1,900 families were on a waitlist for the program as of Aug. 9.
Klath said her family hopes to see a natural easing of childcare costs since her oldest will begin school this year and doesn’t expect her family will qualify for other programs. She will continue to work and remains grateful for the months they did receive help.
“My employer has been adamant about providing real life benefits, and the WPCCR one is one among many that allow my family to live with a little less stress,” Klath said. “I wish more employers adopted that mindset.”
