title: Chesapeake Regional may avoid criminal trial, but former OB-GYN Perwaiz’s patients are still suing
description: By Yiqing Wang/WHRO Federal prosecutors said this week they have reached a tentative deferred prosecution agreement with Chesapeake Regional Medical Center for charges related to disgraced former OB-GYN Javaid Perwaiz. The deal would require the hospital to admit certain facts, accept an independent monitor, repay health care programs and create a $12.8 mill[...]
text:
Chesapeake Regional Medical Center on Battlefield Boulevard. The hospital is facing ongoing civil claims from former patients of Javaid Perwaiz, while a tentative federal agreement could resolve its criminal case without trial. (Photo by Katherine Hafner/WHRO)By Yiqing Wang/WHRO
Federal prosecutors said this week they have reached a tentative deferred prosecution agreement with Chesapeake Regional Medical Center for charges related to disgraced former OB-GYN Javaid Perwaiz.
The deal would require the hospital to admit certain facts, accept an independent monitor, repay health care programs and create a $12.8 million fund for Perwaiz’s former patients. If finalized, the deal would let the hospital avoid a criminal trial.
Legal experts previously told WHRO a federal conviction could cut Chesapeake Regional off from Medicare, Medicaid and other federal health care payments — a punishment that they said could put a hospital out of business.
Perwaiz was convicted in 2020 of health care fraud and false statements after prosecutors said he performed unnecessary surgeries and sterilizations.
Between 2010 and 2019, the hospital received $18.5 million from public and private benefit providers for procedures Perwaiz performed, including some prosecutors allege he misclassified.
Federal prosecutors have then charged Chesapeake Regional with conspiracy to defraud the United States and health care fraud, alleging officials at the hospital were aware of Perwaiz’s conduct and did nothing to stop him.
Court filings describe the civil litigation as involving more than 1,040 plaintiffs and care Perwaiz provided between 1984 and 2019, and the former patients allege Chesapeake Regional was negligent in hiring, retaining and granting privileges to Perwaiz.
The hospital pleaded not guilty to the charges in January 2025. This week, Chesapeake Regional confirmed to WHRO that a deal has been reached, but said it cannot comment further because the agreement is not finalized.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office said the proposed $12.8 million patient fund would be available to people whose medical records show they had procedures performed by Perwaiz at Chesapeake Regional.
But the fund would only cover losses allowed under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act, such as the cost of medical procedures or therapy. It would not cover emotional distress or similar damages.
A class-action lawsuit against the hospital including more than 1,000 former patients is still ongoing.
A court order entered this week has shown multiple civil cases have been consolidated into one and several plaintiffs have dropped claims against the hospital and three former executives: James Reese Jackson, Peter Francis Bastone and Wynn Lawton Dixon Jr.
Claims remain pending against two former Chesapeake Regional CEOs: Donald S. Buckley, who quietly left the post in May, and Christopher Mosley, who the Virginian-Pilot reported in 2010 “resigned abruptly” after 5 years leading the hospital.
Chesapeake Regional has argued that the civil claims are barred by Virginia’s statute of limitations because the procedures happened years ago.
Plaintiffs said the legal deadline should not block their claims because of the hospital’s alleged conduct and the related criminal case.
A spokesperson for Victoria Wickman, who is representing the plaintiffs, told WHRO the former patients will next seek evidence from the defendants and ask the court for permission to update their complaint.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Legislators didn’t allow local bans of gas-powered leaf blowers. Va. localities are doing it anyway.
description: Three years in a row of losing in the legislature might persuade some people to give up trying to get what they want. For members of the group Quiet Clean Virginia, their losing record simply challenged them to seek another path to victory.  Quiet Clean Virginia and its affiliate groups in Northern Virginia advocate for […]
text:
A landscaper blows leaves off a lawn in preparation for annual “leaf pickups” by Fairfax County public services, October 31, 2023. (Photo by Getty Images)Three years in a row of losing in the legislature might persuade some people to give up trying to get what they want. For members of the group Quiet Clean Virginia, their losing record simply challenged them to seek another path to victory. 
Quiet Clean Virginia and its affiliate groups in Northern Virginia advocate for local bans on gas-powered leaf blowers, machines that are either essential to modern suburban living or the scourge of it, depending on your point of view. 
Their pollution-spewing, two-stroke engines are linked to asthma, heart attacks and even global warming, and their headache-inducing roar is the bane of the work-from-home set, parents of napping children and night-shift workers who must sleep during the day. 
But on the plus side, they are really good at blowing detritus off people’s lawns. 
These days electric leaf blowers can also move leaves around, with no pollution and less noise. So advocates believe the gas version should no longer have a place in dense, urban environments where clean air and tranquility are already scarce. 
Prohibitions have been in place elsewhere in the country for years, including in the District of Columbia since 2022, and in Maryland jurisdictions including Montgomery County since 2025. 
Many residents of Northern Virginia would like their region to be next. A survey conducted by Arlington County showed almost three-quarters of residents support a total ban.
The problem is that even Democrats in the General Assembly have balked at giving local jurisdictions the express authority to regulate or ban gas-powered leaf blowers.   
In a Dillon-Rule state like Virginia, localities have only the powers expressly delegated to them by the state. And the General Assembly has never said anything about what local governments can do about lawn care equipment. 
Bills to grant localities this power have failed repeatedly in the House and Senate, and the votes weren’t even close. According to Quiet Clean board member Margaret McKelvey, lawn-care companies and leaf blower manufacturers lobbied hard against the measure, asserting it would cause economic ruin. 
Still, the failure of the initiative wasn’t the end of the story. 
Legislation would have been nice, but was it actually necessary? The Virginia Code gives localities the power to adopt “such measures as it deems expedient” to secure the “health, safety and general welfare” of their residents, including through enforcement of noise ordinances. That seems like enough authority.
Indeed, Alexandria attorney Jamie Conrad, a supporter of the legislation, told me in a phone call that several legislators he spoke with felt localities already have sufficient authority to enact a ban under the police powers delegated to them in the Virginia Code, and this was why they voted against the bill. 
Proceeding cautiously, the City of Alexandria asked their  then-local delegate (and former vice mayor), Elizabeth Bennett-Parker, to request an opinion on the topic from then-Attorney General Jason Miyares.  
On August 12, 2024, Miyares replied with a letter confirming the city’s authority to ban gas leaf blowers simply by amending its noise ordinance. 
Miyares, a Republican, acknowledged that the General Assembly had voted down legislation giving local governments express authority to regulate leaf blowers, but cited case law in rejecting any inference of legislative intent from those outcomes as speculative. Alexandria, he concluded, was clearly within its rights to ban the equipment.
Alexandria used that green light to amend its noise ordinance in May of 2025 and begin an 18-month phaseout of gas leaf blowers. A full prohibition is set to take effect on November 17, 2026.
Miyares’ opinion had leaned heavily on the authority in Alexandria’s city charter, though the power of counties to enforce noise ordinances under the Virginia Code is similar. Nonetheless, Arlington chose to move more slowly, holding extensive outreach sessions and soliciting feedback, including through a survey. 
The county collected more than 3,500 written comments, the great majority of which favored a ban. Reading through the comments linked from the survey, noise is clearly the driving factor behind support for the ban, with pollution and health impacts as secondary concerns. 
Most opponents cite the financial impact to homeowners and lawn care companies from having to buy new equipment. Complaints about government overreach make up a small (but often colorful!) part of the negative feedback.  
Not surprisingly, Arlington’s survey also showed most lawncare companies oppose a ban, saying it would impose an economic hardship. More surprisingly, though, nearly one-third of companies said they were “very comfortable” with a total ban, suggesting that the electrification of leaf blowers is already underway. 
With that support, last month the Arlington County board amended its noise ordinance to ban gas-powered leaf blowers effective January 1, 2029. The 30-month lag time is intended as a transition period giving owners of gas equipment time to change their equipment as it wears out, a frequent suggestion in the comments. The county transitioned all of its own landscaping equipment to electric in 2025.  
McKelvey says other jurisdictions have been watching, but so far none have followed Alexandria and Arlington.
The path to do so is straightforward; most localities already have noise ordinances, and many already apply time restrictions and decibel limits to the use of loud machines. Fairfax County, for example, already bans the use of all lawn equipment between 9 p.m. and 7 a.m. 
Lawn care isn’t alone; other loud activities also have time restrictions. Even dog parks have to close at night, and indeed the quiet hours for dogs are longer than those for lawn equipment. (Clearly, the dogs didn’t hire the right lobbyists.)
Still, localities will have no interest in banning gas leaf blowers as long as their residents don’t demand it. The idea likely won’t even be discussed in rural counties, unless as an occasion to ridicule Democrats. With technology on the side of batteries, the market will eliminate the two-stroke engine long before most governments do. 
That’s cold comfort to the exhausted parent whose colicky baby has just been jolted awake. When that happens, even an avowed libertarian may waver on the sanctity of lawn equipment choice. Politics crumble when the baby is screaming.  
As for whether Alexandria and Arlington have set off on a slippery slope to banning everything having to do with fossil fuels, McKelvey thinks not. For one thing, the price differential between gas-powered lawn mowers and electric is too great to make a similar restriction reasonable; for another, as I can attest, gas leaf blowers are just uniquely irritating. 
I asked Del. Rip Sullivan, D-Fairfax, the House patron of the leaf blower ban legislation, whether he would put the bill in again next year, now that the localities that wanted it had gone ahead with their bans. 
He told me he hadn’t decided, but added, “I’m glad to see Arlington taking this step, and I hope it sets an example for other localities that want it.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Who’s in the running for two open Rhode Island Superior Court seats
description: Rhode Island’s former U.S. attorney, along with a labor lawyer and policy adviser to the House of Representatives, are among a total of eight finalists under consideration by Gov. Dan McKee to fill two vacancies on the state’s Superior Court. The state’s Judicial Nominating Commission sent two lists of recommendations to McKee following the panel’s […]
text:
Former U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Cunha, left, shown grilling Rhode Island Department of Transportation Director Peter Alviti, right, seen from behind, during a November 2025 joint House and Senate oversight committee hearing on the Washington Bridge, made the shortlist of finalists for an open seat on the Superior Court. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Rhode Island’s former U.S. attorney, along with a labor lawyer and policy adviser to the House of Representatives, are among a total of eight finalists under consideration by Gov. Dan McKee to fill two vacancies on the state’s Superior Court.
The state’s Judicial Nominating Commission sent two lists of recommendations to McKee following the panel’s Aug. 12 interviews with applicants to fill the seats formerly held by judges Jeffrey Lanphear and Joseph A. Montalbano.
By law, the governor has 21 days to pick a nominee after the commission interviews and selects finalists to fill vacancies on the bench. Nominees for these lifetime appointments will require confirmation by the Rhode Island Senate. 
That gives McKee up until Sept. 2 to announce his two nominees, a week before the Sept. 9 primary.
“As we always have, we will take the time necessary to thoroughly vet candidates for these important positions,” Olivia DaRocha, a spokesperson for McKee’s office, said in an email to Rhode Island Current. “We are currently reviewing the candidate background information received from the JNC. As of Friday afternoon, McKee’s office had not yet started interviews.
The base salary for a Superior Court judge is $211,734.
The contenders for Montalbano’s old seat
Five finalists were selected to fill the vacancy created by Montalbano’s ascension to presiding justice of the state’s top trial court in April: Angelyne Cooper-Bailey, Family Court Magistrate Denise Cassisi Finkelman, labor attorney Carly Iafrate, Superior Court Magistrate Amanda Valentino, and Assistant Attorney General Ania Zielinski. 
Valentino was the only applicant to receive unanimous support from the nine-member panel. She was appointed magistrate in 2023 by then-Presiding Justice Alice B. Gibney where she oversees many of the Superior Court’s specialized programs and calendars, including those for drug treatment, diversion and early termination of probation, as well as cases involving sexually violent predators.
Valentino worked as an assistant public defender from 2012 through 2022 before a one-year stint as deputy chief of legal services for the state Department of Revenue, according to her resume.
Iafrate received support from eight members to fill Montalbano’s seat. She is a labor and employment lawyer who has operated a private practice since 2003, her resume notes. Iafrate helped negotiate the three-year contract the state reached with multiple public employee unions in 2024. That same year, she represented then-Senate Majority Whip Valarie Lawson before the Ethics Commission over whether her former career as a teacher and her position as president of a state teachers’ union prevented her from voting on pension-related legislation.
Iafrate was among the five finalists the commission recommended in February to fill the Superior Court seat now occupied by Maria Ferro Deaton. Iafrate received five votes to make the shortlist to fill Lanphear’s vacancy.
Zielinski was recommended by six members of the Judicial Nominating Commission. She is a longtime state prosecutor who has handled hundreds of criminal cases, including murder, child molestation, sexual assault, robbery and white-collar and financial crimes.
Between 2021 and December 2023, Zielinski served as deputy chief legal counsel for the Rhode Island Department of Business Regulations before she rejoined the office of attorney general where she now works as senior trial counsel.
Cooper-Bailey, who received support from five commissioners, is the executive counsel for the Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training and serves as a judge for the Cranston Municipal Court. Since 2021, she has worked as an adjunct professor at Roger Williams University School of Law, where she graduated cum laude in 2008.
Cassisi Finkelman, who was appointed Family Court magistrate in 2021 by Chief Judge Michael B. Forte, also received five votes from the commission. She presides over several Family Court calendars, including contested divorces, custody, placement, parenting time, child support, grandparent visitation, restraining orders, and relocation trials.
Labor attorney Carly Iafrate, right, sits next to then-Senate Majority Whip Valarie Lawson during a Rhode Island Ethics Commission on June 4, 2024. Iafrate is on the shortlist for two Superior Court vacancies. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)
The finalists for Lanphear’s seat
For the opening created by Lanphear’s retirement at the end of April, the Judicial Nominating Commission advanced Iafrate, former U.S. Attorney Zachary Cunha, and Joelle Rocha.
Cunha, who was appointed Rhode Island’s top federal prosecutor by President Joe Biden in 2021, received five votes from the commission. Under his tenure, Cunha’s office pushed the city of Pawtucket to ensure Spanish-speaking voters have proper assistance during elections, sued CVS for allegedly contributing to the opioid crisis, and pushed the nation’s oldest community bank to address claims it discriminated against Black and Hispanic borrowers in Rhode Island.
He stepped down from the U.S. Attorney’s office in 2025 after President Donald Trump took office. He now works in private practice as a partner at Nixon & Peabody LLP in Providence. 
Cunha was hired by General Assembly leaders last November to question then-Rhode Island Department of Transportation Director Peter Alviti at length during a joint oversight hearing on the ongoing closure of the westbound Washington Bridge.
Rocha practices with Adler Pollock & Sheehan, where she’s focused on real estate development, land use and real estate litigation since joining the Providence-based firm in August 2025. 
Since 2022, Rocha has served as a legal and policy adviser for the state’s House of Representatives where she drafted and analyzed housing-related bills between the 2023 and 2026 legislative sessions.
Her resume notes she’s provided legal, procedural, and policy counsel to the Speaker of the House, committee chairs in committee hearings and floor debate. Rocha received the support of five commissioners.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Kettering University student sues Genesee County, alleges they withheld records on Flock cameras
description: Joshua Tewolde, a student at Kettering University in Flint, has filed a lawsuit against Genesee County, alleging that the county illegally withheld records in a Freedom of Information Act request for information on Flock automated license plate reader cameras in the county. The records requested under FOIA, according to the complaint and accompanying records[...]
text:
A Flock license plate reader camera in Southfield. July 3, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Joshua Tewolde, a student at Kettering University in Flint, has filed a lawsuit against Genesee County, alleging that the county illegally withheld records in a Freedom of Information Act request for information on Flock automated license plate reader cameras in the county.
The records requested under FOIA, according to the complaint and accompanying records, included “records governing the County’s contractual relationship with Flock Group,” audit and search logs for the county’s Flock system, the county’s policies “governing Flock technology and data, data sharing, and public disclosure of data,” and the locations of county-contracted Flock cameras. He also requested all of the license plate reader records for his own vehicle, as well as prior FOIA records relating to Flock. 
“I submitted these FOIA requests because I wanted to understand how surveillance technology is being used in my community,” Tewolde, who is represented by lawyers from the Mackinac Center Legal Foundation, part of the Mackinac Center for Public Policy, a free-market think tank, said. 
“The public deserves access to basic information about government surveillance, especially when it involves technology that can track people’s movements. This lawsuit is about transparency and accountability, so citizens can have an informed conversation about the balance between public safety and privacy,” Tewolde said.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The county did provide responsive records to two parts of Tewolde’s FOIA: the portion relating to contracts between the county and Flock, and some records relating to prior Flock-related FOIA Requests. 
“The County incorrectly disclaimed ownership of public records which it must release and incorrectly applied the exemption applicable to law enforcement investigative records,” the complaint, filed Aug. 18 in the Genesee County Circuit Court, states.
That specific portion of the complaint relates to the county’s response to Tewolde’s FOIA, which specifically states that, though the sheriff’s office has a contract with this company and can access the system, the “data within it does not belong to this public body, i.e., Genesee County.”
The contract between the county and Flock, however, does indicate that Genesee County is the owner of the data collected by the city’s license-plate reader system. 
“Under the plain language of the County’s contract with Flock, the County retains legal ownership of any data it shares with Flock,” the complaint states. “This expressly includes any footage captured by Flock cameras whether owned by the County or provided to the County by Flock.”
Tewolde’s Mackinac Center lawyers have argued that the broader question at the center of the lawsuit is whether government agencies can avoid Michigan FOIA obligations by routing surveillance operations through private vendors. 
Jared Field, the director of communications for the county, declined to comment on the lawsuit to Michigan Advance, writing, “Genesee County is aware of the complaint. As a matter of practice, the County does not comment on the specifics of a pending litigation. The County will respond to the complaint through the appropriate legal processes.”

title: Amid housing crisis, Maine mobile home residents make strides to protect themselves
description: People who live in mobile homes in Augusta last week succeeded in gathering enough signatures to put a lot rent stabilization ordinance on the city’s November ballot. It’s the latest in a series of efforts by mobile home residents and the state to keep the homes affordable. Residents in Augusta began meeting last fall as […]
text:
Augusta mobile home park residents gather signatures for a lot rent stabilization ordinance. (Photo courtesy of the Maine Labor Climate Council)People who live in mobile homes in Augusta last week succeeded in gathering enough signatures to put a lot rent stabilization ordinance on the city’s November ballot. It’s the latest in a series of efforts by mobile home residents and the state to keep the homes affordable.
Residents in Augusta began meeting last fall as they struggled to handle rent hikes with many on fixed incomes through retirement funds, veteran benefits or disability, which is the case for Vanessa Decker, 65, who has lived in Riverside Drive mobile home park with her fiancé for about three years.
“The rent has gone up every year since I’ve been here,” Decker said, also noting that her property taxes and utilities have increased, too. “If I was by myself, I’d be screwed.” 
Affordability is a concern for people in various types of housing across Maine, as a massive shortage in supply confronts stagnant wages, high building costs, and an influx of residents in part due to an increase in remote workers.
The state is on track to slightly exceed its annual goal of building new units, but new housing is largely concentrated in seasonal communities and affordable units make up just 13%. 
While mobile home residents often own their physical homes, they have to rent the underlying land, leaving them vulnerable to skyrocketing monthly lot rents, especially when corporate or out-of-state investors buy parks. 
In Augusta, where residents are aiming to pass the rent ordinance, there are eight mobile home parks with roughly 300 lots, but only three parks — or 25 lots — have ownership licenses registered in Maine, according to data released in a new dashboard by the Maine Office of Community Affairs.
The dashboard is intended to track housing needs and affordability, with insight on each of Maine’s 475 mobile home parks. 
The average monthly lot rent in Maine is $479. The state currently has 19,348 lots, and 2,383 are unoccupied.
Maine has implemented several new laws in recent years to address the state’s housing shortage, including some of the nation’s strongest protections for mobile home park residents. 
In 2023, lawmakers passed a law that requires mobile home park owners to notify residents of their intent to sell and give them at least 60 days to make an offer. In 2025, they passed another law that gave mobile home owners the right of first refusal to purchase a mobile home park if the owner intends to sell. 
On July 30, the first resident buy out under that law occurred when residents of the Hidden Circle Mobile Home Park bought the park from its out-of-state owner for about $1 million. It was financed by donations from the Maine Community Foundation, the Brunswick-based Genesis Community Loan Fund, and the state’s Mobile Home Park Preservation Fund. 
All the ways, big and little, Maine lawmakers tried to alleviate the housing crisis this session

The latter had been a temporary fund but became permanent through a law proposed by Sen. Cameron Reny (D-Bristol) that took effect earlier this year. 
Administered by the Maine State Housing Authority, the law is funded by a fee of $10,000 per lot paid by certain buyers of manufactured housing communities or mobile home parks. State and municipal housing authorities, resident cooperatives and small companies and individuals with a net worth less than $50 million are exempt from the fee as a means to encourage small local businesses or residents themselves to own the parks. 
Rising rents are not exclusive to mobile homes, Erik Jorgensen, senior director of government relations and communications for MaineHousing, said when testifying in support of the measure at the time. But apartment tenants have the option to move to a different or lower-priced unit. Options for mobile home owners are more limited, Jorgensen said, because “moving a manufactured home is at best, an expensive option, and at worst, impossible.”
During a celebration of the Hidden Circle Mobile Home Park purchase last week, Gov. Janet Mills said that the fund is expected to preserve more than 900 homes across six parks. 
Another law passed this year made some changes to the 2023 law, limiting lot rent increases to once per year and making it easier to develop new homes in mobile home parks. However, another proposal for a large bond package, which included a pilot program supporting the construction of new homes in mobile home parks, failed.
The ordinance the mobile home owners in Augusta are pushing to get passed in November would not apply to resident-owned parks. 
It would limit annual lot rent increases either to meet inflation or 3%, whichever is lower. But it would also create a process for park owners to seek higher increases when needed for major improvements or unexpected hardships. 
City councilors will meet on Sept. 3 to formally approve the ordinance as a ballot measure. 
“Getting this on the ballot in November gives me hope. It gives me hope that I’m not going to be priced out of my home,” Decker said. “We may have done the process and gotten it on the ballot, but the fight is not over yet. We need everyone to vote yes to keep our parks affordable.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Why nuclear, why New Hampshire, why now?
description: At a moment of big changes in U.S. energy use and policy, with electricity bills pinching consumers and discussions on climate and emissions both high stakes and deeply politicized, New Hampshire’s executive branch has locked in on a vision for one specific path forward.  “What we do best right now looks like nuclear, and I […]
text:
Seabrook Station nuclear power plant, viewed from across the Blackwater River. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)At a moment of big changes in U.S. energy use and policy, with electricity bills pinching consumers and discussions on climate and emissions both high stakes and deeply politicized, New Hampshire’s executive branch has locked in on a vision for one specific path forward. 
“What we do best right now looks like nuclear, and I think we can benefit from expanding that,” said Thomas Barrasso, director of energy innovation for the New Hampshire Department of Energy at a public meeting this June. 
At the direction of Gov. Kelly Ayotte, the department has spent the summer pulling together a nuclear playbook for New Hampshire. The goal, as Ayotte laid it out in March, is to find a way to get more nuclear generators running in the state. 
In the run-up to a preliminary September deadline for that “road map,” the discussion has brought in perspectives from some of New Hampshire and New England’s biggest energy institutions and regional experts. Yet, at a series of Department of Energy-hosted stakeholder sessions this June and in interviews with the Bulletin after, some hedged on whether nuclear can deliver all the benefits the region’s governors hope it will — while others openly contradicted that idea. 
Meanwhile, the positivity of those driving the conversation forward, including the department, some state representatives, and industry players, hasn’t wavered. 
The discussion sheds light on a unique moment, electrically, in New Hampshire, and on the array of problems — current and anticipated, local and global — still unsolved.
Governors stress rising price, demand
The road map project is one result of a March executive order in which Ayotte wrote investing in more nuclear power could lower costs for ratepayers and reduce emissions. Emerging nuclear technologies, she said, have the promise to be safer and more reliable than existing plants. 
New Hampshire is already familiar with nuclear power. The Seacoast hosts Seabrook Station, one of New England’s two remaining nuclear power plants, owned by energy giant NextEra Energy Resources. And Portsmouth Naval Shipyard has long hosted some of the United States’ military nuclear submarines and the experts who work on them.
A few days after her March executive order, Ayotte joined governors from the rest of New England in a joint statement championing nuclear power. New England, they said, needs more electricity, and nuclear could provide it.
Electricity use in New England has been on the decline since the mid-2000s, thanks in part to increases in energy efficiency, according to ISO-NE, which operates the region’s electric grid. (Lately, New England has experienced “record” low levels of demand, said Eric Johnson, executive director of external affairs for the ISO, during a meeting in June.)
But now, he said, “we’re in an inflection point.”
The ISO now expects energy use to trend upward. There are several reasons for that change, one of which is the projected addition of large loads from data centers and cryptocurrency mining — things that aren’t yet prevalent on the New England grid, according to the ISO, but could potentially become so. 
Other factors include the shift of high-energy sectors, like vehicle transportation and home heating, from direct fossil fuel use onto electricity. 
But electrification doesn’t automatically remove fossil fuel from the equation. In New England, over 50% of electricity is generated with natural gas, according to the ISO. That links back to the cost concern raised by New England’s governors: Dependence on natural gas, according to the New Hampshire Department of Energy, is a major reason New Hampshire’s electric bills — and those in other New England states — often rank among the highest in the nation. 
Those elements aren’t the only factors that explain New Hampshire’s high and rising electric rates. Intricacies and recent changes in the way energy is bought and sold in the region, and how rates are set, also contribute, according to energy professionals. 
Promises and limitations
Nuclear energy is constant and reliable, Rep. Keith Ammon, a New Boston Republican who has pushed for more nuclear energy in New Hampshire, said during opening remarks at the June meetings. He added that the technology was changing, and that new reactors were safer, more flexible, and more cost effective. 
“Nuclear doesn’t care about the weather. It just runs,” he said, comparing the technology to wind and solar power, which, with output tied to weather conditions, are considered “intermittent” power sources. (Clean energy proponents point to battery storage as a way to spread this power out over time.)
In terms of political palatability under the Trump administration, nuclear also seems to have the upper hand over wind and solar projects. While President Donald Trump has blocked offshore wind developments nationwide and elsewhere in New England, his administration favors nuclear energy and is pushing for widespread development with executive orders and funding opportunities for states and industry.
But how would it affect costs for New Hampshire consumers? At the June meetings, utility experts weighed in. 
Additional electricity-generating capacity from new nuclear generation would indeed help New England as a whole meet rising demand, said Justin Pelkowski, director of wholesale power contracting for Eversource Energy, New Hampshire’s largest electric utility. 
But zero in on New Hampshire, and the equation looks different, he said. 
That’s because New Hampshire is already a net exporter of energy, generating more within its borders than residents and businesses use. Additional generation would simply increase the net amount of electricity sent out to the regional grid from within New Hampshire. And New Hampshire ratepayers, who would likely finance it, would not see a direct, local benefit, although there would be a regional one.
Because the New Hampshire grid does not want for power, additional generation would not fill a local gap — meaning it is less likely a company would see an incentive to choose New Hampshire to construct generation, Pelkowski said. 
New Hampshire has little control over where the electricity generated in-state is sold. That’s because generators may contract with buyers out of state for their electricity. A proportion of the electricity generated at Seabrook Station, for example, is sold out of state.
“Just because an asset is located in the state of New Hampshire doesn’t mean we buy the energy or benefit from the energy,” said Rep. Kat McGhee, a Hollis Democrat, in an interview. 
In McGhee’s view, this fact means that the idea of boosting in-state generation to immediately lower costs for New Hampshire ratepayers is a fallacy. But on the House Committee on Science, Technology, and Energy, on which McGhee is ranking member, other members “did not have that understanding,” she said. 
Depending on where it is sited, a new facility could also trigger a need for significant transmission infrastructure upgrades to handle the added power, Pelkowski said. This would also affect rates.
According to the Eversource representatives, a new nuclear plant would not address New England’s reliance on natural gas, and thus high costs. Extensive buildout would be necessary to make a meaningful difference on high-demand winter moments, when gas is most constrained, that have the largest impact on bills, Pelkowski said.
“It’s not going to solve the issue,” Pelkowski said. 
A financing dance
Courting more nuclear generation would also require finding a way to finance it.
Prospective generation owners are interested in security that they will recoup profits on an investment, said Michelle Gardner, executive director of northeast regulatory affairs with NextEra Energy Resources.
“The most important thing I want to emphasize is the need for long-term revenue certainty,” she said during the June meeting. “Developing nuclear is very capital intensive, and even on a SMR (small modular reactor) scale, it has a long development cycle, and there are still a number of risks.”
Developers are unlikely to move ahead with projects unless they feel certain they will recoup their investment, she said.
“No one, and I’m happy to be challenged, is going to develop nuclear without a contract,” she said. 
But those contracts tend to be costly for ratepayers, said New Hampshire Consumer Advocate Don Kreis. 
New Hampshire has laws designed to prevent capital projects from having an outsized impact on rates, some of which originated after the construction of Seabrook Station went massively over budget, bankrupting the utility Public Service of New Hampshire and leaving ratepayers on the hook.
More recently, the Vogtle nuclear plant in Georgia — the first new nuclear plant built in the U.S. in decades — finished $17 billion over budget, drove Westinghouse Electric Co. into bankruptcy, and left ratepayers with a heavy burden.
Kreis said he wasn’t convinced a project could be pulled off without a negative impact on ratepayers.
For new nuclear in New Hampshire, “nobody has demonstrated a good or even plausible economic case,” he said in an interview.
In the long-term — for instance, now that the cost of Seabrook Station has been paid off, and the plant continues to run — nuclear power can seem instantaneously inexpensive compared to other power sources. But the lifetime cost and initial impact are another thing, said Rep. Michael Harrington, a Strafford Republican.
“If you think you can sell to ratepayers the fact that we’re going to have a big increase in electric costs because 10 or 15 years from now it’ll seem cheap, well, I’ll sell you a bridge in Brooklyn,” he said during the Department of Energy meeting.
During a public comment period at the stakeholder meeting, some shared hope that the state would find a creative way forward to continue pursuing more nuclear. 
“It’s clear to me in many, many discussions that there is a bipartisan acceptance that nuclear is the way to go,” said Rep. John Schneller, a Bedford Republican. “It’s certainly part of a larger solution.”
Others, including Doug Bogen of the Seacoast Anti-Pollution League, shared reservations. 
Bogen said he was concerned about the financial, environmental, and safety impacts of new generation. One of those impacts, Bogen said, is the cost of directing funds to nuclear that may otherwise yield a more immediate benefit.
“If we’re going to spend billions of dollars promoting and building these nuclear plants, what are we not doing instead? Where are we missing out on renewable other sources, even efficiency improvements, that could save us a lot more money?” he asked.
To Bogen, the conversations at the three-day Department of Energy conference didn’t delve deep enough into the reasoning behind the choice to pursue additional nuclear generation over alternatives. He said the focus felt ideological. 
“Are there real issues here,” he asked, “or is this just politics?”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana lawmakers looking at license plate cameras amid growing privacy worries
description: A petition to ban automated license plate readers in rural Lawrence County garnered 500 signatures in four days. The Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department is investigating one of its officers for reportedly accessing the department’s license plate network for personal use, which the Washington Post reports went undetected until one of its reporters dis[...]
text:
A license plate reader outside Avon, Indiana. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)A petition to ban automated license plate readers in rural Lawrence County garnered 500 signatures in four days.
The Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department is investigating one of its officers for reportedly accessing the department’s license plate network for personal use, which the Washington Post reports went undetected until one of its reporters discovered it.
The Bloomington Police Department did not renew its contract with vendor Flock Systems — and other cities across the state are debating whether to do the same.
Public backlash to license plate reader networks is intensifying, but Indiana law says little about how police and commercial entities can use the technology.
The cameras are widely used by law enforcement agencies to capture still images of license plates for criminal investigations.
A state law enacted last year bans homeowners’ associations from deploying the technology to monitor residents and visitors, unless the cameras are operated by law enforcement — the sole restriction to date.
But several lawmakers plan to revisit the subject next year as their constituents express fears of mass surveillance and misuse.
Lawmakers seek ‘guardrails’
“License plate readers have proven to be a very effective tool for law enforcement,” said Rep. Jim Pressel, R-Rolling Prairie. “It’s something that I think we need to preserve the good that it does, while at the same time putting up guardrails to protect Hoosiers from surveillance.”
Rep. Jim Pressel leads a committee meeting on March 31, 2025. (Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Pressel, chair of the House Roads and Transportation Committee, authored the HOA license plate reader ban as an amendment to House Enrolled Act 1150. He’s now drafting a bill to set a minimum standard for how law enforcement should use the technology.
The bill will likely require law enforcement agencies to perform regular audits of license plate reader searches to identify misuse, with additional yearly audits by Indiana State Police, Pressel said.
Pressel is also considering minimum standards for how long police agencies should be allowed to retain license plate data and when that information can be shared with outside agencies.
Walker Lasbury, a DePauw University student who is a founder of Eyes Off Indiana, wants lawmakers to set a seven-day data retention limit on information about license plates that do not appear on hot lists — a digital database of vehicles of interest to law enforcement.
That suggestion mirrors the new default storage limit recommended by Flock Safety, the most well-known vendor of license plate readers.
Flock Safety tightens safeguards as states, cities question surveillance network

Lasenby said the system’s “evidence mode” feature allows detectives to preserve specific data for active cases, though the company’s own research shows more than 90% of searches are performed within one week.
Eyes Off Indiana estimates 3,604 automated license plate readers are in use across the state, with at least one camera in 84 of Indiana’s 92 counties.
The cameras are accessed by thousands of law enforcement agencies, including hospital and airport security, university police, state prisons and natural resource officers.
The Indiana Department of Correction uses the data to find escapees or parolees who violate the terms of their supervision.
The Indiana Department of Transportation accesses license plate data to monitor tolling operations, construction sites and safety zones.
Powerful, ‘unregulated’ systems
Police say the systems allow them to locate missing persons, stolen vehicles and homicide suspects.
The Bloomington Police Department used Flock cameras to find a vehicle after officers rescued a severely beaten woman from a burning home days before the city lost access to the network in April.
The Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department credits license plate readers for the swift apprehension of a serial rape suspect — hours after a national DNA database connected the man to a series of sexual assaults spanning more than a decade.
So, too, with the arrests of three men and two teenagers suspected of stealing $2 million worth of cash and jewelry from an Indianapolis jewelry store.
Indianapolis police say investigators used license plate readers to locate an 86-year-old man who forgot how to get home; three missing foster children whose non-custodial parents were attempting to flee with them to Mexico; and the killer of a 2-year-old Indianapolis girl whose body was hidden in an abandoned southern Indiana home, among other cases.
But the department learned this month that one of its own was using the database for personal reasons.
A Washington Post investigation found the officer, who has not been publicly identified, allegedly searched for his wife and acquaintances as many as 3,759 times in 10 months.
IMPD suspended the officer and initiated an investigation on Aug. 6, around the time the Washington Post reports it contacted the department about the searches, though Chief Tanya Terry told other outlets the officer came forward the same day.
Terry recommended the officer’s termination.
“The problem right now is the state of Indiana, (license plate readers) are left completely unregulated,” Lasbury said, “meaning that any protections that Hoosiers do have come from departmental policy, and departmental policy can change overnight.” 
Do internal polices go far enough?
The IMPD Public Affairs Division said the department instituted a new policy this month with stronger language around the auditing process and appropriate use of the database.
Only officers who undergo training and acknowledge IMPD policies are granted access.
“It includes stronger language regarding system use, emphasizing that ALPRs are powerful investigative tools that must be used responsibly, legally, and only for legitimate public-safety purposes,” an email statement said. “Ongoing auditing enables us to efficiently identify potential misuse and intervene early.”
The department did not provide a copy of the policy to the Indiana Capital Chronicle as of Friday.
Indiana State Police policy requires troopers to complete a dispatch or case number entry each time they search the agency’s license plate database.
District investigative commanders are responsible for auditing the records at their discretion, a safeguard that agency spokesman Capt. Ron Galaviz said has been in place since the deployment of the technology.
The policy also prohibits using the license plate reader system or hot lists to infringe upon a person’s First Amendment rights.
Flock will soon require case codes for law enforcement searches.
Meanwhile, law enforcement agencies using Flock will need to adopt the company’s audit assistance tool, which suspends users whose activity appears suspicious so an administrator can review.
The Indianapolis Fraternal Order of Police issued a statement this month calling on state lawmakers to establish standards so the technology isn’t misused.
Lasbury is also in talks with lawmakers to set a minimum standard, which he hopes will include transparency, audit requirements, a ban on commercial sharing or selling of license plate data and criminal and civil penalties for anyone who misuses it.
Lawmaker wants to ‘preserve the good’
“I tell people all the time: I don’t think we suspended the Fourth Amendment to the Constitution anytime recently, so we should probably look at this topic,” said Sen. Aaron Freeman, R-Indianapolis.
Freeman, who chaired the Senate Corrections and Criminal Law Committee and introduced Pressel’s HOA amendment to the Senate version of HEA 1150, wants to see a comprehensive analysis of how license plate readers are used in the next legislative session.
Sen. Aaron Freeman speaks during a committee meeting on March 25, 2025. (Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
“Who can have access to this stuff? How long do you keep it?” Freeman said. “When you’re looking for somebody who’s cheating on their spouse, can you use it for that? Somebody runs for office — can we use it for that?”
Pressel and Freeman are among several lawmakers engaging the subject, though it is unclear how many bills will be introduced when the General Assembly convenes in January.
Gov. Mike Braun has signaled his support for the effort.
“Gov. Braun will always support law enforcement with the resources they need to ensure public safety,” governor’s office press secretary Griffin Reid said. “Guardrails are important and should be considered anytime personal information is involved.”
Still, backlash is brewing across the state.
A Change.org petition to ban license plate readers in Lawrence County — population 45,000 — attracted more than 500 signatures as of Friday evening.
“I don’t want to live in a society where there are cameras on every corner,” said organizer Nikki Luallen, who started the petition after she noticed license plate readers popping up in her county six months ago.
She’s spotted 16 license plate readers in the southern Indiana county, known for its limestone, underground caverns and forests.
The cameras differ from private security cameras in Luallen’s mind because they sync into a nation-wide database accessible by outside parties, enabling large-scale tracking capabilities.
Pressel said the cameras have their proper uses.
“I don’t think anybody wants to see them go away, and we need to preserve the good while protecting Hoosiers from any kind of misuse,” he said. “That’s the goal, and I think that is going to hit the sweet spot. Time will tell.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: CVS doesn’t deserve all to blame for the opioid crisis. But can we be honest about its complex role?
description: Election years aren’t a great time for nuance.  I’ve been reminded of this as Gov. Dan McKee and Democratic challenger Helena Buonanno Foulkes head down the home stretch of their bitter gubernatorial primary rematch.  In particular, I’m concerned with how their arguments about the opioid epidemic — a “modern plague” that has claimed hundreds of […]
text:
Democratic challenger Helena Buonanno Foulkes, a former president of CVS Health, makes a point while Gov. Dan McKee looks on during the WPRI debate at Sapinsley Hall at Rhode Island College on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Corey Welch/WPRI 12)Election years aren’t a great time for nuance. 
I’ve been reminded of this as Gov. Dan McKee and Democratic challenger Helena Buonanno Foulkes head down the home stretch of their bitter gubernatorial primary rematch. 
In particular, I’m concerned with how their arguments about the opioid epidemic — a “modern plague” that has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives, a complex ongoing public health crisis, the basis for some of the most complex litigation in American history — have veered into black and white territory. 
If you listened to McKee — who has hammered Foulkes via websites, TV ads, social media posts, campaign statements, and debate remarks for her alleged ties to the crisis as a former CVS executive — you might think that CVS was solely responsible for the opioid epidemic. 
This clearly isn’t true. 
A long list of people, parties, or organizations share some responsibility for this crisis, including pharmaceutical companies, medical distributors, doctors, pharmacists, regulators, and insurance companies. Investigative reporting has pointed the finger at others: judges, consulting firms, the American Medical Association. We did not get into this mess because of any one company.
Meanwhile, when she’s not sharing her familiar talking points, Foulkes has strongly implied that sharp criticism of CVS is economically dangerous for the state. In the WPRO debate, she said Cumberland voters she met while door-to-door campaigning told her it was terrible what McKee was “doing to CVS.” Many of them work at the company, and don’t like it at all, she said.
She returned to this theme in their WJAR showdown. After mentioning that CVS and its 7,000 Rhode Island-based employees didn’t appreciate McKee’s attacks, she went further, citing a July statement from the executive director of Partnership for Rhode Island, a consortium of local businesses. “The 50 largest companies business leaders in this state wrote a letter to you, asking you to stop criticizing CVS,” she said. “You are going to drive them out of the state.”
Foulkes is not alone. 
In June, Boston Globe columnist Dan McGowan argued McKee was “jeopardizing part of Rhode Island’s economic future” by his campaign’s “sustained attack” on CVS. Describing the Woonsocket-based giant as “one of the state’s most important corporate anchors,” McGowan suggested McKee ought to drop out of the race. In July, Providence Journal columnist Mark Patinkin called McKee’s attacks on CVS “cynical and self-serving” and described his criticism as a “dangerous game…of angering our biggest corporation.”
As someone who has reported on the opioid crisis for years, I am compelled to correct the record. Because while CVS may not be the only party responsible for the opioid epidemic, its role should not be ignored or dismissed.
Do the people rushing to defend CVS know that when the company agreed to pay $5 billion to settle thousands of opioid-related lawsuits, the Associated Press noted, “Only a handful of opioid settlements have had bigger dollar figures”?
Do they know that, in 2021, in Ohio, CVS and other chain-pharmacies lost a six-week jury trial over civil claims that the companies had fueled the opioid crisis?
Do they know about all the settlements CVS has reached over the years after U.S. Department of Justice investigations into various kinds of misconduct, from poor record-keeping to filling fraudulent prescriptions? $22 million in Florida? $8 million in Maryland? $5 million in California? $3.5 million in Massachusetts? And, after two separate cases — in 2015 and 2019 — a total of nearly $1 million here in Rhode Island?
Have they read the opioid-focused civil complaint against CVS and other chain pharmacies filed by Attorney General Peter Neronha in 2023? It reads, in part:
“[A]ccording to [DEA] ARCOS data, a CVS location in Wakefield purchased over 750,000 dosage units in 2014, in a community of 8,911 people. A CVS location in North Smithfield purchased enough dosage units of opioids in 2012 alone to supply 80 dosage units to every resident of the town.”



Quotation







As someone who has reported on the opioid crisis for years, I am compelled to correct the record. Because while CVS may not be the only party responsible for the opioid epidemic, its role should not be ignored or dismissed.


When it comes to CVS and opioids, the situation calls for nuance.
CVS is by no means the only company implicated in the opioid crisis, as McKee might have you believe. It isn’t even the only chain pharmacy implicated. 
But at the same time, it is true that the company contributed to the opioid crisis in notable ways. 
Ignoring CVS’s role for the sake of how many people it employs or its economic impact is reminiscent of how we got into the opioid crisis in the first place. The subtitle of one medical journal article about the ill-fated marketing of OxyContin reads: “Commercial Triumph, Public Health Tragedy.”
But I hope that, whoever wins, we can return to discussing this crisis — which still claims hundreds of lives every year in our little state — as the complex, multi-faceted problem it is. 
Flattening the issue may help a candidate gain a brief political edge. But it doesn’t serve the public. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia school district accused of illegally delaying enrollment of foster children
description: A state agency is accusing the Muscogee County School District of violating state and federal law by delaying the enrollment of foster children. The Georgia Division of Family and Children Services says the disagreement centers on the interpretation of a bill signed into law this year intended to help get kids in foster care enrolled […]
text:
The Georgia Division of Family and Children Services says Muscogee County Schools is delaying children in foster care from enrolling in schools, a claim the district denies. Getty ImagesA state agency is accusing the Muscogee County School District of violating state and federal law by delaying the enrollment of foster children.
The Georgia Division of Family and Children Services says the disagreement centers on the interpretation of a bill signed into law this year intended to help get kids in foster care enrolled in new schools more quickly.
According to the letter, Muscogee is interpreting Senate Bill 431, which passed both chambers unanimously this year and was signed into law by Gov. Brian Kemp in May, to require a foster child’s case manager to directly enroll the child in school. According to the state agency, any department-approved custodian, like foster parents, or agency personnel, not just case managers, are allowed to enroll students.
The state agency says Muscogee is the only Georgia district to interpret the law this way, and the result is more than 30 students missing the first week of classes, including more than 20 with individualized education plans and special education designation. And the division says around 50 other students in foster care who had already enrolled could be at risk of being withdrawn from school if they are not enrolled by their case manager.
“After years of working through enrollment issues with Muscogee, this is the latest in a long line of efforts by Muscogee County School District to delay, defer, or refuse enrollment of children in foster care into their school system,” reads an Aug. 14 letter from DFCS attorney Dana Carroll to the Regional Education Service Agency overseeing the area and the Georgia Department of Education.
“This unlawful practice violates the rights of these students to be enrolled in school and delays their educational opportunities,” the letter continues.
The letter, which was obtained by the Georgia Recorder, was sent as the central Georgia school district is now three weeks into the new school year.
In an emailed statement, Muscogee County Schools communications director Kimberly Wright said the district is not violating the law and did not receive a copy of the letter from DFCS.
“The suggestion that MCSD failed to enroll students who are eligible for enrollment is incorrect,” she wrote. “The District is working cooperatively with the Department of Family and Children Services on this issue to ensure that all required information is obtained for enrollment.”
“If DHS, the RESA, or any collaborating agency has any questions about the way in which MCSD is undertaking to follow the law regarding enrollment, MCSD is happy to discuss those issues,” she added.
Foster parents sometimes have difficulty enrolling children into a new school when they change locations, sometimes having to take days off work to deal with paperwork and logistics. Lawmakers attempted to ease that struggle with SB 431, which requires districts to enroll foster students within three school business days of receiving a completed enrollment form.
The bill’s sponsor, Marietta Republican Sen. Kay Kirkpatrick, expressed disappointment.
“We passed SB 431 to be sure foster kids would be immediately enrolled to prevent disruptions to their already challenging lives,” she said. “I am disappointed to hear that one of our school districts either has not gotten the message or is deliberately not complying. Hopefully this can be resolved quickly.”
John DeGarmo, founder of an advocacy group called the Foster Care Institute and a foster parent to more than 60 kids in Georgia, said around half of foster children do not finish school. He said he fears Muscogee’s policy will further discourage them from focusing on their schoolwork as well as force foster parents to take off work to watch the kids instead of sending them to school and risk piling on to vulnerable children’s list of problems.
“They might see it as ‘the school doesn’t want me because I’m a foster kid,’” he said. “So that might further traumatize or bring additional anxiety to that child, additional anxiety that the foster parents have to address because that child is living in their home, not going to school. The child might be feeling that anxiety because they think ‘the school doesn’t want me. Yet again, adults have betrayed me, failed me, don’t want me.’”

title: Southern University board chairman wants dress code for its campuses
description: The leader of Southern University’s Board of Supervisors said he wants the system to follow the lead of other historically Black colleges and universities and adopt a dress code.  Board chairman Tony Clayton, who’s also the district attorney for Iberville, West Baton Rouge and Pointe Coupee parishes, said he wants to pull together the chancellors […]
text:
The F. G. Clark Activity Center at Southern University in Baton Rouge is also known as the "Mini-Dome" and is a multi-purpose facility used for campus and community events. (Photo provided by Southern University)The leader of Southern University’s Board of Supervisors said he wants the system to follow the lead of other historically Black colleges and universities and adopt a dress code. 
Board chairman Tony Clayton, who’s also the district attorney for Iberville, West Baton Rouge and Pointe Coupee parishes, said he wants to pull together the chancellors from Southern’s five campuses to discuss the idea ahead of their next meeting on Sept. 18.  
“I walked around campus the other day. I think we need it,” Clayton told board members at Friday’s meeting in Baton Rouge. 
The HBCUs Clayton referred to include Tuskegee University, a private school in Alabama where the new dress code has been met with criticism from some students. It prohibits students from wearing revealing clothes, as well as “bedroom shoes, bonnets, or (do rags)” to their classes or the campus cafeteria, according to a letter its president released over the summer.
Tuskegee students on campus for their first day of class Wednesday had mixed opinions about the new dress code, the Alabama Reflector reported.
Serenity Mitchell, a junior at Tuskegee majoring in biology, said the public manner of sharing the dress code painted students in a bad light.
“I think that releasing it in the way that they did made it look like students were kind of walking around here looking any type of way, and that’s just not true,” Mitchell said. “We as a student population represent ourselves well, so I think publishing the dress code like they did just makes us look bad.”
Tuskegee University declined to comment on its new dress code policy, which does not include any specifics on enforcement or penalties.
Student attire policies vary at other HBCUs. Hampton University and Fisk University have dress codes, while Howard University and Morehouse College have rules that do not apply campuswide.
Andrea Tinker with the Alabama Reflector contributed to this report.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Minority owned businesses were never a diversity initiative
description: Gov. Mike Braun and Attorney General Todd Rokita have made their position clear: Indiana’s use of race and sex-conscious measures in state contracting is, in their view, unconstitutional. The Braun administration is now moving away from those measures and toward what it calls a system based on “Merit, Excellence, and Innovation.” As Black Hoosiers, we […]
text:
The division was created in 1983 to actively promote, monitor and enforce the standards for certification of minority, women, and veteran business enterprises. (IDOA)

Gov. Mike Braun and Attorney General Todd Rokita have made their position clear: Indiana’s use of race and sex-conscious measures in state contracting is, in their view, unconstitutional. The Braun administration is now moving away from those measures and toward what it calls a system based on “Merit, Excellence, and Innovation.”
As Black Hoosiers, we have spent time thinking about what that message means — not simply politically or legally, but personally. And we keep returning to one truth: We were never a diversity initiative.
Women and minorities do not become talented because government recognizes them. They do not become entrepreneurs because a program certifies their businesses. They do not become worthy competitors because someone establishes a participation goal.
We were capable before DEI had a name.
We have built businesses, created jobs, educated children, cared for families, served our country, led churches, invented, manufactured, farmed, practiced medicine and law, constructed buildings and strengthened communities. We have contributed to Indiana’s economy and America’s prosperity even during generations when the doors of opportunity were not simply difficult to open but were intentionally closed.
That history matters in this debate.
State targets ‘discriminatory’ DEI practices, cancels minority business conference

Indiana created its supplier diversity program in 1983 to increase participation by minority and women-owned businesses in state contracting. The state itself has commissioned disparity studies examining whether minority-owned firms face barriers and whether their share of government contracting dollars reflects their availability in the marketplace. Those studies consistently show the marketplace does not favor our labor.
When we talk about “merit,” we should remember that Black businesses have demonstrated merit under circumstances in which access to capital, relationships, networks and government opportunities has not always been distributed equally. And by the government’s own admission, not one majority owned business has suffered due to the inclusion of “other” in this statutory scheme.
We competed anyway. We built anyway. We succeeded anyway.
That is why the Greater Indianapolis NAACP refuses to allow this moment to become a message to Black Hoosiers that our value is somehow disappearing due to the exclusion from a government program.
Braun can eliminate an initiative. Rokita can issue an advisory opinion. The state can change its procurement policies. But no government action can repeal our value.
To every Black entrepreneur wondering what comes next: compete. To the young Black professional wondering whether Indiana still has a place for your ambition: build. To Black-owned companies pursuing state contracts: walk into those rooms knowing you belong there— not because someone lowered a standard, but because generations before you succeeded while carrying burdens their competitors often never had to face.
And Indiana should understand something, too.
A “level playing field” cannot simply be a slogan. If merit is truly going to be the standard, then opportunity must be visible, procurement processes must be transparent, relationships cannot determine who gets through the door, and every qualified Hoosier business must genuinely have the chance to compete.
Removing a diversity goal does not automatically remove disparity and Black Hoosiers are not asking Indiana to manufacture our excellence. Our history already proves it.
You are seen. You are heard. You are valuable.
And our businesses, labor, leadership, creativity and purchasing power are necessary to Indiana’s future.
DEI did not create Black excellence. Government did not give it to us, and government cannot take it away.
As Indiana enters its next chapter, we will be there; building, competing, contributing and reminding state leaders that women and minorities were never the initiative. We were and always will be part of the advancement of Indiana’s culture and economy and deserve to be respected as such.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Task force starts work to tackle illegal dumping in Louisiana
description: Lax enforcement and gaps in state law are among the reasons Louisiana has not been able to curtail illegal dumping throughout the state, especially as it involves furtive waste tire disposal.
text:
A task force the Louisiana Legislature created is evaluating how the state handles illegal dumping as well as the laws created to punish violators. Old tires are chief among the items found in cities and rural areas around the state. (Getty Images stock photo)Lax enforcement and gaps in state law are among the reasons Louisiana has not been able to curtail illegal dumping throughout the state, especially as it involves furtive waste tire disposal.
A group the legislature created will make recommendations to lawmakers ahead of next year’s session to bolster enforcement and raise public awareness about the problem. State Rep. Alonzo Knox, D-New Orleans, is one of its members and authored the resolution that created the Task Force on Illegal Dumping Prevention and Enforcement.
“This is not an isolated problem,” Knox said Friday during its first meeting at the Capitol. “This is really beyond a nuisance … This is a public health issue and a public safety issue.”
Sage Michael Pellet, an organizer with Healthy Gulf, is also part of the task force. He has been active in New Orleans’ efforts to combat illegal tire dumping in the city. He noted the state’s relatively low fines do not discourage scofflaw businesses, namely used tire shops, from hauling their refuse to remote areas. Some out-of-state shops will pay haulers to bring their tires to eastern New Orleans because they know penalties and enforcement in Louisiana are minimal, he said.      
“They can afford to pay the fine and do the crime,” Pellet said.
Louisiana law includes provisions specific to illegal tire dumping, including fines up to $32,500 a day. But local law enforcement most often handles offenses as gross littering, a misdemeanor with fines that start at $900 for a first offense. 
A handful of states treat illegal dumping as a felony offense. Texas, for example, punishes the illegal commercial disposal of more than 1,000 pounds or 200 cubic feet of waste with jail time ranging from 180 days to two years in jail and fines that can reach $10,000.
In addition to Louisiana’s less stringent laws, task force members were told prosecution of littering laws is uneven in a presentation from Kevin Scott, director of LDEQ’s criminal investigation division. Some jurisdictions, such as New Orleans, pursue illegal dumping more vigorously, while other district attorneys rarely pursue cases law enforcement brings to them, he said.
Scott cited a case in Caddo Parish where his agency filed an arrest warrant for illegal tire dumping, but the statute of limitations lapsed before the case could be tried.
Task force member Susan Russell, executive director of Keep Louisiana Beautiful, suggested the task force identify more deterrents to illegal dumping that tie the acts to businesses involved. The loss of an operating license or permit might discourage the behavior, she said.   
“Right now there is no such thing, and we need to hit them in the pocketbook,” Russell said.
Scott shared data on illegal waste complaints to LDEQ showing a marked increase over the past five years. The department received 91 leads for criminal investigations in fiscal year 2021-22, compared with 458 last year. So far in 2026-27, complaints are on pace to exceed that number, Scott said.
Knox suggested the data be used to create an online portal where officials and the public could track where illegal dumping has been reported and the steps taken to address it. State officials acknowledged their existing technology didn’t allow for that option, and any upgrades were likely to come at a cost.  
Scott also pointed out the imbalance between what it costs the state to clean up illegal dumping and the penalties for violations that are most frequently enforced. According to Keep Louisiana Beautiful, it costs between $230 and $600 per ton to clean an authorized dump site with much higher amounts when hazardous materials have to be handled. 
“If you cite someone for gross littering, which is kind of the norm around the state, for someone who dumped hundreds of tires, you cut them a break because the [maximum fine] is $900, but the cost of doing proper business would exceed that,” Scott said.
Russell stressed that the task force should address funding as it considers additional measures to tackle illegal dumping.    
The state collects a fee for every tire sold in the state, ranging from $2.25 for standard sizes up to $10 for industrial and farm equipment tires. The Department of Environmental Quality places the money in an escrow account it uses to pay recyclers for each tire they repurpose. 
The state fee is separate from the recycling fee garages charge customers when they replace their tires. That money stays with the business, which typically uses the money to pay haulers to bring old tires to approved disposal sites.
In addition to tires, the task force also mentioned illegal dumping involving old appliances and mattress sets. Knox said furniture often has to be discarded after evictions and when homeless encampments are cleared in New Orleans.
Other members of the task force include representatives from the state departments of Environmental Quality, Transportation and Development, Wildlife and Fisheries, and Louisiana State Police, the Louisiana Sheriffs’ Association and New Orleans officials in charge of sanitation and pest abatement.
LDEQ Deputy Secretary Nathan McBride, who chairs the task force, said it will meet monthly through January with the goal of finalizing its recommendations to lawmakers by February. He intends to schedule meetings in different locations around the state, starting with New Orleans.
