name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: State paying $625K to settle lawsuit over Braun firing utility commission member
description: The state is paying $625,000 to settle a lawsuit in which a former member of the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission claimed he was illegally fired by Gov. Mike Braun.
text:
Andy Zay, then the chair of the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission, leads a daylong utility affordability hearing on March 24, 2026, at the IURC's downtown Indianapolis headquarters. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The state is paying $625,000 to settle a lawsuit in which a former member of the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission claimed he was illegally fired by Gov. Mike Braun.
The governor’s office announced the deal Saturday with former utility commission member Andy Zay, calling it a “mutually agreeable settlement.”
Zay argued in his suit filed Aug. 10 that Braun lacked sufficient reason to replace him on the commission and described a pattern of the governor’s office infringing on the commission’s statutory duty as an “impartial fact-finding body.” 
Braun’s attorneys had responded to Zay’s lawsuit with claims that Zay, a former state senator, had improperly spent thousands of dollars in campaign funds on gifts to commission staffers and improperly awarded bonuses to IURC employees.
Deal covers Zay’s salary and legal costs
Neither side admitted any wrongdoing under the settlement terms that were released by the governor’s office.
“This Agreement does not constitute an admission by any Party that any of them have violated any law, and each specifically denies having done so,” the terms said.
The settlement includes $485,000 in payments to Zay that were described as “the reasonable net present value of the remaining salary and benefits if Zay had served through March 31, 2030.”
That date is when Zay’s term as one of the five IURC commissioners was to expire.
IURC head, governor talk Zay firing and AES hike reconsideration

The remaining $140,000 will be paid to Zay and the Indianapolis law firm Betz + Blevins to cover his legal expenses. The law firm Kroger, Gardis & Regas was representing the governor’s office in the case.
Braun announced in December he was appointing Zay as the new chair of the commission that determines what residents and businesses in most of the state pay for electricity, natural gas, water and other utility services.
Zay, a Republican from Huntington, resigned from the state Senate seat he had held since 2016 on Jan. 8 and began work at the IURC on Jan. 12.
But Braun demoted Zay from the chair position in June, days after he was part of a 3-1 commission majority that  approved a contentious $71 million rate hike for AES Indiana electricity customers.
Braun denounced that rate hike and said “affordability is my top priority” in announcing he was removing Zay as commission chair.
The governor went further on Aug. 3 in firing Zay from the commission entirely. Braun soon replaced him with former Indianapolis City-County Councilor Joshua Bain.
The Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor and Citizens Action Coalition have asked the commission to reconsider the AES rate increase decision.
Braun, Zay amicable in statements
Zay said in a statement released by the governor’s office that he was proud of his work with the IURC “balancing the affordability of services needed by all citizens …  against the costs for maintaining and supplying those services.”
“I am disappointed that I will no longer be directly involved in this important work, but I believe resolution with the State is in everyone’s best interest at this time,” Zay’s statement said. “I appreciate Governor Braun’s willingness to reach satisfactory terms so that we can all move forward in a positive direction.”
Gov. Mike Braun speaks with reporters on July 15, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Zay’s lawsuit described meetings and phone calls involving Braun and top administration officials seeking to discuss the AES rate case. Zay claimed those crossed into banned “ex parte” communications — seeking to sway a decision-maker in a case without the other parties to the case present.
A Marion County judge had scheduled a court hearing for Thursday on Zay’s request for an order reinstating him to the commission.
Braun said in the governor’s office statement that he was pleased with the resolution.
“This agreement allows all involved to move forward constructively in the best interest of Hoosiers,” Braun said. “I want to recognize Andy for his service to the state. Public service is demanding work, and I appreciate his contributions over the course of a decade on behalf of Hoosiers.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Ag secretary candidate Chris Jones touts systemic changes to Iowa agriculture
description: The Democratic candidate for Iowa secretary of agriculture told Iowa State Fair attendees Saturday that “the outrage has finally arrived” for the state of Iowa’s water, and said systemic change rather than incremental fixes is the way to clear up waterways and improve other areas of Iowans’ lives. Chris Jones criticized “Band-Aid approaches” to fixing […]
text:
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture candidate Chris Jones speaks to Iowa State Fair attendees on Aug. 22, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Democratic candidate for Iowa secretary of agriculture told Iowa State Fair attendees Saturday that “the outrage has finally arrived” for the state of Iowa’s water, and said systemic change rather than incremental fixes is the way to clear up waterways and improve other areas of Iowans’ lives.
Chris Jones criticized “Band-Aid approaches” to fixing Iowa’s environment and rural economy during his Des Moines Register Political Soapbox speech, including President Donald Trump’s decision to import more ground beef and infusions of money by the state into initiatives that haven’t fixed things.
Jones joined Iowa cattle farmers in expressing disappointment at Trump’s Friday announcement that he is suspending tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of imported ground beef, saying the move isn’t helpful to farmers in and outside of Iowa.
“High demand creates better profitability for cattle production, so why is the president, you know, kicking farmers in the gut with this 660 million pounds of hamburger that’s only going to be around for 90 days,” Jones said.
Jones is running against incumbent Republican Mike Naig, who spoke on the soapbox Aug. 17.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Iowa has been taking an incremental approach to trying to fix Iowa’s water quality and other problems, Jones said, like encouraging voluntary adoption of conservation policies and spending $1 million at a time in different areas of “the corn-soy system and the CAFO system,” and these efforts have not worked.
The “most important thing” Jones said he shares with people about creating a more resilient and thriving agriculture industry in Iowa, as well as Iowa’s water quality, is to diversify farm operations. Some have told Jones this practice would send Iowa agriculture backward, to which he responded that going forward the way things are “looks pretty bad” to him.
Farmers need to grow more than just corn and soybeans but expand into fruits and vegetables, Jones said, as well as create more pastures for cattle in order to rebuild Iowa’s cattle industry. These practices would help with sustainability as well as diversify the agriculture economy in the state, he said.
“We need systematic change in this farming system if we’re going to get the environmental outcomes that we want,” Jones said. “At the same time, we need to do that in a way that preserves farmer incomes, preserves their livelihoods, preserves their way of life, but also help(s) us.”
“Common sense regulations” on concentrated animal feeding operations and corn and soy production would help clean up Iowa waterways, Jones said, alongside taxpayer-supported off ramps to help farmers transition into better practices.
Jones said he also wants to support small-scale livestock production as well as in-state meat and grain processing to keep those economic benefits in Iowa rather than sending them to another state. If Iowans diversify their crops and begin growing more fruits and vegetables, Jones added that Iowa could grow its own food for its own residents rather than import the majority of what Iowans eat. He said he would commit $10 million annually to growing food in Iowa for Iowans to eat.
Diversifying crops comes with additional labor needs, Jones said, and farmers would need “certainty on labor” if they were to make this kind of transition. He said the “big effort to send people back to their home countries” from the federal government is harming the potential workforce in this area.
“These are people that could help repopulate rural Iowa, they can provide labor for fruit and vegetable farmers. They want to do these jobs, right? A lot of these people that come from other countries, they have agricultural backgrounds,” Jones said. “This is the work that they want to do, and so we need policy that’s going to make labor available to these sorts of farmers.”
Jones said he’d like to see practices like fall tillage and fall anhydrous ammonia application reduced or done away with through restrictions or taxes on the practices, as they aren’t necessary and can cause problems like increased soil erosion and nutrient loss.
Another topic impacting Iowa’s water and land is data centers, which Jones responded to an audience question about by saying he wants to see at least a one-year moratorium on data center construction in the state.
Iowa land should be used for its “highest use,” he said, which he identified as growing food. He said restoring small livestock production and meat processing in rural Iowa would be a better way to bring in jobs than building data centers.
“If we want more farmers, if we want more young farmers, if we want these vegetable crops and these other diverse crops, if we want cattle on pasture, we can’t have data centers, you know, gobbling up all this land,” Jones said.

title: Libertarian Jacob Heard committed to fight for party’s ballot access
description: The Libertarian Party’s new nominee for the 3rd Congressional District race in Iowa gave two reasons to Iowa State Fair attendees for why he shouldn’t have the chance to speak with them on the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox stage. The first was that Marco Battaglia, the initial Libertarian candidate in the congressional race, was […]
text:
Iowa 3rd Congressional District candidate Jacob Heard speaks to Iowa State Fair attendees on Aug. 22, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Libertarian Party’s new nominee for the 3rd Congressional District race in Iowa gave two reasons to Iowa State Fair attendees for why he shouldn’t have the chance to speak with them on the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox stage.
The first was that Marco Battaglia, the initial Libertarian candidate in the congressional race, was supposed to be up there but didn’t qualify to be placed on the election ballot, as ruled by the State Objections Panel and upheld by a Polk County District Court judge. The second was that Heard himself has not been deemed qualified to run, either.
“The Libertarian State Committee voted about two weeks ago to replace Marco, as well as Nick Gluba and Jules Cutler for the governor and lieutenant governor seats,” Heard said. “When we turned in our nomination papers this last Monday, two days later, the Secretary of State’s Office said that the proper procedure wasn’t filed with their office in time, and therefore he’s not accepting … my candidacy as well as the governor and lieutenant governor’s candidacy to appear on the Nov. 3 general election ballot.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Like Libertarian gubernatorial candidate Nicholas Gluba said after his own soapbox speech, Heard told reporters he is confident the “petition for writ of mandamus” filed by the candidates will force Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate to allow their names to be placed on election ballots. He believes the Secretary of State’s Office is using a “novel interpretation” of Iowa code detailing processes for non-party political organizations to fill vacancies in candidacies.
A ruling on the petition is expected to come on Aug. 27, Heard said. If the case goes up to the Iowa Supreme Court, Heard will argue for the Libertarians.
Heard focused his speech to fairgoers on the risks he sees to having a two-party system in Iowa, but told reporters he’s focusing on constitutional amendments in this campaign “that will try to fix Congress.”
These amendments would include requirements for single-subject bills rather than omnibus bills like those seen at the federal level, repealing the 18th Amendment relating to the direct election of senators and adding an amendment to “force Congress to spend within their means.”
“Congress is, in my opinion, our most dysfunctional branch of government, both federal and state level,” Heard said.
Pulling back the War Powers Resolution to limit presidential powers in engaging in acts of war without congressional authority are other priorities Heard shared.
In his time working as a legislative analyst for Iowa Senate Republicans and as chief of staff to then-Iowa Senate President Jake Chapman, Heard said he learned that Iowa Republicans and Democrats agree on one thing — they will remain the only two political parties in Iowa if they can help it. This was clear in 2024 when Libertarian candidates were taken off ballots, he said, and it’s clear now.
Two-party systems like the one in Iowa cause problems whether the parties have split control over state government or if one has the majority, he said, like nothing getting done if a policy issue keeps the parties at odds or the pendulum effect of the majority party passing its preferred policies then policies swinging the other way when control shifts.
In Iowa’s current case of Republicans being in charge of state government, Heard said the checks that are supposed to be in place go away “because that party isn’t going to want to embarrass or reduce the power of their governor, so to speak.” An example of this he said was during the COVID-19 pandemic when Gov. Kim Reynolds passed executive orders banning certain gatherings.
Iowans are also given a “false choice” at the ballot box that makes them believe they’re wasting their vote if they cast their ballot for a Libertarian or other non-major party candidate, he said.
“Every Iowan can have a good idea, have a good policy solution, but when you limit it to just Democrats and Republicans, it gives you a false choice and a false idea or premise that there’s only two solutions,” Heard said.

title: Auditor candidate Taylor Wettach says he’ll work to reverse law limiting audits
description: The Democratic candidate for state auditor told Iowa State Fair attendees Saturday he wants to build on the good work Rob Sand has completed in the office — hopefully with Sand as a partner in the governor’s office. Taylor Wettach spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox to detail his bid for the state […]
text:
Taylor Wettach spoke to Iowa State Fair attendees and reporters during the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox on Aug. 22, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Democratic candidate for state auditor told Iowa State Fair attendees Saturday he wants to build on the good work Rob Sand has completed in the office — hopefully with Sand as a partner in the governor’s office.
Taylor Wettach spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox to detail his bid for the state regulatory position, saying his career as a lawyer will aid him in holding people and institutions accountable even with limitations that have been placed on the auditor’s office.
“I have experience and understanding to look into those financials, and then as a lawyer, I have experience and understanding to make sure that where there are problems that we do find, we can do something about it,” Wettach said. “So I’m excited to take that background and leverage it.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Saturday is the final day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair.  Here’s the schedule.
Republican U.S. Senate candidate: Ashley Hinson
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate: Thomas Laehn
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic gubernatorial candidate: Rob Sand
Libertarian gubernatorial candidate: Nicholas Gluba
Republican secretary of agriculture candidate: Mike Naig
Democratic attorney general candidate:  Nate Willems
Republican attorney general candidate: Brenna Bird
Democratic secretary of state candidate: Ryan Peterman
Republican secretary of state candidate: Paul Pate
Democratic state treasurer candidate: John Norwood
Independent 1st Congressional District candidate: Michael Bridgford
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate: Joe Mitchell
Democratic 2nd Congressional District candidate: Lindsay James
Independent 2nd District Congressional District candidate:  Dave Bushaw
Libertarian 2nd District Congressional candidate: Rick Stewart
Republican 3rd Congressional District candidate: Zach Nunn
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott
Republican 4th Congressional District candidate:  Chris McGowan


In his work as an attorney, Wettach said he’s negotiated complex financial matters involving millions of dollars and “working with some of the best auditors in the country.” He told fairgoers he resigned from Simpson Thacher & Bartlett LLP, his former firm, in protest of pressure on the firm from President Donald Trump’s administration “to cut a deal to do $125 million worth of free work in support of their priorities.”
The state auditor’s office is supposed to be an “independent watchdog” in service of Iowans and their tax dollars, Wettach said, a role he added Sand has filled successfully despite efforts from the state to restrict access the office has to information. The Iowa Legislature in 2023 passed a bill, later signed into law by Gov. Kim Reynolds, that limits the auditor’s office’s ability to access personal information when investigating matters.
Lt. Gov. Chris Cournoyer, Wettach’s Republican opponent in the state auditor race, did not participate in the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox.
One of Wettach’s focuses will be trying to get rid of that law, he said, as well as continuing Sand’s work, including the operation of the Public Innovation Efficiencies program and maintaining the office’s independence.
“With the school voucher program, Rob was still able to pursue an audit of what was going on there,” Wettach said. “Now, did he get all the information he needed to do it in a really fulsome way? No, he didn’t. But he was able to dig in, look at the challenges, and put that forward. So, I think it’s important to note that while we talk about threats to that office in that sort of way, this office can continue to do a lot of good.”
In response to an audience question about the first thing he’ll focus on if he is elected to the auditor position, Wettach said he would turn the office’s eye once again to Education Savings Accounts for non-public schools. He also wants to further expand support from the auditor’s office to rural areas in order to provide resources and services for local citizens trying to fight corruption.
“It’s kind of like primary care versus, you know, expensive treatment … when you already are sick, right,” Wettach said. “If you can provide more support up front for these areas, we’re not going to have all the pain of playing whack-a-mole in the back end, trying to find the problems and fix things when they are already problems.”
If Sand is elected as governor alongside Wettach as auditor, Wettach said he hopes to have a partner in Sand as someone who understands the work of the office and Wettach’s drive to combat fraud, abuse and misuse of Iowa tax funds. However, if Republican Zach Lahn wins the seat rather than Sand, Wettach said that doesn’t mean the auditor’s office won’t be able to get anything done.
It will still be just as important to serve the state as an independent watchdog, he said, and to reverse the law that has somewhat tied the auditor’s hands.
“It shouldn’t matter if the governor is a Democrat or if the governor is a Republican, if I’m elected, I’m going to work to undo that law because that’s how it’s supposed to be done,” Wettach said. “Because the folks in that office deserve to be able to get the information they need to fight for the taxpayer, and that doesn’t matter who’s in charge.”

title: DeBoyer officially wins LG nomination as Michigan Republicans focus on leadership change in Lansing
description: MT. PLEASANT – Republicans gathered for their nominating convention on Saturday with a focus on changing Michigan after eight years of Democratic leadership in Lansing and 25 years of Democratic representation for Michigan in the U.S. Senate, as delegates voted in the party’s slate of statewide candidates for lieutenant governor, attorney general, secretary[...]
text:
The top of the Republican ticket for the November general election: Gubernatorial nominee John James, lieutenant governor nominee Jay DeBoyer and U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers at the Michigan Republican Party nominating convention in Mt. Pleasant. Aug. 22, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. MT. PLEASANT – Republicans gathered for their nominating convention on Saturday with a focus on changing Michigan after eight years of Democratic leadership in Lansing and 25 years of Democratic representation for Michigan in the U.S. Senate, as delegates voted in the party’s slate of statewide candidates for lieutenant governor, attorney general, secretary of state, state supreme court, state board of education and the boards for three state universities.
“For eight years, Democrats have run the governor’s office in Lansing, and look at the results,” gubernatorial nominee U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) said. “We’re 46th in the nation. Schools are failing. Energy bills are crushing families. Young people are leaving. Eight years of broken promises. Michigan is in decline. Our house is on fire.”
State Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay), who James named as his running mate earlier in August, was officially named the party’s nominee for lieutenant governor. In his speech to the convention, he emphasized his background chairing the state House Oversight Committee and issuing subpoenas to Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor. 
“I will not run scared, and I will fight on a daily basis for the conservative principles that we so dearly stand for,” DeBoyer said. “And I’m going to tell you right now, conservatism is back.”
Republican lieutenant governor nominee Jay DeBoyer at the Michigan Republican Party nominating convention in Mt. Pleasant. Aug. 22, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Candidates and party leadership repeatedly attacked their Democratic counterparts as socialists. U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers told the crowd, “We have a state to save,” after calling his Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed a “con man” and an ideological extremist who wants to “abolish ICE, abolish voter ID, abolish gas-powered cars.” 
While El-Sayed has campaigned openly to abolish Immigrations and Customs Enforcement, he has not said he wants to abolish voter ID, instead saying he opposes “mandatory Voter ID laws like the ‘SAVE Act’ that impose unnecessary barriers to citizens voting.” As for Rogers’ claim about gas-powered vehicles, El-Sayed has supported a transition to clean energy and electric vehicles but has denied he wants to ban gas-powered vehicles.
None of the nominations put forward by the party were challenged, so all positions were uncontested at the convention — a fact that party pundits said was helped by the choice of DeBoyer as a running mate for James. 
Michigan Republican Party Chairman Sen. Jim Runestad said of the unity within the party behind DeBoyer, “I tell you, this is very rare. There’s usually critics in some of these factions around the Republican Party. Everybody’s united. I can’t talk to a single person who doesn’t say that Jay is a great decision.”
One point of interest at the convention came from Paul Jacob, chair for Americans for Citizens Voting, the citizens-only voting measure that the Bureau of Elections recommended against putting on the November ballot due to a shortage of valid signatures. Jacob said that the group is challenging that decision — the Bureau of Elections said that their sample was 17 signatures short, but Jacob said the group had collected 23 affidavits affirming their valid signatures on the ballot petition.
The group has filed a response that “shows three times that many voters are on that petition who they disqualified, but they are qualified registered voters in Michigan,” and the decision on whether the measure will make the ballot will go to the Bureau of State Canvassers on Monday. 
Runestad said that there were around 1,900 attendees at the convention at the Soaring Eagle Casino and Resort in Mt. Pleasant, many waving signs reading “Take Back Michigan.”
Delegates overwhelmingly supported state Rep. Jay DeBoyer for lieutenant governor nominee in a voice vote at the Michigan Republican Party nominating convention in Mt. Pleasant. Aug. 22, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Anthony Forlini and Doug Lloyd were officially nominated for secretary of state and attorney General, respectively, after both winning the party’s endorsement at its March convention. 
Lloyd, asked by reporters after the event how he would handle his relationship with President Donald Trump — who sitting Attorney General Dana Nessel has repeatedly targeted with legal action since he took office for his second term — said that he felt it was the state attorney general’s responsibility to focus on the people of Michigan. 
“If there are positive things the attorney general can work with the federal government on, we will. But if the federal government is intruding on the citizens of Michigan, we’re going to fight it back. It’s just that simple,” he said, a departure from some Republican candidates who have said in debates that they could not identify where they might break with Trump’s policies. 
In response to questions about fundraising — given that Democratic nominees in those roles have outraised them significantly — Forlini questioned where that funding for Democrats is coming from, saying, “We’ve been working pretty hard, and we’ve had fundraisers, and our money is coming between the borders of Michigan on the east and west coast of Michigan, not the East and West coasts of this country.”
The party also nominated candidates for its other statewide positions on Saturday. To the Michigan Supreme Court, the GOP nominated Judges Michael Warren and Casandra Morse-Bills, and for the State Board of Education, Bree Moeggenberg and Terence Collins were nominated by the party. 
For state university boards, Julie Maday and state Sen. Roger Victory were nominated to run for the Michigan State University Board of Trustees, Lena Epstein and Michael Schostak for the University of Michigan Board of Regents, and Christa Murphy and Andy Anuzis for the Wayne State University Board of Governors. 
GOP Attorney General nominee Doug Lloyd and Secretary of State nominee Anthony Forlini at the Michigan Republican Party nominating convention in Mt. Pleasant. Aug. 22, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Party leaders also emphasized unity within the state Republican Party throughout the event, with Maday noting in a speech, “The Democrat coalition in the state is splintered; ours is not.”  
Runestad similarly said in an opening speech to the convention, “Our message is simple: there is a place for all of the voters in the Michigan Republican Party, and we’re going to build that party starting now for people who work hard, for parents who want better schools, for entrepreneurs who want to build, for farmers, manufacturers, veterans, police officers, firefighters, working families — all have a place in the Michigan Republican Party.”
House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township) also asked delegates to “give us a little bit of help up there in Lansing” by electing Republicans to the offices of governor, attorney general and secretary of state.  
“What we’ve done is we’ve unified the Republican Party. We unified the House Republicans, and we’ve done it by saying, look, we’re going to do the things we said we were going to do when we campaigned,” Hall said, emphasizing the importance of maintaining control of the House and taking the Senate for Republicans in November. 
DeBoyer also spoke to reporters about the platform for Republicans, should they win a trifecta in the state government. 
“It’s actually just a pretty simple common sense platform, which is we are going to make education at the top of the nation again in the state of Michigan, we are going to make law enforcement and public safety a primary thing,” he said. “We are also going to efficiently look at government, and we are going to right-size government.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Ole Miss QB Trinidad Chambliss welcomes pressure that comes with fame and aims to refine his game
description: FILE - Mississippi quarterback Trinidad Chambliss (6) throws during the second half of the Sugar Bowl NCAA college football playoff quarterfinal game against Georgia on Jan. 1, 2026, in New Orleans. (AP Photo/Matthew Hinton, File)
text:
When Mississippi quarterback Trinidad Chambliss watches the Houdini acts from last season that made him a college football sensation, there is a part of him that would rather avoid doing that again.
The ability to escape converging pass-rushers, and seemingly ad-lib his way into clutch gains on the ground or through the air, was never more evident than during the Rebels’ CFP quarterfinal victory over favored Georgia in the Sugar Bowl.
When Chambliss saw the post-game highlights, one of his first thoughts was: “That was kind of dumb in the moment. Like, if I would have gotten sacked or I would have fallen down, I’m putting myself — and I’m putting my team — in a really bad position.”
Chambliss appreciates that some of the crazy plays he pulled off during a heady first season with Ole Miss have inspired analysts to refer to him as “the face of college football” in 2026. EA Sports even considered putting Chambliss on the cover of a new edition of its popular college football video game, but decided against it because of a legal dispute with the NCAA over whether he would be eligible to play this season.
As Chambliss enters his final season, with Ole Miss ranked ninth in the preseason AP Top 25 poll, he aims to work with new offensive coordinator John David Baker on a more mature, composed and refined style of play.
Bound for the NFL?
“I’m trying to attack this year more as a pro … knowing that I’ll be draft eligible and I’ll be going to the NFL,” Chambliss said. “So, just making sure that my football IQ is increasing, leadership role is increasing, and just clean up the little details as a quarterback and as a leader on the team.”
In 2024, Chambliss played at Division II Ferris State in his native Michigan. Before that, he says he nearly quit football in favor of playing point guard for a Division III basketball program. But after leading Ferris State to a Division II national championship, he took an offer to be a projected backup at Ole Miss in 2025.
An injury to season-opening starter Austin Simmons thrust Chambliss into the spotlight, and his ability to run circles around frustrated pass-rushers while finding receivers breaking open downfield made him such a hit in Oxford, Mississippi, that fans there began flying flags of his namesake Caribbean island nation, Trinidad and Tobago.
“The Ole Miss fans, they’re very creative and it’s awesome to see,” Chambliss said.
Meanwhile, Chambliss said that while serving as a counselor at the Manning Passing Academy in Thibodaux, Louisiana, this summer, he met a Trinidad and Tobago native who told him that many in his country have become captivated by Ole Miss football in the past year.
All that attention can mean a lot of pressure for quarterback who doesn’t even have one full season as a Division I FBS starter on his resume yet.
“Pressure is a privilege. I prayed to be in this situation,” Chambliss said. “It’s what I’ve asked for. So, I’ve just got to do what I’ve been taught to do, what I’ve been doing my whole life, which is just play ball.”
This year, Chambliss could have opted to transfer to any number of programs, including perhaps LSU, where his former coach, Lane Kiffin, accepted a job right after the 2025 regular season — a decision led Ole Miss to order Kiffin out immediately and promote defensive coordinator Pete Golding as Kiffin’s successor heading into the 2025 postseason.
Leaving behind a legacy
But Chambliss wanted to the chance to capitalize on what he accomplished at Ole Miss, to honor relationships there and leave a more lasting legacy.
“If you know me, you know that I’m a very loyal person. I value relationships a lot,” Chambliss said. “There was just too much at Ole Miss and too many relationships that I couldn’t just throw away.”
While Chambliss had no prior relationship with Baker, the new coordinator had worked under Kiffin at Ole Miss before. He is familiar with the offense and asserted that whatever tweaks he makes will cater to Chambliss’ strengths.
“If Trinidad likes it, then I like it, because it’s got a great chance to work,” said Baker, who joined the program during its CFP run last December as more of an observer before officially taking over this season.
Baker said he expects Chambliss to have a supporting cast with which he can win.
Whatever happens, Chambliss will lean on the perspective he’s gained from working his way up from Division II, persevering through legal uncertainties in the offseason and navigating changes on the coaching staff — all in the span of little more than a year.
“Everyone’s journey is different,” Chambliss said. “I’m grateful for that journey — and I wouldn’t change it.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas political trailblazer Nancy Landon Kassebaum Baker dies at 94
description: A champion of bipartisanship and common sense, former U.S. Sen. Nancy Landon Kassebaum Baker, dies.
text:
Former U.S. Sen. Nancy Kassebaum of Kansas talks about her Senate career, relationship with the late U.S. Sen. Bob Dole and erosion of a commitment to bipartisanship during an appearance at the Dole Institute of Politics in Lawrence. (Photo buy Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Nancy Landon Kassebaum Baker, who fractured a political glass ceiling as the first woman to represent Kansas in the U.S. Senate, died Friday.
Kassebaum, 94, grew up in Topeka and began her personal journey in politics as a member of the Maize school board. In 1978, she defeated eight Republicans to seize the nomination for U.S. Senate in a contest to determine who took the seat held by retiring Republican U.S. Sen. James Pearson. She prevailed in that general election with 53% of the vote but easily won reelection contests in 1984 and 1990 with more than 70% of the vote.
The Kassebaum family confirmed her death in a statement reported by KSNT that noted her remarkable life and appreciation for Kansas.
“For 94 years she relished the support of family and friends from all over the world. Her years were filled with remarkable successes, challenges and above all a deep love for Kansas,” the statement said.
The family intends to conduct a private memorial service at an unspecified date. Memorial donations are to be directed to the Capper Foundation and the Kansas 4-H Foundation, the statement said.
Kassebaum, the widow of retired U.S. Sen. Howard Baker of Tennessee and the daughter of 1936 presidential nominee and Gov. Alf Landon, had the distinction of being the second woman elected to the U.S. Senate without her spouse having previously served as a member of Congress.
Kassebaum was known for her political independence, moderate sensibilities and advocacy of bipartisanship on domestic and international affairs during her 18 years in Washington, D.C.
She supported the Equal Rights Amendment, abortion rights, a ban on assault weapons and the end of apartheid in South Africa. She was among Senate champions of creating a federal holiday to honor the late Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. After leaving elective politics, she voiced objections to GOP President Donald Trump and endorsed Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly.
In 2022, she said during a program at the Dole Institute of Politics at the University of Kansas that it would have been impossible for her to win elective office in the modern era.
“I know full well I could not be reelected today,” she said. “It’s not that I’ve changed so much.”
In the Landon home, her father had been skeptical of her underdog campaign to win a cherished seat in the U.S. Senate. He understood defeat after getting crushed by President Franklin Roosevelt in 1936.
“I talked to the family about it, who all sort of rolled their eyes. My father did not want me to run. I think he thought I would lose,” Kassebaum said.
She decided to run and took note of her father’s reputation among Kansans with the campaign slogan: “A Fresh Face: A Trusted Kansas Name.”
Kassebaum said U.S. Sen. Robert Dole of Kansas, who died in 2021, assisted her campaign by convincing Republicans that she would be a capable senator for Kansas. In 2015, Dole told the Wichita Eagle that Kassebaum had been one of the most popular politicians in the state.
“Nancy has a way about her that she gets along with everyone. She has never tried to be a moderate or a conservative,” Dole said.
Kassebaum was born July 29, 1932, and grew up in Topeka. She earned a bachelor’s degree at the University of Kansas and a master’s degree in diplomatic history at the University of Michigan.
She married her first husband, John Philip Kassebaum, and they had four children — John, Linda, Richard and William. The Kassebaum’s divorced in 1979.
After deciding not to seek a fourth term but still a member of the U.S. Senate, she married Baker in 1996. The Rev. John Danforth, the former senator from Missouri, performed the ceremony. President George W. Bush appointed Baker to serve as ambassador to Japan. Baker and Kassebaum lived in Japan for four years. Baker died in 2014. She resided on a ranch in Morris County.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: It’s time for Noem to ride off into the political sunset
description: The latest addition to Pierre’s Trail of Governors stands out. It’s not because it’s the only statue of a woman. It’s not because it’s the only one accompanied by half a horse. It represents a career of political tumult. A career from which it’s unlikely there’s a chance to bounce back. Kristi Noem made a […]
text:
Former Gov. Kristi Noem speaks with attendees at the unveiling of her statue on the Trail of Governors on Aug. 7, 2026, in Pierre, South Dakota. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)The latest addition to Pierre’s Trail of Governors stands out. It’s not because it’s the only statue of a woman. It’s not because it’s the only one accompanied by half a horse. It represents a career of political tumult. A career from which it’s unlikely there’s a chance to bounce back.
Kristi Noem made a career out of overcoming adversity. Her book tour for “No Going Back” went horribly wrong from the start. She was forced to defend her decision to shoot an unruly dog and a smelly goat. She saw it as an example of her ability to make tough decisions. Others saw it as cruelty to animals.
She also had to explain how her book included a false story about her facing down North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un. Putting the blame on her ghost writer didn’t seem like an acceptable excuse. Where have all the proofreaders gone?

At an event on Aug. 7, 2026, in Pierre, former Gov. Kristi Noem and artist John Lopez get a closer look at his statue of Noem leading her horse, the latest addition to the South Dakota Trail of Governors. (Photo by Meghan O’Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)

The book was written as a way for Noem to show off her conservative bona fides to Donald Trump in hopes that he would select her to be his running mate in 2024. With her book tour fast becoming a favorite topic of late-night comedians, it was easy to write off her chances at higher office.
However, after Trump was elected to a second term, he appointed Noem as his secretary of Homeland Security. That appointment, handled the right way, could have cemented her place among 2028 Republican presidential contenders. That may have been the case if she had approached border security and immigration control with a modicum of empathy and professionalism. Instead, she chose hubris and instilled in ICE a gunslinging mentality that led to the deaths of two American citizens in Minneapolis.
In a presidential administration noted for sloughing off criticism as fake news, Noem’s antics and the level of criticism she faced were too much even for Trump. She joined a long list of Trump Cabinet secretaries who have been sent packing. In Noem’s case, when she was shown the door, a job was created for her as special envoy for the Shield of the Americas.
Maybe she’s working hard to help other countries secure their borders. Maybe the job was created so that both she and the president could save face.
At the unveiling of her statue, Noem told South Dakota Searchlight that she wasn’t ruling out a political comeback. After all, she’s undefeated when it comes to elections. “Oh, I wouldn’t take it off the table,” Noem said about running for office again. “I may someday, but you know, we ran 13 races and won them all, so campaigns don’t scare me, but I’ve got a lot of other things to do, too.”


 Listen to this episode of the Searchlight Report podcast to hear Kristi Noem’s speech at her statue unveiling and her interaction with reporters.
There was speculation this year that Noem would challenge U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds for the Republican nomination for his Senate seat. Those looking ahead to 2028 see her as a possible primary opponent for Senate Majority Leader John Thune.
Perhaps it would be best for Noem if she just went back to the farm. Any attempt to get back into South Dakota politics would be met with a crowded field.
There’s a trend in the state’s Republican politics that no office should go unchallenged. Gov. Larry Rhoden just defeated three primary challengers. Rounds faced a primary challenger, too. Marty Jackley’s record as a popular state attorney general didn’t keep him from having to fend off a Republican challenger for the nomination for the U.S. House of Representatives.
Noem ‘not planning to run’ but doesn’t rule out a political future as her statue is unveiled

These days, incumbency and name recognition aren’t enough in Republican politics to keep challengers off the ballot. Potential challengers aren’t all that Noem would be running against. There’s also an internet full of memes chronicling her strained relationships with dogs, goats and her husband.
At this point, no one in politics is going to step aside just because she was once the governor or for a brief time the Homeland Security secretary. Challengers are going to see her as damaged goods. If she runs for office again, the internet will rejoice, handing her opponents a fresh round of memes and a backlog of comic monologues.
Challengers and dog jokes aside, Noem would also be running against her record as governor, a time when she didn’t exactly cover herself in glory. She treated the National Guard like her private army, sending them to the southern border at taxpayer expense whenever it suited her political ambitions. She labeled it fake news when anyone pointed out that her pursuit of freedom during the pandemic caused South Dakota to lead the league in per capita COVID deaths. She failed to lead on property tax reform and wasted millions of dollars on a prison site that was abandoned. Unfortunately for the former governor, the list goes on.
Noem has bounced back from political adversity in the past, but there’s likely no coming back from the ridicule that’s been aimed at her from all directions and her sketchy record as governor. It’s time for her to use that half a horse to ride off into the sunset.

name: VTDigger
title: Middlebury submits state’s first CHIP application
description:
The Community & Housing Infrastructure Program is attractive to local officials because it harnesses state education fund dollars to pay down infrastructure debt.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Middlebury submits state’s first CHIP application.
text:
A rendering of townhomes at a groundbreaking event for Stonecrop Meadows, a mixed-income housing project in Middlebury, in Feb. 2025. File photo by Carly Berlin/VTDigger and Vermont Public

This story by John Flowers was first published in the Addison Independent on Aug. 20, 2026.
MIDDLEBURY — Middlebury last week became the first community to dip its toe into Vermont’s new Community & Housing Infrastructure Program. Through CHIP the town would be able to borrow money to build municipal infrastructure and pay down that debt over 20 years with tax money raised from the 74 future new homes in the Stonecrop Meadows neighborhood that would be served by that new infrastructure.
The board voted 5-0 — with selectboard member Fred Dunnington abstaining and member Farhad Khan absent — in favor of a housing infrastructure agreement with Summit Properties, the developers of Stonecrop Meadows, a new mixed-income neighborhood off Seminary Street Extension that’s eventually to include around 250 homes.
The agreement, among other things, allows Middlebury Town Manager Mark Pruhenski to submit, to the Vermont Economic Progress Council, Summit’s application to use CHIP as a tax increment financing tool to pay for infrastructure — such as roads, streetlights and sidewalks — for the next 74 homes (phase two) of Stonecrop.
Workers are currently finishing the first phase (61 units) of what’s to be the biggest residential subdivision in the county’s shire town.
Summit Chief Operating Officer Zeke Davisson and Chief Executive Officer Tom Getz have been looking for resources for Stonecrop’s phase two infrastructure. They told the selectboard at an Aug. 4 public hearing that they can’t pass along those estimated $4.4 million in costs to future Stonecrop renters and homebuyers, due to the mixed-income commitment.
The duo returned to the board Aug. 11 seeking Middlebury’s buy-in on what will be the state’s first CHIP application to help underwrite phase two’s curbed roads, water and sewer lines, sidewalks, public space and stormwater treatment.
In short, the CHIP program — administered by VEPC — allows municipalities to leverage tax increment financing from municipal property taxes and state education fund property taxes to help pay for infrastructure that enables new housing development on a single parcel or a group of contiguous parcels.
Starting in the first year in which the developer incurs debt for the housing infrastructure, Middlebury would annually remit to Summit 85% of the municipal property tax increment generated by parcels located within the Stonecrop site, according to the CHIP agreement between the town and Summit. This would occur annually for up to 20 years, or until the phase two infrastructure debt is paid off.
What makes the agreement more attractive, according to town and Summit officials, is that the CHIP program also harnesses state education fund dollars to pay down infrastructure debt. Specifically, the education tax will cover 60% of the infrastructure debt, Getz said.
The state developed CHIP as a tool to encourage more residential construction during the current housing crisis.
But while the state would cover a majority of the debt, the cost to Middlebury wouldn’t be inconsequential.
In exchange for new housing and the promise of an expanded grand list, Middlebury would be forgoing some municipal tax revenue at a time when the demand for services from new residents would be rising.
Pruhenski said town staff estimated the Stonecrop growth could add 1.5 cents to the tax rate during the early years and 2.5 cents toward the end of the potential 20-year tax increment finance period. A penny on Middlebury’s tax rate raises roughly $100,000.
Data furnished by Pruhenski shows $164,500 in potential annual service cost increases generated by the phase two Stonecrop homes, ranging from $10,000 for the library to $40,000 for road maintenance and snow removal.
Pruhenski acknowledged that calculating the cost of future municipal services is an inexact science.
“There is no tool we found to perfectly capture municipal costs. We tried to quantify them to the best of our ability,” he told board members. “The goal here was to illustrate that there is a municipal cost, so you’re going into this with eyes wide open.”
Alex Armani-Munn, executive director of Addison County Economic Development Corp., has been helping Summit and the town navigate the CHIP program. He’s seeking a consultant to perform an independent economic impact analysis that will provide the town with more information about the financial implications of CHIP.
He noted that VEPC, during its 90-day review of the Stonecrop application, will also take a deep dive into the cost variables.
Dunnington, the selectboard member who abstained, asked Davisson how Summit would proceed if the board said no to its CHIP request.
“We wouldn’t build as many houses,” he replied.
Dunnington voiced concern about the potential CHIP impact on municipal property taxpayers, particularly those who are struggling.
He also asked about the impact of potential future CHIP requests — such as one that will soon be submitted for the Middle Housing project.
“If other (developers) come along and ask, how would we say ‘no’ to them?” he asked.
“I don’t think it sets a precedent that if we say ‘yes’ to one, that we’re going to say ‘yes’ to every single one,” selectboard member Isabel Gogardy replied.
Selectboard member Dan Brown agreed.
“We can say ‘no’ to whoever we want. But the choice here is if we don’t do this, we don’t build houses, we don’t increase the grand list, and we don’t see anything with future taxes. And then we’re still in a housing crisis,” he said.
Selectboard Chair Andy Hooper argued that the tax increment financing provision of CHIP is analogous to Middlebury’s current capital improvements process: The town each year prioritizes road, culvert and sidewalk work in various neighborhoods using money provided by all municipal taxpayers.
“In this case, the (Stonecrop) residents haven’t arrived yet,” he said.
The selectboard on Aug. 11 seemed prepared to endorse the Stonecrop CHIP application and then plug in a specific tax increment financing cap for the phase two infrastructure later — after the upcoming study on its economic impacts. But Davisson and Getz persuaded the board to approve a not-to-exceed number of $4 million. Having a specific number provides predictability in a housing industry that has seen its share of upheaval recently, they said.
That $4 million number — and other provisions of the agreement — could change during VEPC’s upcoming review of the CHIP application.
“This is just the next step in a process,” Armani-Munn said.
