name: Washington State Standard
title: Striking workers will need to seek jobs to qualify for WA unemployment benefits
description: Pressed by the federal government, Washington is making a big change in its new law extending unemployment benefits to striking union workers. Starting Sunday, workers involved in labor disputes must comply with the state’s rigorous job search requirements to receive benefits. This means actively seeking work and recording efforts to find another job. Since[...]
text:
Workers at Hilton’s Embassy Suites in Seattle’s Pioneer Square neighborhood went on strike in June. Some could be affected by a rule change concerning striking workers who seek unemployment benefits. (Photo courtesy of UNITE HERE Local 8)Pressed by the federal government, Washington is making a big change in its new law extending unemployment benefits to striking union workers.
Starting Sunday, workers involved in labor disputes must comply with the state’s rigorous job search requirements to receive benefits. This means actively seeking work and recording efforts to find another job.
Since Jan. 1, when the law took effect, Washington’s Employment Security Department waived that requirement because it deemed those involved in labor disputes to be “attached to an employer.”
But this week the U.S Department of Labor told the state agency that this approach does not conform with federal law. 
Federal officials said the state’s employer-attached waiver “does not apply in the case of a strike because the employer did not initiate the separation,” Chris Barron, communications director for the Employment Security Department, said Friday.
“While we cannot provide specifics about the number of current claimants, this only impacts a handful,” he added. Barron said the agency is reaching out to those individuals to inform them about the job search requirements.
This requirement will apply to all new claims during a strike. It will not impact previous claims.
The agency filed an emergency rule Friday and will conduct a formal process to adopt a permanent rule change.
The news is not a total surprise. The state and federal agencies have discussed the law throughout its development and passage. These conversations span the past presidential administration of Democrat Joe Biden and the current one under Republican Donald Trump. 
Earlier this year, the Department of Labor issued a “questions and answers” document spelling out its position on state laws that provide unemployment benefits for striking workers.
Stephanie Sams, the state agency’s government relations director, informed members of the House Labor and Workplace Standards and the Senate Labor and Commerce committees of the change on Tuesday. 
“It is good news,” said Rep. Suzanne Schmidt, R-Spokane Valley, the lead Republican on the House labor committee. As a policy matter, it assures all individuals follow the same rules in order to receive unemployment benefits, she said. 
Schmidt also pointed to talks between Boeing and its professional engineers union, who voted Friday to reject the company’s contract offer. Barring a deal in the coming weeks, roughly 16,000 workers could go on strike Oct. 7 and be eligible for benefits not long after.
“This might weigh into whether or not the union ends up negotiating in the next month,” she said. “Workers will know if they do strike, they will not be eligible for benefits if they are not seeking another job.”
April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, one of the forces behind the legislation, had a different view.
“It is a concern. We are still assessing the on-the-ground impact it might have,” she said. “I don’t think this rule change will stop workers from exercising their power to go on strike.”
‘Actively seeking suitable work’
Unemployment insurance is available in Washington to those who have lost their job through no fault of their own. For example, it applies for those who are laid off or fired, or who quit for certain reasons. Other circumstances include a temporary layoff or furlough or an injury.
In 2025, Democrats overrode Republican opposition to pass the law expanding the benefits to union workers who are on strike or locked out by their employer.
It marked a major win for Democrats and their labor allies who view the benefits as a backstop for rent and food when striking workers are not getting a paycheck. Critics argued the availability of benefits would incentivize striking and squeeze businesses.
Through Aug. 5, the Employment Security Department made payments to 151 people, totaling 741 weeks of pay and $565,714.
Workers on strike can receive up to six weeks of benefits. Unemployment is available following the second Sunday after a strike begins, plus a one-week waiting period. Typical unemployment insurance is offered for up to 26 weeks. The six weeks for striking workers was the result of negotiations between House and Senate Democrats.
A person seeking unemployment benefits must show they are available and actively seeking suitable work. For each week they submit a claim, the person must complete three job search activities and keep a record of their efforts. They also must be signed up with a WorkSource employment center in the state, or an equivalent if they live in another state.
Striking workers will be subject to those conditions starting Sunday. It is recommended that they log their efforts. The agency does reviews and might deny benefits if a log is missing or not complete, or the person is viewed as not making a genuine attempt to find a job.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: After 20 years of failure, a risky mining plan doesn’t deserve the benefits of its past permits
description: In the legal fights over the federal government’s ruthless immigration crackdown, defense lawyers have recently enjoyed a great deal of success with a novel argument: Because of a well-established pattern of dishonesty and deceit in their filings, federal prosecutors should no longer enjoy the “presumption of regularity” — the notion that public officials ar[...]
text:
(Drone photo by Rob Levine/Minnesota Reformer)In the legal fights over the federal government’s ruthless immigration crackdown, defense lawyers have recently enjoyed a great deal of success with a novel argument: Because of a well-established pattern of dishonesty and deceit in their filings, federal prosecutors should no longer enjoy the “presumption of regularity” — the notion that public officials are presumed to act honestly and in good faith.
The simple logic: A conversation with a well known prevaricator is fundamentally different from a conversation with a person who has a track record of honesty. The first instance calls for maximum skepticism, not good will.
This principle comes to mind reading a press release from a company called NewRange Copper Nickel — formerly known as PolyMet — as it touts a set of “project enhancements” for its long stalled copper-nickel mine near the northeastern Minnesota city of Babbitt. The announcement makes many nice-sounding promises about plans for the state’s first copper-nickel mine, including its goal of “reducing environmental impact.”
To anyone who has followed the NorthMet saga as it has wound its way through the courts for the past eight years, this triggers a warning light. The glacial progress of this project is not a consequence of regulatory overreach or delay; it is the inevitable outcome of shoddy geological, engineering and legal work.
NewRange wants to kickstart its ill-conceived plan without doing the work that it demands. The company says the project holds “21 of 24 permits required to begin NorthMet operations.” Sounds good, right? Except that those three missing permits happen to be the most crucial, including the overarching permit to mine. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources approved the permit to mine in 2018, but it was reversed by the Minnesota Court of Appeals in 2020. That decision was affirmed by the Minnesota Supreme Court in 2021.
In press announcements touting the revived proposal, neither New Range nor the DNR mentioned the status of the permit to mine. The company’s message is that the proposed mine meets all of Minnesota’s “tough” mining standards.
Among the many problems with the proposed NorthMet project, however: The plan for the storage of the tailings — the waste left over from processing, which is 99.7% of everything to be mined from the low-grade ore. Though NewRange hasn’t yet applied for amendments to its permit to mine, the company now says it won’t store the waste in an existing tailings pond on site. That was the plan for the past 20 years, despite compelling arguments that leakage from the pond would pollute nearby surface waters. 
Under state law governing reactive mine waste, mining companies are obligated to develop a mine closure plan that ensures the safe storage of mine waste. For good reason: If mining waste spills into public waters, a chemical reaction ensues that creates a toxic slurry filled with heavy metals and neurotoxins. NorthMet would be the first test of these so-called “sulfide” mining rules.
At every turn NewRange’s plan to satisfy this law was filled with dubious claims. For example, the previous plan had been  to store the tailings in a man-made basin whose design was suspect, that was built to leak, and whose underlying geology was unexplored.
Tony Runkel, lead geologist with the Minnesota Geological Survey and an expert on how groundwater flows through bedrock, submitted comments on the DNR’s 2,169 page PolyMet supplemental draft environmental impact statement, noting that “well-known techniques” were not applied in the hydrogeologic studies at the mine site and tailings basin area. 
In his comments on the final Environmental Impact Statement from 2015, Runkel concluded that a clearer picture of the bedrock could have been achieved by “…including information derived from a number of well-established, common practice techniques that provide greater insight into [water] transport through fractured bedrock.” In other words, they didn’t do the basic work. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The most preposterous part of New Range’s plan to address mine waste? It wanted to spread bentonite — basically, the clumping agent in cat litter — into the tailings pond, under the premise that this would forever prevent water from contacting the toxic tailings.
That was too much for the Minnesota Supreme Court, which ordered a hearing on the plan in 2021. Despite relentless advocacy from the DNR and NewRange, Administrative Law Judge James E. LaFave ruled that it would not work. NewRange’s own engineer testified that 298 million gallons of water would traverse the tailings every year.
MPCA was ‘arbitrary and capricious’ in granting PolyMet permit, Supreme Court rules

This was not the only problematic aspect of NewRange’s plans. The water pollution permit issued by the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency was invalidated first by the appeals court and then the Supreme Court in 2023, which “rebuked the MPCA for its irregular procedures and ‘arbitrary and capricious’ decisionmaking in issuing the permit.”
The Wetlands Destruction Permit, granted to PolyMet in 2019 by the Army Corps of Engineers, also fell apart under scrutiny because the company violated the Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa’s water quality rights and standards.
Last year the main engineering firm contracted by NewRange split with the company. A few months ago the outside law firm defending the permit to mine in court abruptly withdrew. Neither development was mentioned publicly but it’s hardly a wild inference to read these as signs of a troubled project.
The project also has new owners and operators, and, most importantly, a lawyer representing the company informed the DNR last month of an entirely new plan to store the mine tailings, following years of inaction in the face of a Supreme Court ruling calling for a contested case hearing on the bentonite — kitty litter — reclamation technique, needed to satisfy the DNR’s reactive waste rule. 
To date, NewRange has never modeled for climate change risks, such as the 500-year flood that deluged nearby Duluth in 2012, or the 200-year rainstorm event in 2024 that caused major damage to the tailings basin. The latter required emergency remediation.
In their new proposal NewRange said it will change the way it mines the ore, the way it processes the ore, the way it will transport the ore, and the way it stores the waste tailings. 
At what point does the DNR think that NewRange should start over with an entirely new environmental impact statement, rather than just tweaks to the existing one, even though the project is hardly recognizable from the previous plan? NewRange and the DNR are thinking they can change nearly everything about the proposal yet still retain permits that are already deeply flawed or non-existent. Even Microsoft makes you get a new Windows license if you replace too many parts on your PC.
The DNR and NewRange say “trust us.” But virtually everything they’ve done in this 20-year project screams neither are trustworthy. They want us to forget the history of this project and avoid the public scrutiny, transparency and costs that would be part of a brand new process.
At this point the responsible thing to do is start over. This time the DNR should force NewRange to follow the rules.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Congratulations, Gov. Gianforte: We’re leading the nation
description: Please join me in congratulating Gov. Greg Gianforte. Under his leadership, Montana is leading the nation. In what?  Guess. No.  Not education. Republicans still won’t fund pre-K.  Our students’ reading and math scores are closer to the bottom than the top of the nation. Ok.  I’ll tell you. Prison rape. Sadly. I’m not making this up. Montana leads the […]
text:
President Joe Biden on Thursday, Dec. 12, 2024, commuted the sentences of roughly 1,500 people and granted pardons for 39 individuals with convictions for nonviolent crimes. (Photo by Caspar Benson/Getty Images)Please join me in congratulating Gov. Greg Gianforte. Under his leadership, Montana is leading the nation.
In what?  Guess.
No.  Not education.
Republicans still won’t fund pre-K.  Our students’ reading and math scores are closer to the bottom than the top of the nation.
Ok.  I’ll tell you.
Prison rape.
Sadly.
I’m not making this up.
Montana leads the nation in reported sexual assaults at the men’s prison in Deer Lodge. We lead in two categories. Inmate-on-inmate sexual assault allegations (62) and staff-on-inmate sexual assault allegations (11). Yes. Staff. The people we pay to keep inmates safe.
There is actually a federal law, called “PREA,” the Prison Rape Elimination Act of 2003. President George W. Bush signed it. President Barack Obama strengthened its implementation.
Under PREA, the federal government investigated. It surveyed inmates, interviewed inmates and staff in Deer Lodge and then  wrote a 130-page report.
One hundred thirty pages, single-spaced, just on sexual assaults at the prison in Deer Lodge.
The rate of sexual victimization across the nation in prisons is 4.1%.  But, not in Montana. The rate of sexual victimization in Montana – 13.4%,  more than three times the national average. Staff-on-inmate victimization was 7.5%.  Translated: Nearly one in seven men in our prison will be sexually victimized each year. These are estimates based upon reports, surveys, and interviews. Still shocking.
This is serious. Insidious. Rape. Sexual assault.  In prison. By staff –an egregious abuse of power and authority. It is a moral failure. A betrayal of public trust.
This is not something I wanted to write about. It is beyond my education, my experience and  my knowledge.  I write because a Montana prisoner told me about frequent rapes. Men raped while corrections officers watched Netflix or slept.
I don’t know if the allegations are true, but we need to find out. We cannot be silent when there are allegations of rape and abuse.
Gianforte didn’t create this problem. He inherited it. It’s not political. It’s historic. Sexual abuse in prison has been a problem for a long time.
Gianforte is the one person who can make a difference.  He has the power, authority, and ability to lead.  To create change.
Here’s my plea to Gianforte:

Own The Issue.  Lead. Make this a priority. Make PREA compliance an executive-level priority in your office.  Not the Department of Corrections. Your office.


Speak Up. Hold a press conference. Issue a press release. Make it clear that the State of Montana will not tolerate sexual abuse in prison. Not by inmates. Not by staff. Not by anyone.


Meet and Listen. Show up. Meet with inmates. Hear their stories. Your presence will send an historic message. Find out the truth. Lead by walking through the prison door.


Enhance Reporting. Create new mechanisms for inmates to confidentially report abuse outside of the chain of command in the prison.


Transparency. Publicly report meaningful PREA data, more often than annually. Put sunlight on the problems; make them visible. Invite legislators, state employees, advocates, and the public to help fix this. Let’s solve this together. It’s a Montana problem. You lead. We will follow.

The next time you are at one of Gianforte’s town halls, ask him what he is doing to eliminate rape and sexual assault in our prisons.
Oops, I forgot.  Republicans don’t have town halls anymore. Or solutions, for that matter.
But maybe. Just maybe, this time will be different. Gianforte could be a hero. Could this be his legacy?Gianforte can make Montana better by eliminating sexual victimization in prison.  The only question is: Will he?
I hope he does.  It would be a great legacy.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: USDA wants to revive the cotton industry. Experts aren’t sure that’s possible.
description: A denim-clad rancher poses on horseback, crimson-red shirt against a hazy blue sky. A farmer in a T-shirt stands surrounded by his crop, leaves bending toward weathered hands. “Real Americans wear cotton,” reads bold text over a photo of a sprawling white field. This Americana-laden imagery came in an X post from Agriculture Secretary Brooke […]
text:
(illustration by Caspar Dowdy/Investigate Midwest)
A denim-clad rancher poses on horseback, crimson-red shirt against a hazy blue sky. A farmer in a T-shirt stands surrounded by his crop, leaves bending toward weathered hands. “Real Americans wear cotton,” reads bold text over a photo of a sprawling white field.
This Americana-laden imagery came in an X post from Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, uploaded in late May. The post — and its subsequent reply by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. — accompanied the release of the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s “Great American Cotton Plan,” an initiative with sweeping promises of reviving American cotton production and bringing textile manufacturing jobs back to the U.S.
Over the past half-century, many American clothing companies have moved their factories to China, Indonesia and Bangladesh, decreasing the need for domestic cotton production. Climate change has depleted southern soils and contributed to the nation’s reduction in the cotton sector, moving the U.S. behind Brazil in 2023 as the world’s largest cotton supplier.
The USDA’s new cotton plan hopes to rebuild the industry, primarily by strengthening crop insurance for cotton and increasing direct funding toward American mills.
Rollins’ announcement comes as major voices of the nation’s health and agriculture policy — lawmakers, farmers, researchers and a new wave of online activists — have set their sights on the fabrics we wear and the plant it often comes from.
The political turmoil surrounding today’s textile industry marks a modern chapter in the complex, often painful and historically fraught, legacy of cotton in America. The battle has played out in a distinctly modern setting: in social media disagreements of a health-conscious electorate, weighing the presumed peril of microplastics with the fear surrounding agrochemicals.
But after decades of disappearing cotton acres and textile jobs, some are skeptical that renewed attention is enough to slow the industry’s decline. Some farmers, frustrated by the impact of retaliatory tariffs, say the plan does little to counter the fallout  from other policies under President Trump’s administration.


“Look at any shirt, anything with cotton is made overseas,” said Jonathan Coppess, an associate professor of agricultural policy at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. “And so you’d have to reverse that in some form or fashion, which paying farmers isn’t going to do.”
As the USDA faces mounting pressure from industry groups and internet forums, the plan represents a search for a strategy that will unseat polyester from the majority of America’s closets — and reclaim the nation’s former place as the world’s top provider of cotton.
In the process, cotton has taken on a new meaning in American politics — the waning industry swept up into the center of long-standing debates about both domestic manufacturing and public health.
“It [cotton] doesn’t occupy the same place in the American imagination,” said Trevon Logan, a professor of economics at The Ohio State University. “But it didn’t go away.”



cotton-plan 


 
Generational decline
For more than a thousand years, demand for cotton fabrics from India influenced trade, and later colonization, throughout Eurasia. But as Europeans arrived in North America, they encountered a species of cotton with longer fibers, making for better textiles. After the invention of the cotton gin made it easier to turn the plant’s sticky seeds into workable fiber, Gossypium hirsutum became America’s greatest driver of economic growth, and of the burgeoning system of slavery.
“More than any other commodity,” writes author Thor Hanson in his book “The Triumph of Seeds,” “it gave the young American nation wealth, clout and international prestige.”
By the mid-1800s, the American South was the source of two-thirds of the world’s cotton. A century later, though, global demands changed the ways people bought their clothes. Innovations brought on to meet the demands of World War II meant synthetic fabrics like polyester were gaining traction among consumers. Then, in the 1970s, expanded trade relationships with China opened a new population of inexpensive laborers to American clothing manufacturers.


As U.S. clothing factories shuttered and moved overseas, so too did the other components of a thriving textile industry. The number of cotton mills has dropped from nearly 900 during the late 1800s to just around 100 today, leaving farmers with fewer options to sell their crop domestically.
Agricultural policymakers have tried to address the shrinking domestic industry with a series of programs designed to alleviate the expenses of cotton producers and processors.
Launched in 2016, the Cotton Ginning Cost Share Program paid more than $215 million to cotton farmers between 2017 and 2019 to mitigate the costs of processing raw cotton. Still, in 2025, U.S. cotton mill use was down 50.8% from 2016.
The 2025 Working Families Tax Cuts Act (better known as the One Big Beautiful Bill) included several provisions for U.S. cotton producers, including increased funding for crop insurance, support for milling facilities and clothing manufacturing and new trade protections.
Other proposed legislation, like the Buying American Cotton Act introduced earlier this year, hopes to reinvigorate the domestic industry by focusing on demand for U.S.-grown cotton. The House resolution, sponsored by U.S. Rep. Gregory Murphy, a North Carolina Republican, would provide tax credits for consumers of U.S.-produced cotton goods and implement programs to track the manufacture of domestic cotton products.
In 2025, Murphy’s campaign received $10,000 each from the National Cotton Council, a Cordova, Tennessee-based industry trade group, and the American Cotton Shippers Association, based in Memphis.
‘Press-release policy’
Coppess said he wasn’t surprised by the new Great American Cotton Plan — support for cotton production has been a sticking point in American agricultural policy for generations. But he isn’t confident in its ability to reverse the direction the domestic cotton industry is heading.
“The idea that they’re going to roll this thing out and magically undo something that’s been going on since the 1940s, it’s marketing,” he said. “It’s political marketing, but the realities are really difficult.”
From New Deal provisions for cotton farmers to NAFTA agreements on textile exports, prior administrations pushed for policies — financial subsidies, import quotas, strategic market interventions and domestic manufacturing campaigns — but were largely unsuccessful in slowing the industry’s decline.


The past decade has not been any better. Tariffs implemented during the first Trump administration hit the cotton industry particularly hard, according to USDA analysis, with cotton exports to China dropping by more than 37% between 2017 and 2018.
In the past two years, retaliation from the president’s second wave of tariffs brought down cotton exports to China by 84% between 2024 and 2025, according to researchers at North Dakota State University. Amid the dispute, Brazil extended its lead as the world’s top cotton exporter.


In early April, trade groups across the agricultural sector, including the National Cotton Council, signed an open letter to Rollins demanding an end to the trade war.
Both Murphy’s bill and the Working Families Tax Cuts Act are mentioned extensively in the Great American Cotton Plan. The plan, as a whole, does not outline any new policy the agency intends to pursue.
Rather, the plan describes how existing legislation and initiatives will work in concert, with the ultimate goal of reviving America’s cotton industry.
According to Logan, whose own family history includes several generations of cotton farming, the industry’s decline in prevalence is a natural consequence of America’s economic growth. Cotton no longer determines the nation’s place on the world stage.


“You can think about cotton in the 19th century the way that we think about oil today,” he said. “If green energy comes along … we wouldn’t be talking about oil being so important. There will still be combustible engines using oil, but we won’t care as much about it as we do today.”
Coppess described the USDA plan as “press-release policy,” and said cotton’s issues are much older than the plan seems to address.


“We’re not addressing the underlying problems for the markets and for farmers. We’re just throwing money at it, or in this case, packaging up existing programs, existing funding,” he said. “And it is kind of a pretend thing. We pretend we’re doing something, but we’re not addressing the problems the domestic textile industry has.”
The USDA press office did not respond to multiple email requests to answer questions about the policy. In a press release announcing the new plan, the USDA said it will continue to partner with lawmakers and industry leaders to promote cotton.
Beyond cotton
In the face of an 80-year decline and massive global shift in clothing manufacturing, some experts worry that it might be too late for these policies — or any policies — to reverse the trend. Rebuilding America’s textile industry, Coppess said, might mean looking at new crop markets.
“All of us intuitively know that putting all your eggs in one basket is never a good idea. And so why are we only focused on cotton?” he said. “If we want more fiber production for textiles, then we should be looking at alternative crops.”
One leading alternative is hemp, in large part because of its supposed lower environmental impact compared to cotton. Sarah Stephens, CEO of Kansas-based Midwest Hemp Technology, said business has been improving over the past several years in her still-fledgling industry.
“You’re seeing the interest in hemp because farmers are in a difficult spot,” she said. “Fertilizer is really high. Hemp uses a little bit less fertilizer. And so it really can meet the moment that a lot of these problems feel overwhelming.”


Last year, hemp producers received a blow from lawmakers: a surprise addition from Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky to the bill that would end the nation’s longest government shutdown and would make many hemp operations functionally illegal.


The ban targets any product intended to intoxicate consumers — and so would not impact producers like Stephens, growing hemp for feed or fiber — but she said the news still hit the entire industry hard.
“For us, it hasn’t changed our day-to-day operation here…” she said. “But I do think it’s just one more kind of black eye, or negative headline that people read with the word hemp in it.”
Stephens isn’t advocating to replace cotton with hemp. Instead, she said hemp could allow farmers to diversify their crops to reflect a changing domestic textile market and the growing movement for natural fiber products.
MAHA and microplastics
Almost as soon as the USDA announced the Great American Cotton Plan, its message was shared on the X account of MAHA Action. Tony Lyons, a long-time friend of HHS Secretary Kennedy, leads the nonprofit organization dedicated to supporting the movement’s political ambitions and documenting its legislative wins.
The plan’s warm reception by MAHA’s biggest figures is a dramatic change from the movement’s initial attitudes toward the cotton industry.

The original MAHA report was highly critical of cotton, a crop that relies heavily on fertilizer, pesticides and diverted groundwater. The 2025 report, outlining the supposed causes of the epidemic of childhood chronic illness, placed the industry alongside ultra-processed foods and “overmedicalization.”

But in subsequent meetings between the government commission and cotton industry representatives, a different story emerged.
Marjory Walker, vice president of council operations and communications with the National Cotton Council, a trade organization that lobbies for pro-cotton policies and legislation, argued that agrochemicals were essential to producing natural fibers to clothe America’s children — to keep microplastics off of their bodies, NOTUS reported. That argument caught the MAHA commission’s attention.
Months later, Kennedy and many of his followers have become key voices in raising the profile of U.S. cotton. Both he and the USDA have co-signed the “Plant Not Plastic” initiative, a campaign to raise awareness of the health risks associated with synthetic fabrics.

 
The campaign’s website, a sleek piece of social media-age design, greets visitors with a banner estimating how many microplastic particles the average person has inhaled since the start of the day. Digital specs float across the screen, revealing descriptions of different synthetic fibers as they shift below the cursor. What is much harder to figure out, until you navigate the page and find a press release toward the very bottom, is the fact that the initiative is a project of the National Cotton Council.
During the 2024 election cycle, the NCC spent over $1 million in political donations, the most in the organization’s history. At the same time, as the Plant Not Plastic initiative was making its way across the internet, the trade group’s expenditures totaled $23.4 million, nearly 28% more than the year before.
The council’s hope of raising interest in cotton has, whether as a result of the organization’s spending or not, appeared to come to fruition. Internet searches for natural fibers more than doubled between June 2024 and the USDA’s announcement a year later. Searches for cotton increased by more than 50% over the same period.
On social media, a subculture of sorts has sprung up around the natural fiber fervor. On TikTok, hashtags like #naturalfibers and #antipolyester garner videos with tens of thousands of likes and comments. Scrolling through videos within the larger genre of “non-toxic living” reveals an endless array of influencers in well-lit, earth-toned rooms, parading across the screen in organic cotton yoga sets, sundresses and blue jeans.

A collage of screen grabs from TikTok videos shows creators discussing natural fibers, synthetic clothing and “low-tox” fashion. On TikTok, where much of the natural fibers movement has coalesced, creators can rack up hundreds of views under hashtags like #antipolyester, #organic fashion and #lowtoxliving. (Graphic by Caspar Dowdy, Investigate Midwest)
Through these videos, a common thread emerges: confusion and the supposed remedies to it. Where are you supposed to find “non-toxic” clothes? How do you know what’s real and what’s marketing language? Why is everything so expensive?
Bill Morris, the California Polytechnic-educated materials scientist behind the account @fabricsvetted, said he’s seen those kinds of conversations more frequently on social media. In particular, his videos attempting to educate consumers about textiles have grown in popularity since he first began posting to Instagram and TikTok earlier this year.


“There have been people in my world talking about this for decades, but I would say the general public is starting to talk a lot more about it,” he said.
Morris said he is not part of the MAHA movement and that his social media algorithm doesn’t often bring him into contact with the political side of the natural fiber conversation.


But, as a person who’s been talking about the role of textiles in human health for years, he worries that the narrative around certain issues, like microplastic exposure, might be “getting a little bit ahead of the evidence,” and detracting from known issues, such as harmful additive chemicals, that are perhaps more grounded in science.
“I think it’s tricky for me when I see some of these messages getting a little bit jumbled,” he said.
Though research does support the idea that synthetic fabrics can pose exposure risks for some potentially harmful chemicals, the issue is not exclusive to synthetics. The pesticides and fertilizers used to grow fiber crops can carry with them significant environmental drawbacks, for example, and the dyes used to finish most fabric goods can be a source of irritation.
Joaquim Rovira, a biochemistry lecturer at the University of Rovira i Virgili in Catalonia, Spain, has spent several years studying the human health risks associated with textile production and exposure. While he personally believes switching to natural fibers where possible is a healthier option in most cases, he cautions against the idea that any one material is perfect.


“We need a lot of land, a lot of water, a lot of agrochemicals to produce one kilo of cotton to be one shirt or jeans,” Rovira said. “This is also a problem, but we obtain plastic fiber from oil and these also have an impact on the environment.”


One issue with understanding and mitigating the potential risks of exposure, Rovira said, is the “never-ending story” of regulating harmful substances in manufacturing. He points to the example of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS: consumer product chemicals that were introduced and widely-used, revealed to be harmful to human health and then regulated once the damage was already done.
A potential solution to that cycle, he said, could come from having stronger regulations in the initial phases of a product’s development.
“The problem of the additives that are in the clothes are the same as additives in food, the additives in the furniture, the additives in the paint, all chemical compounds that are added to consumer products,” Rovira said. “The industry goes 10, 20 years in front of scientists and the scientists are the same years in front of the legislation.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: New job for Moran, new role for Benson, new position for Cullison, in political notes
authors: William J. Ford, Danielle J. Brown
description: AFSCME Council 3 President Patrick Moran is moving on up to be president of the national union, outgoing Sen. Joanne C. Benson and Del. Bonnie Cullison won't stray far from the State House, and Prince George's hosts Fashion Week, in political notes.
text:
Patrick Moran, then president of Council 3 of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, with AFSCME national President Lee Saunders, right. Moran was elected Thursday to succeed Saunders. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Well, state officials won’t have Patrick Moran to kick around anymore. Or maybe it’s the other way around.
Moran, the president of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees Council 3, was elected president Thursday of AFSCME International, the 1.4 million-member national arm of the union. Moran, who had been serving as vice president of the union, replaces outgoing President Lee Saunders, who had held the office since 2012.
During the 14 years that Moran was president of Council 3, the state union tripled its membership, according to the national union, and became the biggest unions for state workers in Maryland. A statement from Council 3 said that during Moran’s tenure, “Maryland workers won historic raises, new laws to protect against extreme heat and workplace violence, and a record-breaking wage theft settlement of $23 million.”
In remarks after his swearing-in Friday, Moran said he was honored to accept the job. And Moran, who got his start as an organizer, called on members at the union’s 47th International Convention to continue building the union, which represents everything from correctional officers to higher education workers to healtcare workers.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“Every generation of our union has faced its defining moment. Now it’s our turn,” Moran said. “We will fight and build power like our future depends on it because it does. We will protect our neighbors and strengthen our communities. This is our fight, and together, we’ve got the power to make change.”
His departure comes at a time of increasingly fraught relations with the Moore administration. Late last year, during contract negotiations, the union filed a series of unfair labor practice claims against the state, and in just the last month it has sued the state over raises for university workers and released a report highly critical of pay, staffing levels and workplace conditions at state agencies.
In a statement, Council 3  congratulated Moran and wished him well.
“Our AFSCME family in Maryland will miss his daily presence, but we are excited to see the decades of union experience and organizing spirit that President Moran will bring to our national union,” the statement said.
She’ll be back, sort of
Although Sen. Joanne C. Benson (D-Prince George’s) isn’t seeking reelection, she said Thursday people will still be seeing her face during the 2027 session. She’ll just be on the other side of the table.
Benson, 85, who has served in the General Assembly since 1991 and the informal title of dean of the Senate chamber, said she plans to testify in Annapolis on a few pieces of legislation.
Sen. Joanne C. Benson (D-Prince George’s) during a Feb. 28 press conference. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
“I’m going to retire the first week in January, but I’m going to be highly visible down there [in Annapolis],” said Benson, who currently serves as the Senate majority whip. “I’m going to speak truth to power because people need to understand that they’re not just here for political aggrandizement. They’re not here to pat themselves on the back. They’re here to do a job to look out for the people who sent them here.”
Besides continuing her “mission” to support seniors, Benson said she’s working on a turkey drive during the Thanksgiving holiday in November.
“We’re in positions of authority, and even if we’re not in positions of authority, we have to exercise strong leadership when it comes to ensuring that the life of the people not only in Prince George’s County, but in this country, is worth something,” she said. “People are losing their jobs. People have health issues. People are homeless. Those are the people that we are gravely concerned about. There are a lot of other things that are going on that we need to take care of.”
Gorgeous Prince George’s? Prove it
While Benson continues her community work in Prince George’s, County Executive Aisha Braveboy (D) announced Thursday the jurisdiction will do something it hasn’t done before: Host a fashion week.
The event will run Sept. 23-25 at the Metro Points Hotel in New Carrollton, the same spot where Braveboy, Gov. Wes Moore (D) and other supporters celebrated in March 2025 when she won the special primary election for county executive.
According to a press release, the event is labeled “as a premier celebration of style, culture, creativity, commerce, and community in one of the most vibrant counties in America.”
“Prince George’s County Fashion Week is engineered as a vital platform for fashion designers, creatives, and cultural innovators,” the announcement said. “This premier showcase is designed to elevate the local creative economy and project the county’s distinct fashion landscape onto a global stage.”
Programming is slated to include runway shows, vendors, talent and model discovery and business forums. Those interested in participating or attending, scan the QR code on the flier. Registrations are accepted on a first come, first-served basis.
Chair Cullison
Del. Bonnie Cullison (D-Montgomery) did not seek reelection this year after four terms in the House, but she’s not moving far: Cullison is now serving as chair of the Prescription Drug Affordability Board that she championed as a legislator for several years.
Her appointment took effect on Aug. 7, filling the seat left by former PDAB chair Van T. Mitchell, who announced at the June PDAB meeting he was stepping down after “almost six years” with the board.
Del. Bonnie Cullison (D-Montgomery) on the House Floor during the 2026 session. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
Cullison, who also serves as vice chair of the House Health Committee, has been a longtime supporter of the board’s goal to reduce prescription drug costs in Maryland. Her appointment as PDAB chair required joint approval from House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) and Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City). She said she was “honored” the two appointed her to chair the board.
“At its core, this is responsible budgeting with a clear public purpose: Helping Marylanders benefit from more affordable health care and, ultimately, lower insurance premiums,” Cullison said in a written statement last week. “I look forward to working with Board members and diverse stakeholders across the state as we continue this important effort.”
Established in 2020, the board is currently tasked with reducing prescription drug costs for those on the state’s health insurance, a goal it has not yet accomplished due to years of financial delays, lengthy policy building processes and careful cost review to determine “unaffordable” prescription drugs. But 2025 legislation will expand the board’s authority bring down costs for all Marylanders, if it can first show it can set upper payment limits under its current authority on what the state is willing to pay for two drugs. That process is underway for Jardiance and Ozempic.
Cullison defended both the 2019 legislation that established the board as well as the 2025 bill that will expand the board’s authority on the House floor.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Police chief in Senatobia regularly used racial slurs, private text messages reveal
authors: Mukta Joshi and Joseph Cranney, Verite News
description: A memorial is in place for 1-year-old Kohen Wiley at Walmart in Senatobia on Friday, June 26, 2026. The state Department of Public Safety says a police officer responding to a shoplifting call on Sunday, June 14, 2026, shot at a car that drove in the officer's direction, killing Kohen.
text:
Mukta Joshi is a reporter at Mississippi Today. She is spending a year as a New York Times Local Investigations fellow. Joseph Cranney is a reporter at Verite News. Both report for the Deep South Today Investigative Reporting Center in collaboration with The Times.
SENATOBIA — For many residents of this tiny city about 40 miles south of Memphis, the fatal police shooting of a 1-year-old Black toddler in June became a flashpoint after years of complaints about discriminatory and overzealous policing.
The toddler, Kohen Wiley, was killed when police officers shot at a vehicle he was in after they responded to a shoplifting call at a local Walmart store.
Harold Vanderford, chief of Senatobia police department, seen in a post on the department’s Facebook page. Credit: Senatobia Police Department, via Facebook
Last year, the city’s elected aldermen had forced out its previous police chief after a string of controversies, including an incident in which one of his officers had arrested a 10-year-old Black boy who had urinated in public. But the new police chief, brought in last fall for his “firm, fair and focused” leadership style, routinely used racist slurs in private text conversations with a colleague even after he was appointed, reporters for Mississippi Today, Verite News and The New York Times have learned.
In one text message, the chief, Harold Vanderford, described having a “racist moment.” In another, he wrote that he “almost beat a nigger and white woman’s ass a few minutes ago.”
Vanderford used the racist slur, spelled various ways, more than a dozen times in a series of 10 text conversations dating back to last summer and continuing after he became chief. The texts were provided to reporters by the person who had received them, who said they came from Chief Vanderford. Three other acquaintances confirmed that the phone number associated with the messages belonged to the chief.
Three months before the Walmart shooting, Vanderford texted a colleague to lament Mississippi State University’s performance in a college sporting event, referring to a player using a racist slur.
In at least two instances in April, Vanderford used the slur to refer to himself or his white friend, text messages show. On another occasion, he texted that he was drunk and that he had “screamed” the slur 15 times, loud enough in hopes that his neighbors would hear.
On Thanksgiving Day, the chief texted that he “just had a racist moment on Goodman Road,” a street in Southaven.
Vanderford did not respond to phone and email messages left by reporters, or notes left at his home and the police station. The mayor of Senatobia, Greg Graves, did not respond to a request for comment.
“It is completely unacceptable for any law enforcement in Mississippi to use racial slurs, whether in private or in public, because no official can protect and serve a community while harboring hatred toward its people,” said Charles Taylor, the executive director of the Mississippi chapter of the NAACP.
When he took over the department, Chief Vanderford, a 60-year-old native of Greenville and 29-year veteran of law enforcement, vowed his tenure would focus on “reestablishing and solidifying trust” with the community.
Then, in June, his officers confronted Vellesiya Wiley and Latoya Ferrell after they were accused by people in a Walmart of stealing baby clothes and a pack of diapers. The pair got into a vehicle, and officers surrounded them with raised guns.
Wiley, who was in the passenger seat holding her son, said that as they drove away, she lifted up the boy in an effort to make sure officers saw him. Then she heard three or four shots.
Attorneys representing the family of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley are calling for law enforcement in Senatobia to release body and dashboard camera footage and on Monday June 22, announced plans for an independent autopsy. Kohen would have turned two later this year.  Credit: Ben Crump Law
According to a statement released the day of the incident by the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the shooting, officers had attempted to stop the car, but “the driver drove in the direction of the officers, almost striking one.”
State and local law enforcement officials said they would not answer questions or release body-worn camera or surveillance footage of the incident until their investigation was complete. On Monday, the Mississippi Legislative Black Caucus demanded updates on the state’s investigation from the attorney general.
The Wiley family hired Ben Crump, the civil rights lawyer, who presented forensic evidence suggesting that the police had fired from the side of the vehicle, which, he said, indicated that the officer had not been in harm’s way.
In documents released “in error,” state law enforcement officials identified Sgt. Hunter Foster as the subject of their investigation. In the months leading up to the shooting, Foster had directed racist remarks at two of his co-workers, according to internal complaints obtained by Mississippi Today.
In July, Mississippi Today reported that two days before the Walmart shooting, Foster had directed a racially offensive remark toward a Black co-worker, according to an internal complaint. Six months before the shooting, Foster was also accused of making derogatory remarks toward a fellow officer who is white and has a daughter with his Black partner, according to an internal complaint. The officer, Joshua Griffin, now a deputy with the Tate County Sheriff’s Department, declined a request for comment.
According to the written complaint, Foster told Griffin, “you need to get your people” in relation to a foot chase involving Black people. A week later, Foster made a second remark using a crude sexist epithet, saying that the owner of a suspicious vehicle was Griffin’s “type,” which Griffin took to mean a Black woman, the complaint said.
Foster remained on patrol. In June, two days before the Walmart shooting, he referred to a Black officer in the department using a racist expletive, according to ‌the internal complaint. That officer, Dexter Smith, filed the complaint the day after the shooting.
A lawyer representing Foster, Martin Zummach, hasn’t addressed Foster’s comments, but wrote in an emailed statement that he was “very convinced” that his client would be cleared of allegations of wrongdoing.
Vanderford hasn’t publicly addressed the shooting. The Wiley family said he had not offered condolences.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: British professor Jason Arday and higher education’s new politics of plagiarism
description: After a meteoric rise to the top ranks of British academia, scholar Jason Arday was found dead at his London home on Aug. 14, 2026. Arday had spent weeks fighting plagiarism accusations. The way they took on a life of their own in the media ecosystem is a stark reminder of the steep price people can pay […]
text:
Cambridge professor Jason Arday was found dead at his home in London on Aug. 14, 2026, days after he resigned from his position amid accusations of plagiarism, which he had denied. (Photo by Nordin Catic/Getty Images)After a meteoric rise to the top ranks of British academia, scholar Jason Arday was found dead at his London home on Aug. 14, 2026.
Arday had spent weeks fighting plagiarism accusations. The way they took on a life of their own in the media ecosystem is a stark reminder of the steep price people can pay in a culture that has made originality a kind of moral virtue.
In 2023, at age 38, he had been appointed to a professorship in sociology of education at the University of Cambridge, becoming the youngest Black professor in the institution’s 800-year history.
Nine days before his death, Arday had resigned from his faculty position. He was facing growing criticism about improbable and inconsistent details appearing in his memoir, scheduled to be released in the coming weeks by Simon & Schuster. Arday’s publisher had stood by him, lauding the academic’s “professionalism and integrity.”
But the originality of Arday’s dissertation and his other academic work was also coming under scrutiny, leading to multiple allegations of plagiarism.
Arday vehemently denied the accusations, suggesting that any mistakes were the result of his autism. He also claimed that his accusers were motivated by racism.
The controversy over Arday’s work reflects an ongoing trend of ideological opponents levying plagiarism accusations to undermine one another. I think it’s also worth exploring why such attacks continue to be so enticing — and so effective.
 
Shifting standards for originality
Plagiarism can be defined as the appropriation of someone else’s words or ideas without acknowledgment or compensation.
In the ancient world, plagiarism was viewed quite negatively: The word “plagiarism” actually means “kidnapper” in Latin, and the Roman poet Horace described literary theft like a crow making itself beautiful with stolen feathers.

But in my 2026 book, “Strikingly Similar,” I explore how, throughout the medieval period, the Renaissance and into the early modern era, an ethos of “imitatio” prevailed. Chaucer, Shakespeare and Milton are examples of authors who hewed closely to writers who had come before them. These writers freely borrowed plots, characters and rhetorical devices in the service of their own work.
True originality came to be viewed in a positive light only gradually, and it eventually developed into the modern concept of intellectual property, in which the creative products of human ingenuity are viewed as tangible assets. Treating creative works as property, in turn, created the legal framework to protect them.
The German artist Albrecht Dürer initiated one of the first known intellectual property lawsuits. In 1506, he asked the Venetian government to stop the Italian engraver Marcantonio Raimondi from copying his woodcuts. Dürer was only partly successful: It was decided that Raimondi could continue copying Dürer’s work, but he was prohibited from also copying the artist’s distinctive monogram.
In the 19th century, as the result of lobbying by authors such as Charles Dickens, the British Parliament enacted the Copyright Act of 1842. This statute greatly expanded the protections granted to authors. It would take another 50 years, however, before foreign authors like Dickens enjoyed similar protections under U.S. copyright law.
Today, the situation that existed during the Renaissance has almost totally reversed itself.
In Europe, groups of scholars have banded together to investigate allegations of plagiarism. Using crowdsourcing techniques, VroniPlag Wiki in Germany and Dissernet in Russia have exposed numerous instances of plagiarism by public servants in their dissertations and academic publications.
The work of VroniPlag Wiki alone has led to several German universities revoking doctoral degrees they had awarded to elected and appointed government officials.
 
Plagiarism becomes political
Today, accusations of plagiarism have become a potent way to undermine someone’s credibility. If a claim is substantiated, the plagiarist is seen as sloppy or lazy at best, and fundamentally dishonest at worst.
As a result, partisans of the political left and right routinely use allegations of plagiarism to vilify their ideological adversaries. This serves their goals of undercutting both their target’s work and the institutions they represent.
In 1991, NPR’s Nina Totenberg broke the story of Anita Hill’s allegations of sexual harassment against Supreme Court nominee Clarence Thomas, drawing the ire of the right. As the controversy engulfed the confirmation process, the conservative-leaning Wall Street Journal revived a nearly two-decade-old plagiarism accusation against Totenberg, dating from her time as a reporter for the National Observer.
The most prominent recent example would be the 2023 claim by conservative activist Christopher Rufo that Claudine Gay, then serving as president of Harvard, had engaged in multiple acts of plagiarism.
In 2024, Gay resigned as the school’s president, although she remains on the faculty. (In an ironic twist, the spouse of one of Gay’s most prominent critics, hedge fund manager Bill Ackman, was accused of having plagiarized her own dissertation.)
Conservative voices have also routinely found themselves in the crosshairs.
In 2013, multiple media outlets accused Kentucky Republican Sen. Rand Paul of plagiarizing in his speeches, newspaper column and his 2012 book from a variety of sources, including Wikipedia. And during Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch’s 2017 confirmation hearings, some media outlets claimed that President Donald Trump’s nominee had plagiarized parts of his 2006 book about assisted suicide. Gorsuch went on to be confirmed by the Senate.
The accusations against Arday did not emerge in a political vacuum. They were shaped by the culture wars over race, academia and diversity, equity and inclusion policies.
On July 21, 2026, Nathan Cofnas, an American philosopher working at Ghent University in Belgium, wrote a Substack post detailing how he submitted Arday’s 2015 dissertation to Copyleaks, a plagiarism detection platform. He found “substantial overlap” with a thesis written by another scholar in 2009.
Cofnas added that “Many passages are lifted with minimal editing, sometimes retaining copy-editing mistakes from the original source,” and found similar issues in other papers written by Arday.
In the past, Cofnas has expressed doubts about the intellectual abilities of Black people in comparison to white people. By discrediting the work of a Black professor, he explained, he could also discredit the university that had hired Arday for promoting “the ideology of DEI.”
Ghent University suspended Cofnas on August 20, 2026, while it conducted an investigation into his actions.
 
AI complicates the notion of plagiarism
The rise of generative artificial intelligence has arguably made the public’s desire for original human works even more pronounced. Just a year after the 2022 release of ChatGPT 3.5, Merriam-Webster chose “authentic” as its word of the year.
Copyright laws also underscore the premium we place on originality by granting creators — and even their heirs — long periods of exclusive rights for books, music and other artistic works.
When a student submits a paper written by a chatbot instead of their own work, should this be considered plagiarism? I’ve argued that this is more akin to ghostwriting, since the student isn’t copying from an original source. Instead, generative AI is stringing words together in a probabilistic way that closely resembles human writing.
That isn’t the same as generating a text from a single source. That said, using a chatbot to write without disclosing its use can still be a form of cheating. And most people contend that plagiarism, cheating and ghostwriting are all cut from the same cloth because they all lack the spark that we ascribe to truly original thinking and writing.
The public ultimately expects journalists, scholars and elected officials to behave ethically. In academia, there is no greater sin than passing off another’s work as one’s own. And violations of public trust are typically judged quite harshly.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Don’t let scammers crash back-to-school season
description: Today’s students and young adults are true digital natives, having grown up online, learning to navigate digital spaces as a normal part of daily life. As they transition to college, they turn to digital platforms and social media for everything  from apartment hunting and job searches to shopping, banking and talking with friends. That familiarity, […]
text:
Today’s students and young adults are true digital natives, having grown up online, learning to navigate digital spaces as a normal part of daily life. As they transition to college, they turn to digital platforms and social media for everything  from apartment hunting and job searches to shopping, banking and talking with friends.
That familiarity, however, can create a false sense of security, making younger adults just as much of a target for fraud and scams as older individuals. According to the FBI’s Internet Crime Report, Americans ages 20–29 reported more than $500 million to internet-crime losses in 2025.
As scammers become more sophisticated, including using AI, students need to be more vigilant than ever about fraud and scams. Understanding the most common ones can help you and your children avoid becoming victims.
Common scams targeting students (and the families supporting them)
Online shopping and marketplace scams
Whether your student is furnishing a dorm, moving into an apartment or buying textbooks–or you’re helping them pay for essentials—online deals and secondhand marketplaces can help you save money while also creating more opportunities for scammers.
Buy from official and trusted retailers whenever possible, double check website URLs for misspellings or other red flags, and make sure the site uses https://. Be wary of deals that seem too good to be true as well. Avoid clicking links in unsolicited emails or text messages, including fake “missed delivery” notifications that often lead to fraudulent websites or malware.
Before making a purchase, read seller reviews and ratings. If you’re buying locally, meet in a safe public place and inspect the item before paying.
Job scams
As students return to school this fall, some may be looking for part-time jobs or internships. Scammers target students with fake jobs offering high salaries, flexible schedules or jobs you can do from a residence hall, apartment or home.
If your child receives a job offer by text, email, or direct message – be cautious, especially if they never applied to work at that company. Encourage them to use well-known job boards and then apply directly through the company’s official website. 
Also, if an employer asks them to pay upfront for training, equipment, background checks or application fees, it may be a sign of a scam. Legitimate companies will never charge you to get a job. They also won’t send you money and then ask you to return a portion of it.
Rental and housing scams
Scammers know student housing is in high demand. They’ll often post fake apartment listings or copy legitimate ones to trick potential renters (or their families) into sending money for a deposit.
Rental prices that seem unusually low should raise a red flag. Use a reverse image search to see if photos of the property appear on a different website or in a different location. Research unfamiliar property managers or housing websites before sending money, and avoid paying deposits through wire transfers, gift cards or peer-to-peer payment apps.
Double check the address, read online reviews of the property management company and schedule a tour of the house or apartment before signing a lease or sending a deposit. That way, you’ll know the listing and location is real. 
The influence of AI
Thanks to artificial intelligence, scammers can now create cloned voices and deepfake videos, along with fraudulent emails, text messages and even websites and apps that look real. These AI tools let scammers impersonate family members, employers, banks, law enforcement, delivery companies and trusted brands to get you to send money or share personal information. They may even target parents directly—claiming your child is in trouble and needs money immediately.
How to protect yourself (and your children)
No matter what type of scam you encounter, a few simple habits can go a long way toward reducing your risk:

Limit the personal information you and your children share online and make social media profiles  private whenever possible. This can help reduce the information scammers can use to target you, guess your security questions or attempt to access your financial accounts.


When you’re making a payment, use more protected methods, such as credit and debit cards, which generally offer stronger consumer protections than wire transfers, gift cards or peer-to-peer payment apps. Treat peer-to-peer payments, such as Zelle, like cash — once the money is sent, it’s often difficult to recover.


Scammers can spoof phone numbers to make calls look like they’re coming from your bank, law enforcement or another trusted organization. Don’t automatically trust your caller ID – if you get a call demanding immediate action or claiming there’s a problem with your account, hang up and call back directly using a verified phone number. Banks will never call and ask you for account information, tell you to transfer money to ‘protect’ it or pressure you to act immediately.


Don’t click links or download attachments from unexpected emails or text messages and avoid accessing your financial accounts or making online purchases on public Wi-Fi, where savvy cybercriminals can gain access to your login credentials. 


Perhaps most importantly, slow down. Back-to-school season brings a flurry of financial decisions and scammers know students and families are looking for deals. They often create a false sense of urgency to try to pressure people into making quick decisions. Taking a few extra minutes to verify information can make the difference.

The bottom line
Whether your student is shopping for school supplies, searching for a job or signing a first lease, their status as a student can make them a prime target for scammers—and families can be targeted too.
Stay skeptical of unsolicited offers, verify before you pay or share personal information, and slow down when something feels rushed. Those simple habits can help protect your money, your identity and your family’s peace of mind throughout the school year from scams and fraud.

title: More out-of-state students opt for University of Alaska Southeast, with new in-state tuition rate
description: Under a driving Juneau rain, dozens of new students at the University of Alaska Southeast gathered Friday for orientation and to kick off the fall semester. This year, the public university saw a boost in enrollment of out-of-state students, which officials and students say is largely due to a new policy eliminating the non-resident tuition […]
text:
New students at the University of Alaska Southeast attend orientation at the Egan Library on the Juneau campus on Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Under a driving Juneau rain, dozens of new students at the University of Alaska Southeast gathered Friday for orientation and to kick off the fall semester. This year, the public university saw a boost in enrollment of out-of-state students, which officials and students say is largely due to a new policy eliminating the non-resident tuition rate. 
UAS piloted the new tuition policy this year, called Alaska Unlocked, which offers the standard in-state tuition rate for all undergraduate courses, regardless of the student’s residency.
That’s resulted in an estimated 36% increase this year in out-of-state students enrolling at UAS compared to last year, according to university officials.     

New students at the University of Alaska Southeast attend orientation at the Egan Library on campus in Juneau on Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

“We are so thrilled with that much of an increase,” said UAS Chancellor Aparna Palmer, in an interview after her welcoming remarks to students at the Egan Library. “We know that a high percentage of our graduates stay in Alaska and work in Alaska within one year of graduation. And so most of these students are our future Alaskans.” 
New students have arrived from 28 states, according to university data, with the top home states including Washington, California, Colorado, Idaho, Minnesota and Wisconsin. 
The in-state tuition rate was a draw for 22-year-old Nicole Wilson of Phoenix, Arizona. After classes at community college, she enrolled at UAS to pursue a bachelor’s degree in marine biology with a focus on mammals. “I decided to come here both based on the in-state tuition and also because it was such, like, an ‘open to marine biology’ type school. My original plan was to go out to Hawaii, but it’s extremely expensive from out of state,” she said. 
Wilson said housing was also a factor. “I did the math. If I were to take a dorm, which I would have had to, at any of the major universities in Arizona, it was actually more expensive than coming out to Alaska,” she said. 
Cost of housing was the main consideration for 20-year-old Owen Kellon of Portland, Oregon, who is pursuing a bachelor’s degree in environmental sciences. “It was the bigger concern when it came to the cost of schooling, just because tuition was like a couple hundred bucks per class, which is perfectly reasonable. It’s about how much I was paying back at my community college in Portland, but the housing cost was the biggest factor.”     

The John Pugh Hall student dorms houses 120 beds for students on-campus in Juneau, seen on Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

The standard in-state tuition rate is expected to be available across the University of Alaska system next year. Earlier this month, the UA Board of Regents moved to eliminate out-of-state tuition rates for all locations and degree types, aiming to draw more students to Alaska. 
Currently, out-of-state tuition is double to quadruple the amount of resident tuition, depending on degree type. The Board of Regents is expected to take up a final vote on the policy change in November. 
UAS has the smallest student population of Alaska’s public universities, with roughly 1,800 students last year across campuses in Juneau, Ketchikan and Sitka.
This year’s preliminary enrollment data shows roughly the same number of students as last year, signalling Alaskan student enrollment may have declined. But Palmer emphasized that it’s too soon to tell, as enrollment numbers are subject to change in the next few weeks with more Alaska students possibly signing up for dual enrollment programs or classes beginning later in the fall.     

University of Alaska Southeast Chancellor Aparna Palmer welcomes new students at orientation in Juneau on Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

This year, UAS saw a 21% increase in applications from out-of-state students, and a 36% increase in newly enrolled out-of-state students. More than 80 new out-of-state students have enrolled this year, compared to 60 students last year, according to university officials.
UAS is an open access enrollment institution, Palmer noted. “What that means is, no matter where you are in life, whether you just graduated from high school, in high school, or whether you’re, you know, in your sixties or seventies, there is a way in which you can access UAS,” she said.
Most students are working adults or part-time students, Palmer said, and can enroll in classes in-person or online. “So, we do have a really diverse group of students,” she said.
In Juneau, new students had a jam-packed schedule for orientation week. On Friday, students were welcomed by UAS administrators, a Tlingit elder and student leaders, followed by a campus tour and briefings on campus resources, student clubs, tutoring, career counseling, and anti-discrimination and Title IX rights and reporting. 
Students expressed excitement for the new school year and to be in Alaska, including Owen Kellon of Oregon.
“I love the rain,” he said. “ I am excited to see how the winter months will look like with only like six hours of sunlight. I’m scared, but I’m also excited.”
New students at the University of Alaska Southeast pose for a photo by Auke Lake during a campus tour as part of orientation in Juneau on Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)

title: Is a U.S. Department of Justice investigation about to disrupt Alaska’s U.S. Senate race?
description: On Alaska’s primary election day, NBC News — citing unidentified sources — reported that the U.S. Department of Justice has issued grand jury subpoenas as it investigates whether Petersburg candidate Dan J. Sullivan may have somehow violated federal law.  If that’s true, subpoenas haven’t reached Sullivan, currently running third in this week’s election and[...]
text:
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, talks to staffers on the morning of Aug. 18, 2026, at the intersection of the Seward Highway and Northern Lights Boulevard. The Midtown Anchorage intersection is a favored spot for candidate sign-waving, and Sullivan, who is running for re-election, was there with U.S. Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, also running for re-election. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)On Alaska’s primary election day, NBC News — citing unidentified sources — reported that the U.S. Department of Justice has issued grand jury subpoenas as it investigates whether Petersburg candidate Dan J. Sullivan may have somehow violated federal law. 
If that’s true, subpoenas haven’t reached Sullivan, currently running third in this week’s election and the person that incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan has accused of running a sham campaign.
Subpoenas also haven’t reached anyone in the campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola as of Friday, according to the campaign. That includes Anton McParland, Peltola’s former campaign manager, who is still with the campaign. 
Jalen Lee, a spokesman for the Alaska Democratic Party, said on Thursday that no one at the party has gotten a subpoena. 
Amber Lee, a consultant who helped Dan J. Sullivan start his campaign, said on Thursday that she has not been subpoenaed. Lee is no longer working with Sullivan’s campaign.
A spokesperson for the Alaska Division of Elections said no one with the division has received a subpoena about Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign. 
Dan J. Sullivan said by email on Thursday that he has not received a subpoena. He said he’s refraining from saying more about the issue until he understands more about what’s happening.
In July, NBC News reported that the U.S. Attorney’s office and acting Alaska Attorney General Cori Mills were looking for evidence of wire fraud or a conspiracy to deprive Alaska voters of a free and fair elections process, which could be a civil rights violation.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Reagan Zimmerman-Hartzheim, a spokeswoman for the U.S. Attorney’s office in Alaska, said that under DOJ policy, she could neither confirm nor deny the existence of an investigation.
Throughout his campaign, Dan S. Sullivan has called Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign fake, and a trick to deceive Alaska voters. Dan J. Sullivan, also a registered Republican, has denied that claim.
“My intention is not to trick people,” Dan J. Sullivan told the New York Times in an interview this month. “I would hope people are informed enough to know the difference between an incumbent senator and a teacher.”
Dan J. Sullivan, a Republican, remains on track to advance to November’s general election, alongside Dan S. Sullivan, Peltola and a fourth person. Progressive Democrat David Leslie led the race for that spot on Friday. 
A spokesperson for Dan S. Sullivan’s re-election campaign did not return emails about the possible Department of Justice investigation.
Ahead of this week’s statewide primary election, President Donald Trump took to social media with a statement that closely resembled Dan S. Sullivan’s remarks. 
In the statement, the president claimed Dan J.’s candidacy is the result of “trickery” by “Crooked, Radical Left Dumocrats” who put up another Dan Sullivan “to take Votes away from our Great Senator of the same name.”
The Alaska Democratic Party was not involved in Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy, both Sullivan and the party have said repeatedly.
“I have not spoken to Mary (Peltola). I wouldn’t even know who to speak to,” Dan. J. Sullivan told his hometown newspaper, Petersburg Pilot, in June. 
In the Times interview, Dan J. Sullivan suggested he was worried about the possibility that he could face federal investigation.
“I’m just a guy, and they’re scary,” he said. “Whether you’ve done something right or wrong, it doesn’t seem to matter anymore.”
Across the country, federal judges are tracking an increasing number of ungrounded, politically motivated prosecutions by the Department of Justice. 
These include high-profile failed prosecutions against anti-ICE protesters in Chicago, a man who threw a sandwich at a federal official in Washington, D.C., and a man the president accused of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C.
Last weekend, new U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said he would take the president’s views into consideration when making decisions on prosecutions. 
Traditionally, the Department of Justice has acted independently from presidents and has sought to preserve that independence. 
In 1973, Attorney General Elliot Richardson and his deputy both resigned rather than follow President Richard Nixon’s orders to fire a special prosecutor examining the Watergate scandal. Those resignations spurred impeachment proceedings against Nixon.
Last month, the U.S. Senate confirmed Blanche in office by a 50-49 vote. Dan S. Sullivan, who voted “yes,” was a decisive vote in favor of Blanche’s confirmation. 
Aubrey Wieber is the director of the 907 Initiative, an organization opposing Dan S. Sullivan’s re-election. 
Wieber said he doesn’t know if Dan S. Sullivan is working with the Trump administration to manufacture false claims, but he does see the accusations as part of a broader national pattern, with Trump attempting to sow doubt about elections in general.
“I do think this is bogus,” he said of the accusations against Dan J. Sullivan. “Look how many investigations and how many people have looked into this, and no one has found any indication that Dan J. Sullivan is a sham candidate.”
In the just-completed primary election, third-party groups spent millions of dollars to advertise fringe candidates in hopes that they would finish in the top four and advance to the November general election. Dan J. Sullivan wasn’t generally targeted by those ads.
“If this is the ace in the hole,” Wieber asked, “Don’t you think you would spend to make sure that he makes it into the top four?”
