name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Electric Boat cheers move into new campus at former Crystal Mall
description: Officials said the new campus marks a new economic opportunity for southeastern Connecticut, one that could usher in a wave of growth.
text:
Windy skies and a steady downpour weren’t enough to dampen spirits in Waterford on Friday morning as local officials, construction workers and business leaders gathered to celebrate the groundbreaking of General Dynamics Electric Boat’s new campus. 
Work on the roughly 800,000 square foot facility, which will reuse the former Crystal Mall complex, is well underway. The majority of the mall was acquired last year, and the remaining tenants moved out of the building in the spring. 
When renovation work is completed, the campus will house office and software development space as well as facilities for training and workforce development. Some 4,000 to 5,000 employees are expected to work at the campus, which is expected to open in 2027. 
The facility will make Electric Boat, a defense contractor responsible for supplying the military with submarines of varying sizes, the largest employer in Waterford. The company recently celebrated a $76.6 billion contract with the U.S. Navy, one of the largest shipbuilding contracts ever awarded. 
The contract, which comes amid a hiring push for the company, further cements the need for Electric Boat’s expansion, speakers said Friday. 
“This groundbreaking signifies our long-term commitment in Connecticut but also in  all of you and all the workforce,” said Electric Boat President Mark Rayha. 
But speakers also acknowledged that the campus marks something even greater for southeastern Connecticut: a new economic opportunity, one that could usher in a wave of growth and once-in-a-generation investment in the local workforce. 
It’s a new chance for revitalization and commercial activity in the region, built using a space that supported earlier waves of development. Now, as renovation work begins, supporters say that the reused mall will become the backbone of the region’s economic comeback. 
“For decades, the Crystal Mall was part of the fabric of our community. We shopped here, we worked here, we brought our families here,” said Waterford First Selectman Rob Brule. “Today we aren’t here to talk about what this property used to be. We’re here to celebrate what it’s about to become.”
Crystal Mall is trying on something new
The mall redevelopment, DECD deputy commissioner Matt Pugliese noted, is one of the largest reuses of an existing property in the state. The redevelopment work comes as DECD looks to support projects around the state that will breathe new life into old buildings, part of a larger effort. 

Rob Brule, Waterford first selectman, speaks during a groundbreaking ceremony at Electric Boat’s Waterford Campus, the former Crystal Mall, on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

A place like the Crystal Mall, speakers said, is a natural fit for this work. 
“Malls simply cannot meet the kind of commerce that we see today in the United States of America,” said U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal. “Electric Boat, with typical ingenuity and innovation, is, in effect, putting new wine in old bottles.” 
When completed, the Waterford campus will complement submarine production efforts by providing additional space for administrative staff, software developers and new trainees. Submarine production work will continue in nearby Groton, where Electric Boat’s shipyard is located. 
As renovations continue, parts of the Waterford campus will house temporary training spaces for new employees. A more permanent location on the campus known as SAIL, or the Shipbuilding Advanced Institute for Learning, is set to open in the near future. 
When fully operational, SAIL is expected to support close to 400 shipbuilders and will also include support for welding, advanced technology work and additional innovations. 
“We’re really celebrating bringing this place back to life,” said Courtney Murphy, Electric Boat’s director of talent acquisition, workforce development and compensation. “Seeing this plan take shape and now become reality is truly inspiring because it is more than just a groundbreaking. It’s the start of a new chapter in how we grow, train and support the shipbuilders who carry our mission forward.” 
The growth comes as the company continues a larger expansion, including hiring a projected 8,000 workers this year, more than double what it hired in 2025.
And in a region that has long struggled to find stable economic footing, the hope is that Electric Boat’s growth will have effects that will be felt across Connecticut more broadly. 
“This is just going to be one of those milestones that our children and grandchildren are going to experience,” said U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney. “It’s a big deal.”
A deeper economic shift
The hoped-for economic transformation, coming to a region that has long relied on the manufacturing industry, is expected to bring significant change, and thousands of new workers, to the area. 
Local officials are gearing up to meet the demand and figuring out how to support the workers expected to flood into the region in the coming years. The region is facing a housing shortage, with low stock and rising costs squeezing the market further. The area needs thousands of new homes to support the expected workforce. 
Still, the hope is that the influx will usher in a larger wave of economic activity in the region, rippling out from Electric Boat and driving increases in tourism, recreational activities and other industries. 

Rep. Joe Courtney speaks during a groundbreaking ceremony at Electric Boat’s Waterford Campus, the former Crystal Mall, on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Electric Boat says that for now, its focus is on meeting its hiring and workforce goals.
Local officials, meanwhile, say they are prepared to do their part as the region looks ahead. Hundreds of new housing units are in development, with more on the way. 
“We’ll support responsible housing. We’ll invest in infrastructure. We’ll continue to work closely with DECD. We’ll support our businesses and schools,” Brule said. “Growth isn’t about getting bigger; it’s about getting it right.”

name: WyoFile
title: Cheyenne Roundup: Decision 2026 | Wyoming primary results
authors: WyoFile staff and Wyoming Public Media
description:
Freedom Caucus candidates took a beating in Wyoming’s primary election. But MAGA Republicans found success in congressional races.
The post Cheyenne Roundup: Decision 2026 | Wyoming primary results appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Freedom Caucus candidates took a beating in Wyoming’s primary election. But MAGA Republicans found success in races for federal office. Plus, Democrats envision a new direction; details TBD.
Download the podcast episode.
Maggie Mullen: This is the Cheyenne Roundup: Decision 2026, a look at the candidates vying for Wyoming’s top elected positions, from Wyoming Public Radio and WyoFile.  
Jordan Uplinger: I’m Jordan Uplinger with Wyoming Public Radio.
MM: And I’m Maggie Mullen with WyoFile. 
JU: The primary was on Tuesday. We’re recording this on Thursday afternoon, Aug. 20.
MM: We finally got to hear from voters about the tug-of-war happening within the Republican Party. More than a dozen incumbent Freedom Caucus members and allies lost to challengers, stripping the bloc of its majority in the state House and failing in its goal to grow its members in the Senate.
JU: In the governor’s race, Eric Barlow beat out Trump-endorsed Megan Degenfelder and Brent Bien, who was backed by the Wyoming Republican Party in its first-ever round of endorsements.
MM: Voters swung the other way when we look at the federal races, where a founding member of the state Freedom Caucus took the GOP nomination for Congress, and Trump-backed Harriet Hageman found success in her bid to move from the House to the Senate.
JU: Let’s swan dive right into it.
MM: So, did the Freedom Caucus grow its power? Nope — much the opposite. It looks like the caucus will have about 10 reliable votes in the House. Some notable oustings include former caucus chairman John Bear of Gillette, founding member and Majority Floor Leader Scott Heiner of Green River, Ann Lucas of Cheyenne and Ocean Andrew of Laramie. Plus, Jeanette Ward of Casper and Mark Jennings of Sheridan, who previously served in the Legislature and were part of the caucus, also lost their bids to return to the House. 
Members and allies of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus, including, from left: Reps. Ann Lucas, Nina Webber, Scott Heiner, Bill Allemand, Joel Guggenmos and John Bear, as well as Ken Pendergraft, Pepper Ottman and Joe Webb (in back row, not visible), Rachel Williams and Darin McCann hold a press conference on the opening day of the 68th Wyoming Legislature’s budget session in Cheyenne. All pictured except for Bill Allemand and Pepper Ottman, who was uncontested in the primary election, lost their seats to challengers. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
JU: The caucus also failed to pick up any new seats in the House, and nine newcomers that would’ve likely carried the torch of their Freedom Caucus predecessors came up short.
MM: Bottom line is the caucus voting bloc is no longer big enough to thwart bills on introduction during budget sessions. That’s a tactic we’ve seen various voting blocs use to block legislation. 
JU: As a little bit of framing, Tuesday’s results come after the Freedom Caucus held a press conference in the Capitol rotunda toward the end of this year’s legislative budget session. They made a call for reinforcements to adopt a statewide library book policy, prohibit touchscreen voting machines, strengthen legal recourse if parents feel their rights have been violated and better public access to court documents.
MM: Which all failed, even with the caucus’ majority.
JU: Looking at the state Senate, voters rejected several prominent Freedom Caucus members’ attempts to move up from the House. Chip Neiman, current House speaker, came up short against Sen. Ogden Driskill in a closely watched race in Northeast Wyoming. Ken Pendergraft and Paul Hoeft also failed to move up. And Sen. Bob Ide lost his reelection bid.
MM: This leaves five reliable Freedom Caucus votes in the upper chamber, well below the 16 needed for a majority. My colleague, Maya Shimizu Harris, talked to Gail Symons, a long-time Wyoming politico and Freedom Caucus critic. She likened this year’s results to the flip in the opposite direction that happened in 2024. But she said this is a way larger scale than that.
Gail Symons: I think what happened is they weren’t paying attention to whose ox was being gored.
JU: The team at Wyoming Public Radio and KHOL in Jackson were talking to voters all day and we kind of heard inklings of that from the polls.
Jeanene Esterholt: I’m not sure I completely agree with the Freedom Caucus.  I’m glad they’re conservative. On the other hand, I don’t like the fact that there’s out-of-state places that are swaying our state officials to vote one way or another. 
Bob Woodall: In name only, that’s all they are, that they’re an out-of-state group that is trying to usurp Wyoming and bring their outside influence into our state. In the state Legislature, they’re changing all the rules. That’s why I had to vote, change my affiliation and make myself a RINO [Republican in name only] for the day.  
Kendra Cross:  We’re losing young people. We are losing people having the ability to pay their bills, to have services. We absolutely need strong, stable, reasonable leadership and no more extremism.  
JU: I was also bopping around a few watch parties in Cheyenne, and after some races were called, I made some calls myself. Jessica Crowder is a political newcomer with a career in ag. She beat out Freedom Caucus Rep. Ann Lucas with roughly 63% of the vote. Crowder told me a common question she heard on the campaign trail was, “Are you part of the Freedom Caucus?” 
Jessica Crowder: So it’s certainly on everyone’s mind, and it looks like there’s a shift across the state just based on the results of the night.
MM: For Wyoming’s top five statewide offices, again voters chose traditional Republicans.
JU: In the secretary of state’s race, current Freedom Caucus Chair Rep. Rachel Williams lost by more than 10 points to Converse County Commissioner Robert Short. Where Williams campaigned as a successor to the current secretary’s approach to managing elections and business filings, Short said he wanted to “make the office boring again.” 
Republican candidate for Wyoming Secretary of State Robert Short on Wednesday, July 15, 2026, during a candidate forum at the Albany County Public Library in Laramie. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
MM: Rep. Steve Harshman took the Republican nomination for superintendent of public instruction. He had about 60% of the vote over caucus ally Rep. Tom Kelly’s 31%. Chad Auer, who previously worked as Gov. Mark Gordon’s senior policy advisor, came in third place. 
JU: Worth mentioning: This race also saw a Democratic primary between political newcomer Ana Cordova and former Northern Arapaho Tribal Education Director Sergio Maldonado. Cordova took it with about 63%.
MM: For state treasurer, Curt Meier will have a third term after staving off a challenge from Lingle Rep. Scott Smith, who is listed as a member of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus and who earned the state GOP’s endorsement.  
JU: The governor’s race was an interesting one. You may remember from the many political ads flooding our TV, phones and YouTube, President Trump backed current Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder. While the state Republican Party put its weight behind retired civil engineer and military officer Brent Bien. 
MM: They both garnered about a quarter of the vote, well behind rancher-slash-state Senator Barlow’s 45%. Barlow campaigned on protecting public lands, funding education and solving Wyoming’s healthcare access and affordability issues.  
Republican gubernatorial candidate Eric Barlow speaks during a primary election candidate forum organized by the League of Women Voters of Wyoming on Wednesday, July 22, 2026 at Casper College. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)
JU: The last two times the governor’s seat was open in Wyoming, the Republican nominee handily won the general election. But Barlow will have competition in November.
MM: That comes from Democrat Kenneth Casner of Casper and Constitution Party candidate Rebecca Bextel of Jackson. You may remember earlier this year, Bextel hand-delivered campaign donation checks to lawmakers on the House floor after they’d adjourned for the day. 
JU: Ah yes, I think that was called “Checkgate.”
MM: That’s right. To close that loop: Nine out of the 10 lawmakers who received the $1,500 checks from Teton County donor Don Grasso lost their seats.
JU: Moving on up to the federal races, where Wyomingites had a lot of choices, especially in the congressional race.
MM: Current Secretary of State Chuck Gray carried the day over eight Republican competitors by a slim margin. 
JU: Didn’t we guess this race could be won with something like 25% of the vote?
MM: We sure did, and that’s exactly what happened.
JU: Gray was closely followed by Jackson conservative activist Steve Friess with 20%, Army vet Kevin Christensen with 17% and former Superintendent of Public Instruction Jillian Balow with 10%.
MM: This race really showcased the “big tent” of the Republican Party. Several candidates tried to position themselves as Trump acolytes, though the president did not make an endorsement in the race. Others ran more middle-of-the-road campaigns while a couple voiced opposition to some Trump administration policies, like Trump’s latest funding request for the war in Iran. 
JU: Despite that, after the race was called, candidates were quick to get voters to rally behind Gray.
MM: This was a spendy race, boosted by the candidates’ own money. Four loaned themselves over a million dollars. Gray said that he, like Trump, had to make that kind of investment to take on “the insiders and the media.”
JU: On the Senate side of things, Republican Harriet Hageman and Democrat James Byrd both won by landslides.
MM: Voters first elected Hageman to Congress in 2022 over Liz Cheney and again in 2024. This year she ran a $2 million MAGA campaign eight times larger than her closest competitor, Sam Mead. Mead is the nephew and great-grandson of two former Wyoming governors. He campaigned under the banner of protecting public lands. That struck a contrast with his opponent, who signed onto a Utah lawsuit that claimed the U.S. government’s ownership of land in Wyoming amounted to a justification for war. 
JU: I was at a watch party with Democrat James Byrd, a former state lawmaker and son of the first Black woman elected to the Wyoming Legislature. With MSNBC on a big TV and LED lights flashing, Byrd gave a speech to a small but energetic crowd, talking about a new Democratic Party approach, but I didn’t hear specifics on that idea.
MM: Byrd easily won over his opponent, Billy Benavidez, a greenskeeper from Sheridan. 
JU: If history tells us anything, Byrd has an uphill fight in the general election. The last time this seat was open in 2020, current U.S. Sen. Republican Cynthia Lummis handily won with about 73% of the vote over Democrat Merav Ben-David. But Byrd is undeterred.
MM: A quick programming and process note: We’ve been talking about unofficial results. The state canvassing board still needs to meet on Aug. 26 to certify the results. 
Jordan: It’s unlikely we’ll see any changes in the winners. This is really the process that counties and the state use to cross their Ts and dot their Is. It also gives counties time to run post-election audits. 
MM: For recounts, any race where the winner won by less than 1% will have an automatic recount. Candidates can also request a recount for their race by Aug. 24.
JU: I want to go back to audits, just for a second. This year’s primary and general elections also have a hand-count audit requirement. Clerks will assemble teams to count, by hand, about 5% of ballots cast in certain races. Election clerks we’ve talked to said they think this will be a good chance to show the machine tabulators that counties use are accurate.
MM: So, where does this leave us for the general election?
JU: Republicans are still likely to have a supermajority in the state House, as only 20 Democrats are running out of the 62 House Districts.
MM: We might see some Independent candidates file to run, too. There could also be minor and provisional party candidates, but that list hadn’t been posted by the time we recorded.
JU: A couple seats could see exciting contests come November. 
MM: I’m really curious to see whether this rebuke of the Freedom Caucus and its cut-and-slash budget approach carries over into November’s general election when voters will decide whether to approve a 50% property tax cut. 
JU: Thinking in the long term, I’m interested in the direction of the Democratic Party. James Byrd talked a lot about being a “new Democrat” [and] the state party has gone through some leadership changes. Even if they win all their races in the state Legislature, I don’t think they’re going to be driving policy anytime soon, but it will be interesting to see how they operate without the Wyoming Freedom Caucus majority in the Capitol.  
MM: Another thing I’ll be looking out for: The 69th Wyoming Legislature is gonna have a lot of freshman lawmakers, especially in the House. And there can be a steep learning curve to lawmaking, so they’ll have their work cut out for them when the next legislative session kicks off in January. 
JU: I’ll also be watching to see if the Freedom Caucus will keep up its tradition of wearing red jackets, their way of bringing attention to a potential budget deficit down the line, which was also the justification for the large quote “Spending Reductions” they wanted to make to the governor’s proposed budget earlier this year. 
MM: I’ll also want to point out that our current lawmakers — a lot of whom are losing their seats — are the ones currently working on committee bills that’ll be voted on in next year’s legislative session. They’re the ones shaping policy, so it’ll be interesting to see how the next few months go and how that legislation comes together.
JU: And I also want to point out: Ballpark, 150,000 Wyomingites voted in the primary. That’s about 55% of registered voters, but somewhere like 33% of voting-age Wyomingites.
Poll workers signal to voters as they enter the polling station during the 2026 Wyoming primary elections at North Christian Church on Tuesday, Aug. 18, in Cheyenne. (Dan Cepeda for Oil City News and WyoFile)
MM: The raw turnout numbers were second only to the 2022 midterms, the last time Wyoming’s top five elected positions were on the ballot and when Harriet Hageman successfully challenged Liz Cheney for Wyoming’s U.S. House seat. 
JU: We’re expecting to see more people at the polls for the general election on Nov. 3.
MM: We’ll be back with more Cheyenne Roundup before that, so check our feed.
MM: Thanks, as always, for listening to the Cheyenne Roundup: Decision 2026, a preview of Wyoming’s primary election races, from Wyoming Public Radio and WyoFile.
JU: Make sure to like this episode and subscribe wherever you get your podcasts.
MM: Editing and producing by Nicky Ouellet and Tennessee Watson. 
JU: Keep following our politics and state government reporting at wyomingpublicmedia.org and wyofile.com. Thanks for listening.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico U.S. Rep. Leger Fernández calls for investigation into toxic metals in fire retardants
description: U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) on Friday announced she and fellow members of Congress are urging a federal government watchdog agency to examine the prevalence and potential impacts of hazardous metals that may be present in retardants firefighters use in battling wildfires.
text:
U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández on Aug. 21, 2026, announced she and other members of Congress are seeking an investigation into the environmental and health impacts of fire retardants. Above: Leger Fernández and other officials tour a Mora County acequia Nov. 25, 2025, after elevated levels of toxic metals were detected in dozens of private wells.  (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) on Friday announced she and fellow members of Congress are urging a federal government watchdog agency to examine the prevalence and potential impacts of hazardous metals that may be present in retardants firefighters use in battling wildfires. 
Leger Fernández’s request to the U.S. Government Accountability Office cites unsafe levels of antimony, arsenic and uranium detected in dozens of Mora County private wells last November. The discovery prompted the New Mexico Health Department to issue a health alert. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While the cause of the spike in contaminants remains unknown, health officials noted at the time that the metals are regularly found in fire suppressants used to battle wildfires, including the 2022 Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon fire. 
Subsequent tests from the New Mexico Environment Department have found that levels of the heavy metals are within the limits of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s safe drinking water standards. 
Still, Leger Fernández, in a letter Aug. 4 to the GAO, noted that the United States Forest Service and federal Interior Department have continued to rely on dropping millions of gallons of fire retardant each year. According to her letter, federal agencies dropped nearly 50 million gallons of the material on landscapes in 2024. 
“This mass deployment of fire retardants has raised concerns about whether their use introduces risks to the environment and human health,” Leger Fernández and seven other members of Congress wrote. 
Her letter also cited a November 2024 academic study that estimated aerial retardant drops introduced nearly 840,000 pounds of toxic metals into the environment between 2009 and 2021. 
Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire victims grapple with latest crisis

GAO spokesperson Sarah Kaczmarek told Source NM in an email Friday that the office had received the request and is currently evaluating whether and when to conduct the investigation lawmakers requested. 
The letter asks the office to examine and provide recommendations related to how prevalent the metals are in fire retardants and the potential impacts of retardants on watersheds and human health, including firefighters. It also asks the office to identify alternative, less-harmful fire retardants and other best practices for firefighters. 
“When families finally return home to communities destroyed by wildfires, they should not have to worry if the water coming out of their tap is safe to drink,” the letter says. “This will be a question that more families ask as wildfires continue to threaten communities across the West.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota Sen. Kevin Cramer vows to block future Trump nominees over federal wetlands rule
description: U.S. Sen. Kevin Cramer says he will block confirmation of future Trump nominees until the administration changes a Biden-era wetlands rule he said tramples on farmers. Cramer, R-N.D., said the rule violates private property rights by creating enormous setbacks for drain tile from wetland easements. Those easements are pieces of private land the U.S. Fish […]
text:
North Dakota Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer talks to media July 1, 2026, in Medora, North Dakota, before a speech from President Donald Trump. (Photo by Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)U.S. Sen. Kevin Cramer says he will block confirmation of future Trump nominees until the administration changes a Biden-era wetlands rule he said tramples on farmers.
Cramer, R-N.D., said the rule violates private property rights by creating enormous setbacks for drain tile from wetland easements. Those easements are pieces of private land the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service purchased years ago to permanently protect habitat. Drain tile is plastic pipe that carries away excess moisture.
Cramer said he recently called President Donald Trump to address the matter. The rule majorly affects North Dakota because the state makes up a large portion of the Prairie Pothole Region, he said. That wetland area is important habitat for ducks and geese. 
“This is a left-wing, environmentalist extremist dream rule,” Cramer told the North Dakota Monitor.
North Dakota program seeks to transform less productive cropland into wildlife habitat

Last month, Fish and Wildlife asked for public comments on the 2024 rule. On Aug. 14, the agency said “no further action is planned” as it reviews feedback from more than 200,000 commenters.
“Our administration is dedicated to protecting both the wetland easements purchased by the FWS that are necessary to protect our conservation heritage as well as the private landowners’ use of their lands outside the easement boundaries,” Fish and Wildlife said on social media.
It’s unclear where the agency’s process will go next. Fish and Wildlife did not respond to an email and an online message from the Monitor.
Cramer said, “The Fish and Wildlife Service can say they’re pausing, but as I said, I can’t pause my aggression.”
The senator said he called Trump on Wednesday night when no other officials would call him back. Trump asked how he could fix it and said he planned to call Interior Secretary and former North Dakota Gov. Doug Burgum, according to Cramer. Fish and Wildlife is housed within the Interior Department. 
“I’m more optimistic today than I was before,” Cramer said late Thursday.
The Senate is in recess until Sept. 14. Cramer said he already has put a hold on every pending nominee, which would cause a significant disruption to the chamber’s business if the holds are still in place when senators return to Washington next month.
Cramer said he told Trump the administration needs to evaluate the comments and “pull the pause off of the action.” 
“That’s all you have to do: restore the process that they were under and utilizing,” Cramer said. Ultimately, a class-action lawsuit by farmers might be necessary, he said. 
The issue at hand is Fish and Wildlife and the Natural Resources Conservation Service, both federal government agencies, are playing by different rules when it comes to drain tile setbacks, said Ryan Wanzek, whose family farms in east-central North Dakota in the Prairie Pothole Region. 
“They’ve changed the goalposts,” Wanzek said.
His family farm in Stutsman County has not tiled on easement land because it’s not worth drawing up the plans only to have the federal agencies change their minds, he said.
“It makes it harder for us as farmers to go and get a clear answer when we’ve got two different agencies, both run by the same administration, telling us two different things,” Wanzek said. 
Many wetland easements house zero wildlife and are basically white, salty soil farmers cannot improve, Wanzek said.
“Whether you like it or not, if there’s crop there, it houses wildlife. It feeds the wildlife. If there’s not crop there and it’s white, salty soils, it’s not doing anything for the wildlife,” he said.
The North Dakota Wildlife Federation supports the rule. The rule ensures habitat for ducks and protection for compliant landowners if their easements dry up, Federation Executive Director John Bradley said. The rule also takes soil types and hydrology into account, complex factors that aren’t blanket standards, he said.
The Dakotas produce more than 50% of North America’s mallards, blue-winged teal, pintails, gadwalls and other game ducks, Bradley said. North Dakota has an important job to protect wetlands for everybody, he said.
Landowners were fairly compensated for the easements in the first place, Bradley said. Hunters’ duck stamp dollars purchased the easements, he said. Cramer’s comments are out of touch with the everyday North Dakota duck hunter, he said. 
“To say that it’s either these rich Southern duck hunters or radical environmentalists who have concerns or vested interest in keeping these wetlands – certainly, I’m sure some do, but that glosses over the average duck hunter of North Dakota,” Bradley said. 
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura can be reached at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Legal Marijuana NOW Senate candidate endorses Osborn after suspending campaign
description: Mike Marvin has denied being a plant for Osborn – but his move will likely add fuel to those claims from Republicans.
text:
The official logo for Nebraska's Legal Marijuana NOW party. (Logo courtesy the party | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Legal Marijuana NOW U.S. Senate candidate Mike Marvin announced he can’t put more “energy” into the Senate race because of health issues and endorsed nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn.
“For me, this has always been about defeating Pete Ricketts, and with my worsening condition, I know I cannot put in the effort this race requires,” Marvin said in a statement. “I will be remaining on the ballot, but I am now urging all who supported me to now support Dan Osborn.” 
Marvin didn’t offer specifics of his health problems but said he retired from the Nebraska Association of Public Employees in 2017 for the same reason. He said for anyone who believes “in the cause of the Legal Marijuana Now Party, the choice in this election could not be clearer.”
“Dan has a real chance to beat Pete Ricketts in November if we all get behind him,” Marvin said. 
This announcement comes hours after reporting from the Flatwater Free Press that two Osborn-paid staffers of the 2024 campaign joined an effort to dissolve Legal Marijuana NOW last year. Marvin has been one of the candidates accused of being  “plants” meant to help either incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts or Osborn. Former Democratic Senate nominee Cindy Burbank paid Marvin’s $1,740 candidate filing fee earlier this year. She dropped out of the race one day after the secretary of state verified Osborn’s signatures to be on the fall ballot.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Marvin has denied being a plant for Osborn – but his move will likely add fuel to those claims from Republicans. 
He told the Examiner earlier this month that he never planned to leave the race. Legal Marijuana NOW Party officials said they have never interacted with Marvin. While Marvin is technically still on the ballot, the move might inch the race between Osborn and Ricketts to a “head-to-head” race.  
Legal Marijuana NOW has been part of the twists and turns of this year’s Nebraska Senate race, as well as the 2024 race between Osborn and Republican U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer. 
The Nebraska Democratic Party is facing pending litigation over its effort to clear the field for Osborn, brought by William Forbes, another candidate who was accused of being a plant — a charge he has also denied. 
Forbes was registered as a Republican until 2008 but has been a Democrat since, according to records obtained by the Examiner. The state Democratic central committee will vote this weekend on whether to fill a vacancy caused by Burbank’s dropping out. 
Osborn, in a statement to the Examiner, said he appreciates Marvin’s support and wishes “him well on his health.”
“We hope to earn the support of the LMN voters and hope that we can represent their concerns well in the US Senate,” Osborn said. 
Jessica Flanagain, a consultant for Ricketts, posted on Twitter about the news: “Shocking!”
The general election is Nov 3.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Republican CD2 candidates will debate after all; Mellor, Skoly accept invite from NBC10
description: Ten days ago, it wasn’t looking like Vic Mellor and Dr. Stephen Skoly would meet for a debate ahead of the Sept. 9 Republican primary in Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District. It turns out the pair of Republican candidates — both vying to face Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner on the ballot for the November […]
text:
Republicans Dr. Stephen Skoly, left, and Vic Mellor, right, face off in the Sept. 9 primary for Rhode Island's 2nd Congressional District seat. The winner will face Democratic U.S. Sen. Seth Magaziner in the November general election. (Contributed photos)Ten days ago, it wasn’t looking like Vic Mellor and Dr. Stephen Skoly would meet for a debate ahead of the Sept. 9 Republican primary in Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District. 
It turns out the pair of Republican candidates — both vying to face Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner on the ballot for the November general election — will meet for a televised debate after all.
NBC 10 WJAR plans to host a primary debate between the two candidates on Friday, Sept. 4, the station’s Assistant News Director Dan Paquet confirmed. 
The debate will be taped at WJAR’s Cranston studio that afternoon and is set to air over the weekend twice: first on Saturday, Sept. 5, at 5:30 a.m., and again on Sunday, Sept. 6 at noon.
Mellor declines ‘stunt’ RI GOP debate with Skoly in CD2 primary

Paquet told Rhode Island Current in an email that the debate was organized by the TV station as part of its primary election planning process, rather than at the request of the campaigns.
Mellor spokesperson Jen Nerbonne confirmed to Rhode Island Current that Mellor will participate. 
“WJAR reached out to invite Vic to the debate, and he happily accepted,” Nerbonne said.
Mia Iannotti, a spokesperson for the Skoly campaign, confirmed Friday that Skoly, an oral and maxillofacial surgeon from East Greenwich who won the Rhode Island GOP endorsement in June, will participate. 
The Sept. 4 debate will happen more than two weeks after early voting began Thursday. 
Skoly had wanted to debate Mellor before early voting began. Skoly shared his stated terms for a state GOP-hosted debate online on Aug. 10.
Skoly accepted the invitation on Aug. 4, the same day invites went out, but Mellor ultimately declined about a week later.
Dr. Stephen Skoly, a Republican candidate for Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District, walks through a campaign event at Marasco’s in Cranston on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Mellor, who withdrew from consideration of the GOP’s endorsement in June, objected to the state Republican outfit hosting the debate. 
“I’m not participating in a Facebook event managed by the same people who already endorsed my opponent and have been attacking me,” Mellor said in an Aug. 12 statement. “I will debate Dr. Skoly on Channel 10, Channel 6, Channel 12 — any real television station with an actual audience of Rhode Island voters.”
Mellor additionally countered that Skoly had refused a debate in June hosted by the West Warwick Republican Town Committee.
“It was a bar, a small bar in West Warwick, hosted by a committee that was working against the Republican Party, and I’m like, ‘no,’” Skoly said in an interview before a campaign event Tuesday outside Marasco’s in Cranston.
He told supporters Tuesday night that the June 9 event was advertised at first as a meet-and-greet but later transformed into a debate proper, which he found disingenuous and lacking in transparency. 
“Nobody had attained a position on the ballot, and it was not in the position of one of the local Republican parties to hold the first statewide Republican debate,” Skoly said on the mic. “That was going to be up to the party.”
The candidate was firm on Tuesday that he was still up for a match. 
“If somebody can work out an appropriate debate, I would still debate him,” Skoly said.
Skoly said that he had entered the race with “the Hippocratic oath” in mind, and at first sought to do no harm to his primary opponent.
But Skoly stressed that “the voters and the constituents, they need to know who has the best chance. If they really want change, they need to know who has the best chance to take on the Democratic ideology here.”
“I think if we can’t get by the primary, this candidate [Mellor] will get destroyed in a general election,” Skoly told the approximately 50 supporters gathered Tuesday night for his town hall event.
Mellor’s campaign, as well as his biography, have drawn scrutiny both in and outside the Republican party. An Aug. 17 Providence Journal article detailing Mellor’s campaign financing — prompted in part by a recent series of sleuthing tweets from former GOP gubernatorial candidate Ashley Kalus — raised questions about the source of more than $2 million Mellor reported loaning his campaign. 
Rhode Island Current submitted questions about campaign finances to Mellor, which acknowledged the inquiry and said it was still working on responses.
Accounting specifics aside, Mellor enters the final weeks of the primary with more cash at his disposal. His campaign reported $1.44 million on hand as of June 30, compared with about $52,700 for Skoly. 
Also in June, Mellor reported nearly $2.9 million total receipts through June, with most of it coming from his own contributions and loans to the campaign.
The winner of the Sept. 9 primary will face Magaziner in the Nov. 3 general election.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Experts skewer new Trump administration analysis claiming noncitizens voted in 2020
description: This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access. President Donald Trump this week unveiled another effort by his administration to raise questions about the outcome of the 2020 election he lost: an unusual U.S. Census Bureau analysis concluding with “high confidence” th[...]
text:
President Donald Trump in Rochester, days before Election Day 2020. Trump has continued to struggle to come to terms with his defeat. (Photo by Ricardo Lopez/Minnesota Reformer)This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access.
President Donald Trump this week unveiled another effort by his administration to raise questions about the outcome of the 2020 election he lost: an unusual U.S. Census Bureau analysis concluding with “high confidence” that 24,000 noncitizens illegally voted in the 2020 election.
Trump touted the finding on social media and wrote that it supports his long-running false claims that he actually won the 2020 election.
But experts said there are substantial questions about the Census Bureau study’s methodology and validity. And even if 24,000 noncitizens had voted in 2020, it wouldn’t have been enough to change the election’s outcome.
The seven-page Census Bureau report said researchers examined more than 128 million voters in the 2020 presidential election and determined with “high confidence” that more than 24,000 of them were noncitizens. If so, that number would be less than 0.019% of the sample.
Trump said census researchers are still analyzing another 32 million voters and predicted that the number of illegal noncitizen votes would “explode” after that was done.
The Census Bureau did not respond to a request for comment. But experts said some aspects of the bureau’s release raise fundamental questions.
Most Census Bureau reports identify the authors of the report and detail the reliability of the data they are using. This analysis did neither.
“A properly done Census report would have had that information and the fact that it is missing is glaring and makes me think that they are hiding something,” said Beth Jarosz, a senior fellow at Georgetown University’s Massive Data Institute who has worked as a contractor on Census Bureau reports.
Terri Ann Lowenthal, who served as staff director for the U.S. House of Representatives subcommittee overseeing the Census Bureau from 1987 to 1994, said the report’s minimal methodological information raised questions about the accuracy of the results.
Lowenthal said the report was “beneath the Census Bureau’s stellar reputation.” The failure to include the names of any career staff members, she said, suggested that the work may have been done by someone with a political agenda “and may not reflect the sound, reputable analysis for which the Census Bureau is known.”
Trump administration searches for noncitizen voters
Trump has focused the efforts of his second administration on rooting out voter fraud, especially any instance of illegal voting by noncitizens, which audits, investigations, and studies have found happens only rarely. But the federal government doesn’t possess a comprehensive database of citizens, and efforts to match different data sets have so far yielded inaccurate results.
The administration pushed states to run millions of records of registered voters through a revamped federal data tool to check if they were citizens. But election officials found the system, which cross-referenced federal records from various federal agencies, in some cases erroneously flagged citizens. In June, a federal judge blocked the use of the overhauled tool, finding it threatened privacy and voting rights.
In a televised primetime speech on July 16, Trump said his administration had found more than 250,000 noncitizen voters on the voter rolls of just four states: New Jersey, California, Pennsylvania, and Nevada. Officials in all four states pushed back on Trump’s claims and said they didn’t understand how the administration arrived at those numbers. The Trump administration has yet to provide any detail on its methodology in that case either.
The president has lobbied for federal legislation to require people registering to vote to prove their citizenship, and he repeated that call when releasing the Census Bureau findings Tuesday, describing it as his highest legislative priority. But the effort has stalled in the U.S. Senate. He has also released two sweeping executive orders on elections, but their major provisions have been so far blocked by federal courts.
Questions surround Trump administration’s data analysis
The voting data used in the analysis was provided by Data-Clear, a business in Virginia that secured an $885,000 Census Bureau contract from former President Joe Biden’s administration in 2024. Carolyn Carlson, Data-Clear’s president and founder, said she provided nationwide voting data to the bureau that year as part of a project to try and prevent an undercount of minority voters in the 2030 census.
Carlson said she was surprised to see the data she provided used in the new review of noncitizen voters.
The report says the Census Bureau matched the Data-Clear voter files with federal immigration records to determine if people were citizens and eligible to vote. The report offers only general descriptions of how and when it was able to match verifiable information.
Justin Levitt, an election law specialist at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles who worked in the Biden White House on voting rights issues, said a typical analysis would include caveats around the possible margin of error, and the 24,000 figure for noncitizen voters could be within it. However, the Census Bureau report doesn’t specify one.
“In most statistical exercises, it’s not unthinkable that there might be 0.019% false positives – and if that were the case here, that would turn the total conclusions to zero,” he said.
Should the analysis hold up to scrutiny, the underlying numbers showed that they would not involve enough voters to change the result of the 2020 election. The report said it found 500 noncitizens illegally cast ballots in Wisconsin, which Trump lost to Biden by more than 20,000 votes. The survey said it identified 1,100 noncitizens who cast ballots in Arizona, which Trump lost by more than 10,000 votes. And the report cannot say whether those voters supported Trump or Biden.
In response to questions about whether the release supported the president’s assertion, the White House responded with a link to a social media post by U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
Dion Nissenbaum is Votebeat’s senior national reporter and is based in Houston. Contact Dion at dnissenbaum@votebeat.org.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: NH silent as neighboring governors sound the alarm on proposed utility merger
description: Gov. Kelly Ayotte was absent from a joint letter released on Tuesday by the other five New England governors containing strongly worded opposition to a proposed merger between the utilities NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy. The proposed union would create the largest regulated utility in the world, according to NextEra, and bring New England’s two […]
text:
The proposed union would create the largest regulated utility in the world, according to NextEra. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)Gov. Kelly Ayotte was absent from a joint letter released on Tuesday by the other five New England governors containing strongly worded opposition to a proposed merger between the utilities NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy.
The proposed union would create the largest regulated utility in the world, according to NextEra, and bring New England’s two remaining active nuclear power plants under the same ownership. This includes New Hampshire’s Seabrook Station, which is owned by NextEra Energy subsidiary NextEra Energy Resources.
New Hampshire Consumer Advocate Don Kreis said he was “extremely skeptical” about the proposed merger. But his office has not yet taken a stance, either, he said, adding, “I can’t argue with the governor’s decision to think more about it, as well.”
In fact, consumer advocates from across New England are still studying the merger, Kreis said, and are in the process of requesting a deadline extension for the comment period before the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.
But the governors of Maine, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Connecticut were clear in their stance, writing that the union would concentrate an “unprecedented amount of leverage” in NextEra, which they said had exhibited “anticompetitive” behavior in its past dealings in the region.
“The states’ concern that these companies will act to disrupt and delay infrastructure development is not hypothetical,” reads the statement issued by the New England States Committee on Electricity. 
NextEra Energy is headquartered in Florida. Dominion Energy, an electric utility based in Virginia, is smaller than NextEra but still a sprawling company, including ownership and operation of Connecticut’s Millstone Power Station.
In the statement, the five governors said NextEra had exerted its significant influence already to disrupt needed infrastructure projects in New England. 
They cited NextEra’s opposition to the New England Clean Energy Connect project, a transmission corridor completed early this year that brings hydropower from Quebec through Maine and into Massachusetts.
Acting through community groups and campaign donations, NextEra was involved in an attempt to derail the project, according to reporting by MainePublic. The utility also resisted making updates to its own infrastructure that were necessary to move the project forward, according to the New England governors’ letter. The U.S. District Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ultimately forced NextEra to complete that work, ruling the resistance was “anticompetitive,” according to the statement.
And the utility has “demonstrated disregard for consumers and affordability” in previous infrastructure project proposals, they said.
NextEra did not respond to a request for comment.
The joint letter was issued by the New England States Committee on Electricity, a not-for-profit entity that represents the interests of New England’s governors in regional electricity matters. Ayotte also did not respond to a question about the decision not to join the letter.
Each state’s executive branch is represented on the committee by designees; New Hampshire’s representatives are Department of Energy Commissioner Jared Chicoine and Regional Policy Director Dan Phelan. 
More research by the states’ consumer advocates will illuminate whether consolidating ownership of the two nuclear plants will have a significant impact on energy prices in New England, Kreis said.
The offices are in the process of asking FERC to extend the comment deadline by 2 months, into November, he said. 
The five governors’ letter was “very strongly worded,” Kreis said. But, he added, NextEra does “assert themselves very aggressively.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: JTRAN workers will return Monday under new contract that hikes pay and benefits
description: A post for the 60 line for JTRAN sits outside of Union Station in downtown Jackson on Wednesday, June 17, 2026.
text:
JTRAN employees will return to work Monday under a new tentative agreement with MV Transportation, putting an end to the monthlong strike between the two parties.
Employees will see an immediate 5% increase in their base pay under the new contract and an additional 3% increase over the next two years. Under the old contract, starting pay was $17.18 an hour with senior workers receiving $23 an hour.
The proposal was ratified Thursday by a 29–9 vote and addresses the union’s demands for better pay and benefits.
“We’re just glad that it’s over,” Local 1208 union president Charles Tornes Jr.  said. “It’s hot out there in Jackson, Mississippi, weather.”
The final agreement is set to be voted on next week.
A spokesperson for MV Transportation was not immediately available.
The new agreement also addresses union concerns with MV Transportation’s previous proposal to the city. The plan sought to cut two bus routes, eliminate Saturday service and allow MV to hire drivers without commercial licenses for microtransit services, a ride-hailing system. 
A JATRAN bus sits at Union Station in Jackson on Wednesday, June 17, 2026. Credit: Aaron Lampley/Mississippi Today
JTRAN routes 70 and 20 — which provide service to the Ellis and Woodrow Wilson neighborhoods — will continue in addition to Saturday service. MV is limited to hiring five drivers without a commercial license but the limit rises to seven if JTRAN falls beneath 40 active workers. 
Additional provisions add Martin Luther King Jr. day to the holiday calendar and creates an accident review board within the company. The board will include one representative from the Amalgamated Transit Union and MV Transportation.
While the agreement serves as a win for both sides, compromises were made. The union did not gain lunch breaks. Provisions for workplace incidents will remain the same — meaning employees will go unpaid if placed on administrative leave. 
Tornes said some of the issues not agreed upon are still a work in progress.
Though publicly funded, JTRAN employees have worked for private Texas-based company MV Transportation since 2024 under a $9 million contract with the city. The contract is set to expire Dec. 31, 2027. 
Tornes told Misissippi Today that he doesn’t see a path forward with MV and predicts that another company will take over once bids reopen.
“Companies come and go. But at the end of the day, we’ve been chartered since 1939 at JTRAN ATU. We’re gonna be there”
The two parties had been negotiating a new agreement since December after their previous contract expired. Tensions boiled over in late May after union members learned that Mayor Horn’s administration was planning to present MV’s proposal to the city council — something members previously said would undermine their negotiations. 
JTRAN employees would vote to strike two weeks later.
The company’s contingency plan, which was sought by the city, saw outside workers flown into Jackson in order to continue bus services. 
In a paratransit meeting on July 15, MV senior vice president Leland Paterson said 11 of 12 fixed routes were on the road and that they were 50% on time the first day workers went on strike. Mississippi Today reached out to MV Transportation for updated statistics but MV did not respond prior to publication. 
This is not the first time a strike has happened under the city’s contract with MV Transportation. JTRAN workers previously went on strike in September 2024—halting all bus services in the city for 14 days. The strike ended after seven mediated sessions.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Medicaid to cover doula care in Arkansas in September with rule’s passage
description: Low-income expectant parents in Arkansas should be able to have their doula care covered by Medicaid starting Sept. 1, Elizabeth Pitman, director of the Division of Medical Services for Arkansas Medicaid, told lawmakers Thursday. The Arkansas Legislative Council on Friday approved the rules for Medicaid’s coverage of doulas, part of a 2025 law requiring the[...]
text:
The Arkansas Department of Human Services building on Main Street in downtown Little Rock. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)Low-income expectant parents in Arkansas should be able to have their doula care covered by Medicaid starting Sept. 1, Elizabeth Pitman, director of the Division of Medical Services for Arkansas Medicaid, told lawmakers Thursday.
The Arkansas Legislative Council on Friday approved the rules for Medicaid’s coverage of doulas, part of a 2025 law requiring the program and private insurance to cover such services for Arkansans. The council’s rules subcommittee gave preliminary approval Thursday.
Doulas provide emotional, physical, educational and logistical support to parents-to-be and serve as middlemen between them and other medical professionals. The coverage requirement law was aimed at improving the state’s maternal health outcomes.
Madison Jones of Cabot said she’s looking forward to having a doula’s help when she has her second child in December. She could not afford a doula when she had her first child in 2024, and “another voice in the delivery room” would have helped her push back against the medical professionals that didn’t respect her wishes for her birth plan, she said.
“It’s really hard to speak for yourself when you’re in the middle of a huge transition, a painful transition at that, and you can’t really put your focus into both,” Jones said.
There’s one more bureaucratic hurdle to clear before the state can fully implement the policy: enrolling certified community-based doulas in the program, said Annie Hill, who runs the Bright Blessings doula service in Cabot.

Delayed insurance coverage for doula services frustrates Arkansas parents and providers


Hill said she hopes the state can fast-track enrollment so as many clients as possible can receive care starting Sept. 1 as promised. She also said Medicaid reimbursement will not be financially profitable for her business but will broadly expand her client base.
“I’m incredibly excited that we’re this close to putting it into practice,” Hill said.
DHS missed the legally required Dec. 31, 2025 deadline to put forth the Medicaid coverage rules for public comment, drawing frustration from doulas and their clients who hoped Medicaid would cover their 2026 births. Private insurance companies also were not yet covering doula care in Arkansas at that time, doulas and clients both said.
After DHS made the rules public in February and collected feedback, the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services “engaged in multiple rounds of reviews and questions” before approving the rules in July, DHS spokesperson Gavin Lesnick said.
Insurance coverage for doula care was among the recommendations from a task force Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders created in 2024 to improve Arkansas’ maternal healthcare landscape. Arkansas consistently has among the nation’s highest maternal and infant mortality rates.
Additionally, rural Arkansans face increasingly long drives to hospitals that deliver babies. Several labor and delivery units have closed due to financial strain in the past several years, leaving 53 of Arkansas’ 75 counties without delivering hospitals.
Drive time to Arkansas hospitals for labor and delivery getting longer, report shows

A 2022 study from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists found that longer drives to delivering hospitals increase the risk of health problems for mothers and newborns.
Hill is working to spread the word to expectant parents in Cabot that the state is making doula care more affordable. Biliah Muhammad owns an indoor playground and said she’s advertising the policy to low-income parents among her customers.
Muhammad said she was on Medicaid when she gave birth in February and would have appreciated being able to afford Hill’s services.
“That help wasn’t available to me, and now it is, and we can spread the word and help other mamas who can’t afford it [otherwise],” she said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Republicans on the NC elections board agree to drop Sunday early voting hours in 10 more counties
description: When members of county boards of election disagreed on whether to offer Sunday hours during early voting for this year’s midterm elections, the NC Board of Elections usually went along with plans to cut them.  Ten North Carolina counties that had Sunday voting in the last midterm election won’t have any this year as a […]
text:
The NC State Board of Elections met on Aug. 20 to consider early voting plans for 20 counties. Republicans voted to eliminate Sunday hours in 10 counties that had them four years ago. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)When members of county boards of election disagreed on whether to offer Sunday hours during early voting for this year’s midterm elections, the NC Board of Elections usually went along with plans to cut them. 
Ten North Carolina counties that had Sunday voting in the last midterm election won’t have any this year as a result of state Board of Elections votes this week.
The state board met Thursday to consider early voting plans for 20 counties where local boards of election could not agree on locations, dates, or times.
The Republican majority on the state Board of Elections agreed with decisions of GOP majorities in Anson, Chatham, Columbus, Greene, Harnett, Nash, Pasquotank, Pitt, Union, and Wayne – counties that opened polls on Sundays for voting four years ago – to drop those hours this year. 
Thursday’s decisions continued the contraction of Sunday voting since Republicans took majorities on the state Board of Elections and county boards last year. 
Election boards in about a dozen counties that had Sunday hours in 2022 had already agreed in their unanimous plans to drop them for this fall’s general election, NC Newline reported.
In addition to those ten counties, Lenoir dropped Sunday voting this year. Lenoir elections board members could not agree on an early voting plan, but neither of the options they asked state board members to consider included Sunday hours. 
The partisan disagreement over Sunday voting goes back for years. Democrats have largely supported them, while Republicans are generally opposed. That pattern continued this week in 3-2, party-line votes with Republicans on the state board approving early voting plans that didn’t include Sundays. 
Sunday voting supporters knew those hours were in serious danger of getting chopped. 
A former staffer in state Auditor Dave Boliek’s office, Dallas Woodhouse, encouraged county board chairs to drop Sunday hours. Woodhouse is a political operative and former state Republican Party executive director whom Boliek hired to work with county boards. 
NC auditor’s office liaison invoked state GOP wishes in some county early voting plans

At a rally Thursday, the Rev. Dr. Floyd Wicker of the Lillington First Missionary Baptist Church in Harnett County spoke against cutting Sunday hours, which are important to Black and brown voters.  
“It appears that some people on our state Board of Elections are trying to make it more difficult for people in my community to vote,” he said. 
Republicans argued that Sundays should be reserved for church and family, that opening polls on Sunday isn’t worth the cost, and that Sundays are burdensome and boring for poll workers. 
Democrats argued that Sunday voting hours are important for people who work long or irregular hours, people with long commutes, and people with care-giving responsibilities. 
Older people who don’t drive may only be able to vote in person on Sundays, when family members are available to provide transportation, supporters said. 
In an attempt to refute claims that Sundays are not cost effective, some county board members said Sunday hours cost less per vote. Sunday hours only appear to be under-used, they said, because polls are open only a few hours on Sundays. 
Betsy McCormick, a Democrat on the Harnett board, told state board members that in 2024, the county’s early voting sites served 31 voters per hour on weekdays and 32.5 voters per hour on Sunday. 
Eight percent of early voters cast ballots on Sunday that year, she said, while Sunday hours were only 5% of the total early voting hours available.  
“Sunday voting hours are a cost effective way to provide a wider range of voters the opportunity to cast their vote,” McCormick said.
Krista Savage-White traveled to the NC State Board of Elections meeting August 20, 2026 from rural Gates County.  Savage-White was concerned about a proposal to cut Sunday early voting in Pasquotank County and move the county’s early voting site away from the K.E. White Graduate Center on the Elizabeth City State University (ECSU) campus. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)
Danny Moody, chair of the Harnett County Board of Elections, told the state board that Sunday voting traffic is light, and that he heard no complaints about a lack of Sunday hours for this year’s primaries. 
“I do not believe that Sunday is needed, or perhaps wanted, in Harnett County,” Moody said. At one of the county’s sites, only four people voted on a Sunday in 2020, he said. 
The voting rights group Democracy North Carolina denounced the cuts. 
“The cuts to Sunday voting in many counties will have a chilling effect on voters, full stop,” Brian Kennedy, policy director for Democracy NC , said in a statement. “Cutting Sunday hours and sites not only has a huge impact on working families, it also creates confusion in communities who have grown accustomed to certain hours and locations being available to them during elections.”
Though he is no longer a Boliek employee, Woodhouse has been active in the last week promoting early voting plans. 
Democrats’ objects are rooted in partisan anger over not controlling elections, Woodhouse wrote on X.
“It’s a proud day for North Carolina voters and for me personally, as the GOP-majority State Board gave final approval to a comprehensive 2026 early-voting plan that offers unprecedented voter access for any North Carolina midterm election in history, as measured by total voting sites, total voting hours and even weekend hours,” Woodhouse wrote.

title: US Supreme Court allows $400M Trump ballroom project to proceed
text: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump can continue building a White House ballroom for now, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled Friday, reversing a federal judge's order that barred above-ground construction on the grounds of the former East Wing.The one-page order from Chief Justice John Roberts allows the justices more time to consider the legal arguments as to whether the president can continue with construction. The National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States, a nonprofit Congress created to protect public buildings, sued to block construction late last year. The group charged that Trump violated the U.S. Constitution and federal law when he demolished part of the White House last July without approval from Congress. The trust wrote in its brief to the high court that the trial court’s pause should remain in place because any progress on the project could not easily be undone.“We are grateful for the Decision of the United States Supreme Court,” Trump wrote on social media after the order. “The Military/Ballroom Complex being built on the hallowed grounds of the White House, which is so vital for National Security, will be THE GREATEST OF ITS KIND! Construction is under budget and ahead of schedule.”Trump has argued the 90,000-square-foot ballroom — which the administration said this month will cost $400 million, double the initial estimate — is needed to reinforce security features and provide a larger space to host foreign dignitaries. Trump has said the project is being funded with private donations.The East Wing of the White House was built in 1942. Workers last October demolished it, even after Trump said the ballroom construction would not impact the building. A federal appeals court this month upheld the lower court order that barred further construction of the ballroom above ground, but allowed for below-ground construction. The appeals court stayed its decision for 14 days to give the administration time to appeal to the Supreme Court.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Beef producers ‘disappointed’ by Trump tariff suspension
description: President Donald Trump announced Friday he was suspending tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of imported ground beef to help lower the cost of the meat, in a move cattle producers said would not help their efforts to restore herd sizes.  The president made the announcement in a Truth Social post where he said the imported […]
text:
The Trump administration plans to exempt tariffs on ground beef imports for 90-days in an effort to lower prices of the meat. (Photo by Preston Keres/USDA) President Donald Trump announced Friday he was suspending tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of imported ground beef to help lower the cost of the meat, in a move cattle producers said would not help their efforts to restore herd sizes. 
The president made the announcement in a Truth Social post where he said the imported beef will be sold at 25% below the current market prices.
“This deal will reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again,” Trump wrote in the post. 
National Cattlemen’s Beef Association CEO Colin Woodall said “flooding” the market with “government-subsidized, below-market beef” would not help producers to “rebuild the American cattle herd,” which continues to decline. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the most recent cattle report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, the nation’s herd size is “up slightly” from where it sat in July 2025. Even with the slight increase from the year prior, the cattle and calves inventory – at 94.2 million head – is at about the same level it was in the 1950s. 
Iowa Cattlemen’s Association President Craig Moss said the association was “extremely disappointed” by Trump’s announcement and said it has already “created unnecessary market volatility.”
Cattle market reports from Friday showed “crashing futures” because of the Trump announcement. 
“The drop in the markets will directly impact their profitability and bottom line, and in turn impacts decisions our producers are making about expanding their cattle herds,” Moss said in a statement. “We believe the government should avoid intervention and let the market work.”
At the same time, the price of ground beef has been on a steep increase since around 2023, which was the last time a pound of ground chuck was below $5 per pound. The price, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, has not dropped below $6 per pound since April 2025. 
In his Truth Social post, the president blamed his predecessor Joe Biden for the hike in prices, claiming beef prices “soared at their fastest rate” under the Democratic president. Consumer Price Index data shows ground chuck rose from $4.31 in January 2021 when Biden took office, to $5.58 in December 2024. Prices have risen to $6.85 in the year and a half Trump has been in the office. 
Moss said consumer demand for “high-quality beef raised by U.S. producers has remained strong” and argued that consumers have been “willing to pay for beef.” 
Hinson sides with beef producers
U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, speaking with reporters at the Iowa State Fair Friday, said Trump’s recent decision to increase beef imports was a “bad idea.” 
“We grow the highest quality beef here in Iowa, and so absolutely, I’ll be advocating to the administration because I think we need to be focusing on growing the herd the right way and protecting our cattlemen,” Hinson said. 
Hinson is running for U.S. Senate against Democrat Josh Turek, who has been critical of past efforts to import beef and has called for mandatory country of origin labeling to support U.S. beef producers.
This is not the first time Trump has acted to lower consumer beef prices in a way that has upset cattle producers. In February the president announced a deal with Argentina to import an additional 80,000 metric tons of lean beef trimmings with a goal of lowering consumer prices. 
Moss said the Friday announcement pausing quota tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of ground beef imports, was “another hit” for cattle feeders who learned Aug. 13 that a major Tyson beef facility in Illinois would close.
Woodall with the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association said this time of year is a “critical” time for producers as they make decisions about herd sizes. 
“Cattle farmers and ranchers are responding to strong market signals and historically high demand, and we are already working to rebuild after years of ongoing drought, high input costs and other challenges that have reduced U.S. cattle numbers,” Woodall said. “Today’s announcement and other market interventions throw cold water on the prospect of herd expansion and sacrifices long-term stability for short term messaging.”
