name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: In The SCEA, there’s no D or R only E
description: Since 1967, The South Carolina Education Association (yes, the “The” is always capitalized) has stood as a pioneer in public education. As the first professional organization of its kind in the United States willing to integrate, The SCEA demonstrated a commitment to ensuring every child has access to quality education and every educator is supported […]
text:
Dena Renee Crews, president of The South Carolina Education Association (middle), poses with other educators during the organization's back-to-school drop-in at the organization's headquarters in West Columbia, South Carolina, on Friday, July 17, 2026. (Photo courtesy of The SCEA)Since 1967, The South Carolina Education Association (yes, the “The” is always capitalized) has stood as a pioneer in public education.
As the first professional organization of its kind in the United States willing to integrate, The SCEA demonstrated a commitment to ensuring every child has access to quality education and every educator is supported and valued. Our history is one of resilience, progress, and an unwavering commitment to educational equity.
As president of The SCEA, I am honored to lead an organization with such a rich history.
Over the past year, I have listened to educators across South Carolina and heard stories of both progress and persistent challenges. I have also listened to parents and guardians who are concerned about their children’s public schools and want to ensure educators have the resources and support needed for students to thrive.
Our mission is clear: advocate for equitable resources, fair compensation, and safe, nurturing learning environments.
Achieving these goals requires all of us — educators, administrators, parents, families, and community members — to work together. Public education must remain a unifying force for the public good.
In The SCEA, there are no D’s or R’s — only E’s: Education.
Our commitment is to build bridges, foster understanding, and keep children at the center of every conversation.
We must protect the dignity and value of educators while working together to strengthen the schools our communities depend upon.
Political labels and partisan divides should never prevent us from finding common ground on behalf of our children.
The SCEA Fund for Children and Public Education engages at the local, state, and federal levels on policies affecting public education. More than 90% of South Carolina’s children attend public schools, including 95% of students requiring specialized instructional support.
The decisions made by elected officials directly affect these students, their families, and the educators who serve them.
During my first year as president, I participated in candidate interviews and reviewed questionnaires addressing public education issues. The experience reinforced an important truth: The SCEA’s commitment is not to a political party.
Regardless of party affiliation, we hope that beginning in January, elected officials and their agencies will choose collaboration over division and work with us to strengthen public education.
To encourage meaningful dialogue, The SCEA will host nine town halls through March 2027, bringing together students, families, educators, and elected officials to listen, learn, and discuss the future of public education. They are free and open to the public:

Sept. 22, Spartanburg
Sept. 24, Charleston
Oct. 1, York
Oct. 30, Columbia
Jan. 7, Beaufort
Jan. 21, Orangeburg
Feb. 4, Florence
March 4, Myrtle Beach
March 15, Abbeville

The road ahead demands courage, compassion, and an unwavering commitment to our children and our communities. I invite every stakeholder to join us in this vital work.
Because when it comes to education, there are no D’s or R’s — only E’s: Education.
Together, let us pursue equity, excellence, and opportunity for every child in every South Carolina public school.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Democratic lawmakers call for closure of ICE detention center in southwest Georgia
description: LUMPKIN, Ga. — Democratic members of Congress are calling for an immigration detention center in southwest Georgia to be shut down after conducting an oversight visit this week, describing conditions that included overcrowded cells and lack of adequate medical care. Stewart Detention Center, a facility run by the private prison company CoreCivic, is one of [[...]
text:
Democratic members of Congress, including Rep. Nikema Williams of Georgia, Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington, Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia and Rep. Deborah Ross of North Carolina, speak with reporters outside Stewart Detention Center in Lumpkin, Georgia. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderLUMPKIN, Ga. — Democratic members of Congress are calling for an immigration detention center in southwest Georgia to be shut down after conducting an oversight visit this week, describing conditions that included overcrowded cells and lack of adequate medical care.
Stewart Detention Center, a facility run by the private prison company CoreCivic, is one of the largest detention centers in the country. At least two people have died after being detained at the facility this year, including a man with leukemia whose family said he waited eight days for medical treatment after he began coughing up blood, according to reporting from WABE. He was later transferred to a hospital, where he went into a coma and died. 
Stewart Detention Center, a facility run by the private prison company CoreCivic, is one of the largest detention centers in the country. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
Georgia Reps. Hank Johnson and Nikema Williams toured the facility for roughly four hours Tuesday alongside Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington and North Carolina Reps. Valerie Foushee and Deborah Ross, and spoke with three people detained in the center. U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock also toured the facility Tuesday in a separate visit.
Jayapal, who serves as ranking member of an immigration enforcement subcommittee, called the facility “one of the worst in the country,” citing a 2023 government report detailing substandard conditions within the detention center after an unannounced inspection. She added that lawmakers were initially obstructed from conducting oversight by the prison staff during this week’s visit.
“We had to fight for access and for answers to be here,” she said while standing outside the facility talking to reporters. “We are horrified by the situation here at Stewart, and we believe this detention center should be shut down.”
Staff were also unwilling or unable to provide responses to many of the lawmakers’ questions, Jayapal said, such as the facility’s capacity or how many people were being detained without any criminal convictions on their record.
Johnson, who represents a metro Atlanta House district, also criticized the practice of having private, for-profit corporations running immigration detention centers.
“This whole racket is taking money directly from the taxpayers, the people, the wage earners of this country — those who don’t have the tax breaks that the wealthy have — and putting it directly into the hands and pockets and pocketbooks of these ultra wealthy people,” Johnson said. “They are profiting off of human misery.”
In a separate statement following his visit, Warnock echoed many of the lawmaker’s concerns about the conditions in Stewart Detention Center, citing an 11Alive investigation into recent increases in 911 calls made from the facility to treat detainees suffering from medical emergencies such as head injuries, suicide attempts and pregnancy complications.
“Regardless of your politics, we should all be able to agree on this, that everyone deserves to be treated with basic human dignity and respect,” he said in a statement. “As a member of Congress, I thought it was important for me, as a voice for Georgia, to spend time speaking directly to those in the facility.”
Ryan Gustin, CoreCivic’s senior director of public affairs, disputed lawmakers’ description of the facility, arguing the facility is maintained to the standards set forth by the federal government. He added that medical providers onsite provide the “highest standards of care,” which he said is available to detainees 24/7.
“The safety, health and well-being of the individuals entrusted to our care and our dedicated staff at all our facilities, including Stewart Detention Center is our top priority,” Gustin said in a statement.
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Attorneys push for the release of Georgia immigration activist detained by ICE during check-in

Alexandra Smolyar, an immigration attorney with Asian Americans Advancing Justice – Atlanta, said the lawmakers’ concerns mirror what she’s heard from clients who were detained at Stewart. Recent changes to immigration enforcement under the Trump administration, including the practice of detaining people during routine immigration check-ins, may also contribute to a rise in immigration-related arrests and detentions. 
“People who had periodic check-in requirements, who may well have been living peacefully in the community without incident for many, many years, for decades even, are just being indiscriminately detained at their ICE check-ins,” she said. “That is, to my understanding, unprecedented.”
She added that the detention center’s location in Lumpkin — a town of about 900 people that sits about 45 minutes south of Columbus — might play a role in limiting public awareness about what conditions are like for detainees.
“These are places that are out of public scrutiny, where many, many people are detained,” she said. “And I think that that allows conditions, in some ways, to fester.”

title: Legal Marijuana NOW candidate for Nebraska governor selects running mate
description: LINCOLN — The Legal Marijuana NOW nominee for Nebraska governor announced Friday the pick of an Omaha Housing Authority commissioner and local community ambassador as his running mate. Rick Beard of Omaha selected Keenya “Ruby” Barnes as his choice for lieutenant governor. Beard is a wine professional and private chef. Barnes has been a community ambassador[...]
text:
Rick Beard and Keenya Barnes, both of Omaha, are the 2026 governor and lieutenant governor candidates for Nebraska governor for the Legal Marijuana NOW party. (Photo courtesy of Beard campaign)LINCOLN — The Legal Marijuana NOW nominee for Nebraska governor announced Friday the pick of an Omaha Housing Authority commissioner and local community ambassador as his running mate.
Rick Beard of Omaha selected Keenya “Ruby” Barnes as his choice for lieutenant governor. Beard is a wine professional and private chef. Barnes has been a community ambassador for Omaha Performing Arts, Omaha by Design and Table Grace Ministries. 
She is an appointed resident commissioner for the Omaha Housing Authority. Under state law, the position means she advocates for fellow residents who receive assistance from the OHA.
“Through these positions, she has consistently demonstrated a unique ability to bridge communities, foster meaningful dialogue and champion affordable housing,” Beard’s campaign said in a news release. “The party is thrilled to welcome Ruby to the team as we work together to deliver real progress and representation to Nebraska voters.”
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, a Republican at center, is running for reelection against former Democratic State Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, left, and Rick Beard of Omaha, the nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW party. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Beard’s platform calls for a state-run medical cannabis program, which he sees as a long-term way to stabilize Nebraska’s budget and fund property tax relief. He also would like to legalize an industrial hemp program, get corporate and political action committee money out of Nebraska campaigns, and take a more serious, in-depth look at data centers.
This November, Beard will face Republican Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, who is running for reelection, and former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont.
Pillen is running again with Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, a longtime prosecutor who led the Lancaster County Attorney’s Office before being appointed U.S. attorney for Nebraska in President Donald Trump’s first term.
Walz is running with Ben Steffen of Humboldt, a corn and soybean farmer and ex-Republican.
In addition to Pillen, Walz and Beard, Nebraska could see a fourth candidate for governor.
Former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, an ex-Republican, failed to qualify a nonpartisan petition campaign for governor, in part due to allegations of fraudulent signatures. He’s opened the door to running as the gubernatorial candidate for an existing or prospective third party and join what he terms a “pirate ship.”
The deadline for the Libertarians and prospective America First Party or Nebraska Working  People Party to nominate a gubernatorial candidate is Sept. 1.
The general election is Nov. 3.

title: Nuclear training center, ROTC building named for Lindsey Graham among USC’s 2027 budget asks
description: The University of South Carolina is making plans for a nuclear training center and a new ROTC center in honor of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham.
text:
A University of South Carolina student studies Monday, April 29, 2024, on the historic Horseshoe, the original part of campus one block from the Statehouse in Columbia, South Carolina. (File photo by Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — The University of South Carolina is making plans for a nuclear workforce training center within its engineering school, as well as a new, $60 million Reserve Officers’ Training Corps center to be named in honor of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham.
“With renewed federal investment and private-sector leadership from companies such as Westinghouse, the United States is poised for a nuclear energy resurgence,” reads a statement from the college. “Through partnerships with private industry, federal agencies and the South Carolina Technical College System, USC is preparing to serve as a state and national hub for developing the workforce critical to supporting America’s next-generation nuclear energy ecosystem.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
USC plans to ask state legislators for $100 million in the next state budget cycle, beginning July 1, 2027. That dollar amount will be matched by private investment, the school’s statement said.
The center will be part of the school’s larger plans to renovate and expand its college of engineering and computing. It will train technicians, engineers, specialized construction professionals and operators for both large- and small-scale nuclear reactors.
The announcement comes amid efforts to restart construction of a pair of partially built nuclear reactors in the Palmetto State.
Work continues on a $2.7 billion deal between South Carolina’s state-owned utility company, Santee Cooper, and New York investment firm Brookfield Asset Management for the purchase of the abandoned reactors at the V.C. Summer nuclear plant in Fairfield County.
Decision on potential $2.7B sale of SC nuclear reactors could be 2 years away

Brookfield has until the end of March 2028 to make a final decision on whether or not to go forward with the purchase and reboot.
“By creating a model for developing the skilled talent and technology infrastructure required by the rapidly expanding nuclear energy industry, the center will strengthen South Carolina’s ability to compete for the next generation of nuclear and technology-driven economic development,” according to USC.
A new ROTC center
USC also will seek $20 million in state funding for a new ROTC center named after Lindsey Graham, who died unexpectedly July 11 of a tear in his aorta. He was 71 years old.
“The Senator Lindsey Graham ROTC Center of Excellence will serve more than 2,000 military-affiliated students and ROTC cadets in what will become the Southeast’s premier ROTC training and education facility,” the school wrote in a statement.
Graham served in the U.S. Senate for 23½ years and received two degrees from USC: a bachelor’s degree in 1977 and a law degree in 1981. He served in the U.S. Air Force, S.C. Air National Guard and U.S. Air Force Reserves from 1982 to 2015. Last week, Joint Base Charleston was officially renamed in Lindsey Graham’s honor.
The school has already received $20 million in federal grants for the center. It plans to request another $20 million.

name: VTDigger
title: As heating oil prices remain volatile, Vermonters prepare cautiously for winter
description:
Vermont’s deep reliance on heating oil makes the state vulnerable to price swings. Some residents are trying to find a safer path.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  As heating oil prices remain volatile, Vermonters prepare cautiously for winter.
text:
The reflective side of an Energy Co-op of Vermont fuel delivery truck is seen in Colchester on Tuesday, August 18, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
For Danny McGibney, a Barre Town resident who heats his home with oil, the price cap plan he uses to lock in his fuel costs is substantially more expensive this year than last. Nonetheless, renewing it this summer in preparation for the chilly months ahead was clearly the right call, he said.
“It just guarantees that I won’t pay more than a certain amount,” McGibney said, though that price threshold will be roughly 20% higher than in 2025. “We don’t have choice over the price of oil.”
That much is clear. Recent months have seen wild changes in fuel prices worldwide, with fuel oil costs in Vermont rising from under $3.50 per gallon in September 2025 to over $5 per gallon by May 2026, state data indicates. Despite some price dips earlier this summer following diplomatic advances in the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran, experts expect continued volatility in oil prices. Benchmark heating oil prices have risen in recent weeks, once again nearing their spring heights.
Few states are exposed to these price swings as acutely as Vermont.
More Vermonters use oil for heating than any other energy source, with U.S. Census Bureau data indicating over 35% of homes used fuel oil or kerosene in 2024. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, which estimated in 2020 that kerosene makes up a tiny portion of that category, this reliance on oil makes the state “particularly vulnerable to heating oil shortages and price spikes during the winter months.”
Across the state, fuel vendors and buyers alike are eyeing the winter months with caution.
Price-control tools available to residents like McGibney — which include maximum or fixed rates as well as prebuy contracts — are used by about half of oil customers in northern New England, according to Matt Cota, a lobbyist who represents fuel dealers in Vermont. Those contracts, which sometimes require upfront payment or hundreds of dollars in separate fees, are a way for customers to hedge their bets against the volatile global supply chain, Cota said. 
Unlike budget payment plans, which simply allow customers to even out their month-to-month utility payments without changing the overall cost, oil contracts lock in a price for a set amount of fuel. Some plans — like McGibney’s — allow prices to go down with the market, but not up above a set threshold.
This year, Cota said, there’s been a surge in people across the state choosing to pay more up front or overall to avoid the risk of getting stuck with even higher costs later. But for some, he noted, that’s a luxury beyond their means.
“Not everyone has the resources available to do this in summertime,” Cota said. 
Fuel industry analysts project that prices are likely to decrease over the winter, which has allowed many Vermont dealers to offer oil packages this summer at a lower price per unit than today’s delivery would cost, Cota said. But prices have been fluctuating so quickly that some vendors in the state are offering less wiggle room than usual to their customers.
Rose Friedlander, who leads marketing at the Energy Co-op of Vermont, said the company had delayed launching its prebuy plan due to market instability. 
“We weren’t able to launch it at our normal time, which left some members, you know, nervous for the upcoming season,” she said. “We have just seen incredible volatility since basically March.”
The co-op is also offering fewer such plans than usual for that reason, Friedlander said. And in the week since the program became available, she said in an interview recently, more than half the contracts had sold — a much faster rate than normal.
Anecdotally, Friedlander added, the company has also seen more interest from customers in secondary heat sources this year to decrease their dependence on fuel oil and defray higher costs. 
“Things like a wood pellet stove or a ductless heat pump are both good options for people who are looking to maybe reduce their fuel usage through the winter,” she said.
McGibney, for his part, is seriously considering installing a woodstove, both to cut costs and provide a backup option in power outages. If he were certain of staying in his house for the long haul, he said, he would be thinking about switching over his central heating source too.
Matthew Smith, who leads public relations at Efficiency Vermont, agreed with Friedlander that heat pumps and wood could both be cost-effective supplements to central heating. Heat pump technology has improved and diversified in recent years, he said, with his organization estimating Vermonters have installed more than 80,000 of them in the last decade.
Weatherization improvements to a home — such as insulation and air sealing — can also save hundreds of dollars annually in heating oil costs, Smith added.
“Given Vermont’s old housing stock, weatherization is kind of the invisible element here,” he said. “It’s an investment that will help bring down the energy bills, regardless of how you’re heating your home.”
Vermont offers need-based financial assistance for weatherization and appliance costs through the Department for Children and Families and Efficiency Vermont.

title: Republican PSC commissioner resigns from rate-setting regulatory board
description: Republican Public Service Commissioner Tricia Pridemore is stepping down early next month, 60 days before the election to replace her. In an Aug. 18 email to Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, Pridemore announced her plan to leave the body that regulates Georgia’s utility companies and helps set energy prices for Georgia Power customers. Her resignation was […]
text:
Tricia Pridemore is resigning from the Public Service Commission ahead of November's election. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderRepublican Public Service Commissioner Tricia Pridemore is stepping down early next month, 60 days before the election to replace her.
In an Aug. 18 email to Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, Pridemore announced her plan to leave the body that regulates Georgia’s utility companies and helps set energy prices for Georgia Power customers. Her resignation was first reported by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution.
Pridemore provided a copy of her resignation letter to the Recorder but declined to comment further. Her resignation takes effect Sept. 4.
“It has been an honor to serve Georgia in this position,” wrote Pridemore, who has served since 2018.
Georgia code gives Kemp, who is a Republican, the authority to appoint her successor until the next election. The governor’s office has not yet announced who the replacement will be and did not respond to a request for comment Friday.
The election is set for Nov. 3, when Republican Josh Tolbert is set to face Democrat Sheila Edwards for control of the seat. Tolbert and Edwards did not respond to requests for comment Friday.
Public Service Commission races typically fly under the radar of many voters, but a pair of Democratic flips on the previously all-Republican five-person panel put a spotlight on the utility regulating body. Democrats chalked the wins up to dissatisfaction with rising energy rates under Republican control, but Republicans blamed an off-year election that put the PSC races on the ballot alongside local races in deep blue cities. Republicans currently hold a narrow majority.
The PSC has also come under increased scrutiny during Pridemore’s tenure over the growth of data centers, which proponents say will power the internet of the future, but have been the center of commotion at city council meetings around the state where opponents decry their heavy water and power usage.
Pridemore was appointed to the seat in February 2018 by Republican Gov. Nathan Deal and re-elected for a six-year term that year. Lawmakers went on to postpone PSC elections in 2024, which meant her seat was not up for re-election again until this year.
Pridemore’s tenure already had an expiration date. Instead of running for re-election this year, she filed paperwork to run for the congressional seat held by retiring Republican Congressman Barry Loudermilk but fell short of making the GOP runoff.

name: Mississippi Today
title: ICE detainee fights deportation to be with medically fragile infant son
description: Olinder Calderon was the primary source of income for his family in Alabama and drove his son Oliver David, who  has needed consistent, specialized medical care since birth, to and from medical appointments. Calderon has been away from his family for a month at the Adams County Correctional Center in Natchez as his immigration case proceeds.
text:
Yulia Gómez held her infant son during a doctor’s appointment in Alabama as part of his care for health complications he’s faced since birth. Until a month ago, her husband Olinder Calderon was by her side to translate and help her understand their child’s care. 
But on this day, Gómez was by herself because Calderon is hundreds of miles away in a Mississippi immigration detention center facing deportation to Guatemala, a country he left nearly 20 years ago.  
Calderon plans to ask a judge to cancel removal proceedings against him because of his son and how much of a role he plays in the infant’s medical care. If deported, his wife said she would have to stay so that their American-born son can continue to receive specialized medical care. 
“(It) would completely change our lives,” Gómez said in Spanish in a phone interview from the doctor’s office. “I’d have to start our whole life over, and I think we’d even end up separating because you can’t put love above our baby’s well-being and health.”
The 27-year-old has been especially worried because Calderon was the family’s main source of income and transportation to the baby’s appointments, some hours away.  
Since he’s been away, Gómez said she has used their small savings to continue their son’s medical care. She is looking for support from organizations and searching for a pro bono immigration attorney because money is limited.  
Calderon’s immigration case took a step forward Wednesday with a virtual preliminary hearing with Immigration Judge Larry Downend from the LaSalle Immigration Court in Jena, Louisiana.  
That morning, Gómez logged on through a link provided by the federal government to watch the hearing, but she spent hours in a virtual waiting room unable to see anything before she was kicked off. 
Later that day, she talked with her husband who told her the hearing was brief. Downend, who was appointed to the court in June, asked if Calderon had an attorney and if he needed more time to get one, Gómez said. The judge also asked about the possibility of voluntary self-deportation, but she said Calderon does not plan to do that because of their son. 
His next hearing date is set for Sept. 1. At that hearing or a future one on his case’s merits, Calderon will have the chance to argue why he should stay in the country. 
As Calderon’s case makes its way through immigration court, Gómez said she has been in contact with the office of Alabama U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, who has offered help to look into Calderon’s case, including reaching out to Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 
A spokesperson for Rogers, a Republican who chairs the House Armed Services Committee, was not immediately available for comment Friday. 
Alabama resident Olinder Calderon has been detained in the Adams County Correctional Center in Natchez for a month and faces deportation to Guatemala, a country he left nearly 20 years ago. If removed, he would leave behind a life he built with his wife, their 9-month-old son, and a church community. Calderon sings and plays bass guitar for the church band and he is a worship member.  Credit: Courtesy of Yulia Gómez
Calderon, 37, came to the U.S. through a work visa and he stayed after it expired. He has worked as a painter and joined a Latino Christian church, where he became a member of the worship team, played bass guitar and sang in the church band. A friend introduced him to Gómez, and the couple married three years ago. Their son Oliver David was born in Georgia, near the Alabama border, in November. 
Gómez said she doesn’t have a driver’s license and can’t leave her son with others because of his special care needs. She stopped working during her high-risk pregnancy. 
Oliver developed bacterial meningitis after he was born, and the infection resulted in problems with his swallowing and coordination with his breathing. Gómez said eating poses a choking risk for him. The infant receives therapy at a Birmingham, Alabama, hospital and has appointments at a children’s clinic in Auburn, Alabama. 
Because Gómez and Calderon don’t have family in the U.S., people from church and the community have stepped in to help her get to doctor’s appointments and buy milk and supplies for Oliver. 
In a letter shared with Mississippi Today, Oliver’s pediatrician wrote that Calderon’s absence would have a physical, mental and emotional impact on the infant. The first week Calderon was gone, Gómez said their son had trouble sleeping because the baby was used to sleeping with his father. 
On July 19, Calderon was driving home from church when a police officer in Jackson’s Gap, Alabama, pulled him over. The officer found Calderon had a suspended license due to an outstanding ticket from another state, Gómez said. Then the officer asked Calderson if he was a citizen. He told the truth: No, I don’t have papers. 
Police put cuffs on his hands and legs and put him into the back of a cruiser, which Gómez said she saw through a video call from friends who met Calderon at the scene. 
“What impacted me the most was seeing my husband … accused like a person who committed a crime,” she said, adding that he does not have a criminal record. 
Coordination between local and state law enforcement and ICE is possible especially through the 287(g) program. Participation has exploded during the Trump administration. Jackon’s Gap’s agreement with ICE gives the force some authority to enforce federal immigration laws during routine policing, according to ICE records. 
Similar 287(g) agreements have also been signed in Mississippi, and more departments and state agencies are expected to ink them because a new state law requires all counties with a jail to have one. As of August, 25 of the state’s 82 counties have signed them, as well over 20 police departments, five state agencies and a county constable’s office.  
The Trump immigration crackdown has led to increased immigration arrests and restricted eligibility for bond hearings. At one point, anyone who entered the country illegally at any point in time could not receive bond to leave detention and await court proceedings from home, leading to indefinite detention. In July, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that those arrested are entitled to a bond hearing within 90 days of detention. 
Olinder Calderon, center, has been at the Adams County Correctional Center in Natchez for a month, hundreds of miles away from his home in Alabama. He came from Guatemala nearly 20 years ago and created a life in the United States, including becoming a member of his church community, meeting his wife Yulia Gómez, and having a son Oliver David.  The couple is pictured at their baby shower in 2025.  Credit: Courtesy of Yulia Gómez
Calderon had a bond hearing and provided written support from his church. The pastors highlighted his service and devotion to the church, his family and the community. 
If released on bond, they said the church would continue to support Calderon and his family. The pastors said he earned their trust over the years and they are confident he would attend future immigration hearings, according to the letter shared with Mississippi Today.
Downend denied the request July 30, saying Calderon failed to meet the burden to show he wasn’t a flight risk, according to documents reviewed by Mississippi Today.  
Calderon was moved from one immigration center to another, and Gómez was not able to talk to him. She said she tracked his movement through an app until he ended up in the Adams County Correctional Center in Mississippi.
She talks to him daily, and through a tablet. Calderon can have video calls where he can see their son. 
Since coming to the Natchez facility, Calderon has had a fever and sore throat, making it difficult for him to speak, Gómez said. She worries he has been receiving inadequate medical attention because he has asked a nurse to treat him, but Calderon said he hasn’t received treatment. Others at the immigration detention center are sick, too, he told her. 
“What I want people to take from this story is that Olinder, my husband, is not a criminal. He’s a father, a hard worker, a man who for years has served the church and been part of the community. His criminal record is clean,” Gómez said. 
“I want people to understand that behind an immigration detention there are human beings — families.”

name: VTDigger
title: Law enforcement governance council holds first meeting
description:
Representatives from nine Windham County towns took initial steps toward a long-term regional policing service.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Law enforcement governance council holds first meeting.
text:
The Windham County Sheriff’s Office building on Old Ferry Road in Brattleboro. File photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

This story by Olga Peters was first published in The Commons on Aug. 18, 2026. 
The newly formed Windham County Law Enforcement Governance Council convened for its inaugural meeting Aug. 7, ready to tackle how the Windham County Sheriff’s Office should provide collective policing for rural towns that lack their own police departments.
Selectboards from the initial nine participating towns opted into the pilot program. At the hybrid in-person and online meeting, members elected leadership, discussed their towns’ needs and expectations, and set initial goals.
Towns in Vermont provide law enforcement by relying on the state police, establishing their own police departments, electing or appointing constables, sharing services with a neighboring town, or contracting with their county sheriff’s department.
Currently, 15 Windham County municipalities have their own contracts with the WCSO.
Council members noted that creating municipal police departments would be cost-prohibitive for most towns. However, towns still face challenges such as inconsistent police coverage, insufficient traffic enforcement, concerns about responses to domestic violence or mental health crises, safety risks for emergency responders, and shifting needs in communities with many second-home or seasonal residents.
David Bemis from Athens said he understood that the state police can’t always respond quickly. The state police barracks in Westminster is stretched thin with a handful of troopers, he said.
“They certainly can’t do proactive things in our town like slowing speeders down or house checks, things like that,” he said.
Katy Johnson-Aplin from Newfane recalled that growing up in a rural area often meant police were too far away to help.
“And having grown up like that, we almost never call the police,” she said. “There is no reason to call the police, not for anything, unless it was a life-or-death emergency, where somebody’s trying to break down the door — and I think that this opportunity for our town means that there will be more presence, quicker response times.”
Robert Brooks from Jamaica added that he hopes his town can retain its productive relationship with the WCSO. According to the town’s website, Jamaica has contracted with WCSO since at least 2025.
He said the town’s population is shifting from mostly working-class residents. About 60% to 70% of Jamaica’s grand list — its total value of taxable properties — now includes more second homes, resulting in more vacant properties and fewer full-time residents.
“I would like to explore how we can maintain the wonderful service and our place within the bigger picture, because we’re also a smaller town compared to a Putney or, you know, most other towns,” he said.
At future meetings, the council intends to review a draft set of shared principles and develop bylaws.
Council members set a goal to launch the regional policing service by July 1, 2027, requiring a working service budget by Nov. 1, 2026.
The aggressive timeline is necessary because participating towns must present the program and budget to voters at Town Meeting in March. Therefore, the council aims to submit its budget this fall while towns are developing their fiscal year 2028 budgets.
Sheriff Mark R. Anderson said he sees the pilot program, established by a new state statute, as a “field study.”
“We are attempting to answer questions that have been researched and studied by the Legislature for decades on implementing a service that is shared by many, that benefits many, and is cheaper than doing it by ourselves,” he said.
The sheriff said he has heard the stories from people in the county’s more rural towns who default to calling neighbors in an emergency instead of the police. He recognizes that part of this is a result of gaps in the public safety system. What he worries about, however, is that in place of calling 911, people will resort to a doorbell camera and a shotgun.
He presented a pilot program to the Legislature earlier this year that resulted in the eight-year pilot, Act 104, that set up the Law Enforcement Governance Council.
The meeting facilitator, Windham Regional Commission Executive Director Chris Campany, said: “I really hope this (pilot) succeeds because I think it’ll be very beneficial to everybody involved, especially the towns and the people who live here.”
Selectboard members from the nine towns making up the council are David Bemis, of Athens; John Gregory, of Grafton; Tara Cheney, of Guilford; Robert Brooks, of Jamaica; James Ameden, of Londonderry; Kate Kirkwood, of Marlboro; Katy Johnson-Aplin, of Newfane; Aileen Tulloch, of Putney; and Jean Carr, of Vernon.
The group elected Johnson-Aplin as chair, Cheney as vice-chair and Tulloch as secretary-treasurer.
Beginning Sept. 2, the council will meet every Wednesday in September at 4 p.m. Check windhamcountyvt.gov/regionalpolicing for an updated meeting schedule or to follow the council’s work.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Wu hails White Stadium ruling as cranes and crews keep working
authors: Sam Drysdale | State House News Service
description: City officials cheered that the stadium project will now move ahead without delay, while opponents said the Supreme Judicial Court decision allowing construction to continue does not resolve their concerns about the stadium's size, cost, private use, and impact on the surrounding park and neighborhoods.
text:
CRANES WERE SWINGING over White Stadium about a mile away from where Boston Mayor Michelle Wu on Thursday celebrated the court ruling clearing the way for the major construction project to continue. 
The press conference unfolded on the patio behind the William J. Devine Golf Course clubhouse in Franklin Park, where Wu joined Boston Public Schools students and coaches, city and state officials, and other community leaders for what speakers repeatedly called a “celebration.” BPS band students welcomed attendees as golfers paused to watch, and most of the crowd squeezed into narrow patches of shade cast by the clubhouse, seeking relief from direct sunlight on the 85-plus-degree day. 
At the other end of Franklin Park, construction crews kept working on the mostly scaffolded White Stadium — now with unanimous agreement from the state’s highest court that they can continue to do so. 
The White Stadium project is a partnership between Boston Public Schools and Boston Legacy, the professional women’s soccer organization that plans to make the renovated stadium the home of its National Women’s Soccer League team. The city is rebuilding the nearly 80-year-old stadium as a public school and community athletics facility while Boston Legacy will use it for professional soccer and other events and pay for half the renovations. 
The project became the subject of a three-year legal fight after the Emerald Necklace Conservancy and 20 citizen plaintiffs sued, arguing that the stadium parcel was protected by Article 97 of the Massachusetts Constitution, which generally requires legislative approval for changes to protected parkland. 
The Supreme Judicial Court unanimously rejected that argument Wednesday, ruling that legislative actions in the late 1940s and 1950s had already removed the stadium from Article 97’s protections. 
City officials on Thursday cheered that the project will now move ahead without delay, while opponents said the court’s decision does not resolve their concerns about the stadium’s size, cost, private use, and impact on the surrounding park and neighborhoods. 
The mayor described the renovation as the culmination of decades of demands for investment in a facility that had deteriorated badly. The stadium’s bleachers had crumbled, she said, locker rooms lacked heat and running water, and students were injured playing on a pitted field and running on a cracked track. 
The renovated stadium will provide professional-grade athletic fields, an eight-lane track, new locker rooms, strength and conditioning rooms, study and community spaces, and year-round programming for students and residents, Wu said. 
“Everything looked so different when they would go to meets or games in suburban communities compared to when they were back home in their own city. That, to me, was the final straw,” Wu said. 
The city’s next steps will include decisions about how the stadium operates on game days. Wu said the facility will be open to the public 15 hours a day, seven days a week, after it reopens next year — a substantial change from recent years when its dilapidated state meant it was open for only limited hours and closed on weekends. 
“For so many of our community members who would be walking a dog through the park or coming in for exercise as neighbors who lived in the area, would be that they would see the gates locked and chained up to the stadium itself,” Wu said. “After we cut the ribbon next year, our residents, our communities will be able to use the facilities 15 hours a day, at least seven days a week, open to everyone to come, exercise, be healthy, and get to know your neighbors.”

name: VTDigger
title: Defund Israel’s decimation of southern Lebanon
description:
Sen. Peter Welch can force a Senate vote on Israel's human rights record in Lebanon. He should stop waiting.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Defund Israel’s decimation of southern Lebanon.
text:
This commentary is by Oscar Vulte, a rising sophomore at Brattleboro Union High School and a fellow with Action Corps.
Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., introduced a resolution on June 24 requesting a report on Israel’s human rights practices in Lebanon since Feb. 28, 2026, under Section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act, which allows Congress to request a human rights report on any country receiving U.S. military aid. This is a fantastic piece of legislation, and Welch was right to introduce it. Unfortunately, since being referred to the Committee on Foreign Relations, this resolution has not moved. This is sadly unsurprising considering that the chair of the committee is Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, who is a staunch supporter of Israel, and the committee has never once advanced a measure conditioning U.S. military aid to Israel on its conduct.
The good news is this: With a single motion on the Senate floor, Welch can get every member of the Senate to record their position on the resolution. The only requirement is that the committee has not reported the resolution within 10 days, a threshold it has cleared. The resolution might not pass, and even if it did, I don’t have much faith that our administration would do its due diligence or even attempt to lie convincingly. However, the point is to get our senators on record either voting for transparency in the human rights record of the largest cumulative recipient of U.S. military aid or essentially publicly burying their heads in the sand. A vote to table is still a vote on the record.
In case you haven’t been following the atrocities in the Middle East, Amnesty International has reported that the Israeli military has expanded its use of “everybody-leave” orders — one order in May covered 15% of the country — and followed them with “don’t-come-back” directives barring residents from a zone covering 6% of Lebanon. Lebanon’s Ministry of Social Affairs reported more than 1 million people still displaced as of June 7. On top of this, the Lebanese Health Ministry has reported nearly 4,000 deaths, including 247 children, according to UNICEF. 
These atrocities — and moreover, this tactic of atrocity — are not new: Israeli strategists have a name for it. “Mowing the grass” — kisuach hadeshe — has circulated in Israeli security discourse for years and was formalized in a 2014 paper by two Israeli scholars as a strategy of periodic large-scale operations to degrade an adversary rather than defeat it. Beneath it sits the Dahiya doctrine, which calls for disproportionate force and for treating civilian villages as military targets. Meanwhile, the U.S. is providing the weapons, bulldozers, military intelligence and diplomatic cover for these doctrines of murder. 
Welch’s resolution could prompt further action by Congress and lead to votes to restrict or cut off weapons for what U.N. experts say points to Israel’s pattern of ethnic cleansing of southern Lebanon. Legislators who vote against this resolution — if forced to vote — would have to confront the political consequences of plugging their ears and shutting their eyes in the name of combating terrorism. 
As Vermonters, we are uniquely positioned to help stop the U.S.-enabled ethnic cleansing of southern Lebanon. Welch’s introduction of the resolution is a good start, but he now needs to force the vote. There isn’t much sense in waiting. Don’t get me wrong: The Vermont delegation is probably one of the strongest in Congress in terms of fighting for human rights and progressive values, but we as the constituency do need to nudge them from time to time and not just have blind faith that they are doing their best. 

READ MORE

Some might say that this is the wrong thing for Welch to spend time on, that it won’t pass and that it’s better for Welch to focus on policies for Vermonters that actually have a chance of success. I would rebut these claims by noting that stopping the blank check to oppressive foreign governments is critical for our democracy. Moreover, Vermonters’ taxpayer dollars should be funding construction of housing here, not destroying people’s homes in Lebanon. There is nothing more important than stopping what U.N. human rights experts have described as part of the same pattern of destruction initiated during what they term the genocide in Gaza. If this were 1941, would you say that stopping Nazi Germany should be a secondary pursuit to lowering taxes or passing a policy of paid leave? Both of those could be worthy pursuits, but not as important as stopping ethnic cleansing or genocide. 
Welch should use his position in the Senate to force a vote on the Lebanon human rights resolution the same way Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., — joined by co-sponsors including Welch himself — has repeatedly forced votes on weapons transfers to Israel. Vermonters have a unique power and responsibility to ensure this happens.

title: Winfield resident shocked by Kansas lawmaker’s response to her plea for gun safety
description: TOPEKA — Winfield resident Lisa Spoon emailed every member of the Kansas House to start a conversation about loopholes in state law that allow people convicted of violent crimes to own a gun. Instead, she received a reply from Rep. Rick Wilborn that she views as “void of compassion.” Spoon began her email to lawmakers, […]
text:
The makeshift memorial outside the home on West Ninth Street in Winfield, where four children and their parents were found dead last week in a murder-suicide that has rocked the community. (Photo by Lisa Spoon via Cowley Courier Traveler)TOPEKA — Winfield resident Lisa Spoon emailed every member of the Kansas House to start a conversation about loopholes in state law that allow people convicted of violent crimes to own a gun.
Instead, she received a reply from Rep. Rick Wilborn that she views as “void of compassion.”
Spoon began her email to lawmakers, sent late Thursday, by explaining that she was writing “with a heavy heart and deep frustration” about a mass shooting in her south-central Kansas town of about 12,000 people. Last week, her next-door neighbor shot and killed his wife and their four children before killing himself.
Her email referenced the “critical gaps” in state laws that allow individuals like her neighbor, who have a documented history of violence, to obtain and possess firearms. She urged lawmakers to consider policy changes, such as mandating universal background checks on all gun sales and transfers and considering “threats of violence as a rationale for a warrant, search and removal of guns from a household.”
Wilborn, a McPherson Republican who didn’t seek reelection this year, replied to Spoon, and everybody else, early Friday.
“You folks never miss an opportunity, to promote your gun shaming hypothesis,” Wilborn wrote. “More people are killed by illegals with a criminal record. Please spare me.”
Rep. Rick Wilborn, R-McPherson, appears at a Feb. 3, 2026, hearing at the Statehouse in Topeka. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Kansas Reflector interviewed Spoon after obtaining a copy of the email exchange. She hadn’t yet seen Wilborn’s reply, and read it before answering questions.
“I’m a little shocked to be honest because there was no compassion, no empathy, no nothing,” she said. “You know, when you start an email out that says, ‘you people’ — he doesn’t know me. I tried to write the most logical, sensible email that I possibly could muster, and immediately he went to ‘you people’ and ‘immigrants shoot more people in the United States than anybody else.’ So there was nothing there. I mean, he apparently is somewhat void of compassion.”
“I think he’s wrong,” she added. “Statistically, I don’t think he has a leg to stand on.”
U.S. Customs and Border Protection data show between two and 62 “criminal aliens” have been convicted of homicide or manslaughter nationwide each year for the past 10 years. Research by the gun-safety advocacy group Everytown shows 70 women are shot and killed by an intimate partner every month.
Wilborn didn’t respond to a voicemail or email from Kansas Reflector seeking comment on his fact-challenged response.
Spoon said she has guns in her house — “most people do” — and just wants to live in a safe community. She said she is a longtime registered Republican but now considers herself to be “left-leaning.”
“I’m not advocating that we just randomly go take guns away,” she said, but she wants her community to be safe.
She said it had been 123 years since the last mass shooting in Winfield.
“To be quite honest, there’s something that happens inside you when a mass murder happens 20 feet away from your home,” Spoon said.
Rep. Mari-Lynn Poskin, a Leawood Democrat and gun owner, said Spoon’s email “was so thoughtful and well written,” and that she was “taken aback” by Wilborn’s response.
“It really surprised me because I think of Rep. Wilborn as a kind and conscientious person, and I’ve never known him to be disrespectful,” Poskin said. “But I felt that it was very disrespectful, particularly given the tenor of the sender’s email.”
Rep. Jo Ella Hoye, a Lenexa Democrat and gun owner who previously led the state chapter of Moms Demand Action, said the shootings in Winfield show the need for stronger laws “to keep guns out of the hands of dangerous people.”
“Unfortunately,” she said, “over the past few years, the Legislature’s actually been weakening our gun laws.”
She pointed to House Bill 2058, passed in 2021, as an example. Lawmakers at the end of the session expanded the scope of that bill to lessen the prohibitions on owning a gun for some people convicted of violent crimes. That policy came from a Senate bill favored by Attorney General Kris Kobach that hadn’t received the support of a committee in either chamber.
Wilborn, who was in the Senate at the time, voted to pass HB 2058 and again to override the governor’s veto.
Hoye said she hasn’t seen data regarding Wilborn’s claim that “more people are killed by illegals with a criminal record.” She said a lot of domestic violence is homegrown.
“The continuous weakening of our gun laws would make it easier for any criminal to get a gun, whether they’re documented or undocumented,” she said.
Spoon said she was aware before the shooting that her neighbor, Ronald Williams Sr., was a registered sex offender and convicted felon. She said she was aware that he was capable of violent crime, based on police calls to the house and interactions people had with Williams in the community.
“The fact that Kansas has loopholes in gun laws that allow felons to have guns in their possession just doesn’t really make sense to me, especially when they have particularly violent personal crimes,” she said.
“I don’t know what the answer is,” she added. “I’m not a legislator, you know. I’m speaking from my heart and what goes through my head and trying to make sense of what happened 20 feet away from my side door. It’s disturbing.”

text:
Red rock shores are pictured at Sand Hollow State Park near Hurricane, Utah. Sand Hollow was the most visited state park during the 2025 to 2026 season. (Courtesy of Utah State Parks)For a third year in a row, Utah’s state parks recorded more than 12 million visits between July 2025 and June 2026, Utah State Parks announced in a blog post Wednesday. 
That marks the parks’ third-highest year of visitation on record. 
Over the past decade, visitation to state parks has more than doubled, from 5 million in 2016, Utah State Parks Director Scott Strong said in a prepared statement. 
“As interest in the outdoors continues to increase, we will continue to provide parks full of great recreation opportunities, well-maintained facilities and park rangers ready to help you make lifelong memories,” Strong said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Utah State Parks operates 46 state parks that span across the state, including reservoirs, red rocks in Southern Utah, and museums. 
During the COVID-19 pandemic, which sent droves of people outdoors, visitation to state parks boomed. During the 2019 to 2020 season, visitation increased by more than 2.6 million, according to the agency. The total number of state park visitors in 2020 was almost 10.6 million — a 33% jump from 2019, which saw less than 8 million visitors.
Today, state parks’ visitors continue to surpass pandemic-era popularity. As post-pandemic tourism continues to boom, Utah State Parks officials said they’re working to continue to provide “well-maintained facilities, friendly park rangers and beautiful lands to enjoy for this and future generations.”
Here are the top 10 most popular parks over the last year, according to Utah State Parks:

title: Two Iowa nursing homes added to list of the nation’s worst care facilities
description: The federal government has added two Iowa nursing homes to its list of the worst care facilities in the nation. Oakland Manor in Pottawattamie County and Harmony House Health Care Center in Waterloo have been added to the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ nationwide list of care facilities that are eligible for special-focus status, […]
text:
Oakland Manor in Pottawattamie County and Harmony House Health Care Center in Waterloo have been added to the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ nationwide list of care facilities that are eligible for special-focus status. (Photo by byryo/iStock/Getty Images Plus)The federal government has added two Iowa nursing homes to its list of the worst care facilities in the nation.
Oakland Manor in Pottawattamie County and Harmony House Health Care Center in Waterloo have been added to the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ nationwide list of care facilities that are eligible for special-focus status, indicating a history of serious, recurring resident-care issues.
At any given time, no more than two nursing homes per state appear on the list of federally designated “special-focus facilities,” while 10 others in each state are designated as eligible for such a designation due to resident-care issues.
The 100 facilities that are designated special-focus facilities are subject to a comprehensive, onsite inspection at least once every six months, with the expectation that they will eventually take substantive action to address any ongoing issues.
The two Iowa nursing homes that are currently enrolled in the special-focus program are Garden View Care Center in Shenandoah, and Pine Acres Rehabilitation and Care Center in West Des Moines. Garden View has been in the program for 12 months and Pine Acre for 14 months.
Oakland Manor cited for abuse, staffing issues
In addition to the list of the 100 nursing homes actively enrolled in the special-focus program, CMS also publishes a list of the roughly 500 homes — 10 per state — where recurring, serious resident-care issues have made them eligible for enrollment.
Oakland Manor’s recent addition to the list of eligible homes appears to stem from a number of violations cited by inspectors over the past 16 months.
In July 2025, state inspectors cited the home for 18 regulatory violations related to resident nutrition, abuse and neglect, failure to self-report alleged violations, failure to meet professional standards, overall quality of care, feeding assistance and infection control.
In January 2026, the home was cited for 14 regulatory violations, including failing to provide a safe, clean, homelike environment; failure to self-report violations; overall quality of care; inadequate respiratory care and insufficient nursing staff.
In April 2026, the home was cited for resident abuse after it was determined that hundreds of narcotic tablets were missing from residents’ drug supplies and the cards that had contained the tablets had been tampered with.
Harmony House cited for abuse and medication errors
Waterloo’s Harmony House Health Care Center was cited for 15 regulator violations in August 2025. The violations were tied to abuse and neglect, failure to self-report violations, failure to develop and implement comprehensive resident care plans, overall quality of care, treatment of pressure sores and infection control.
In March 2026, Harmony House was cited for 13 regulatory violations, including failure to investigate cases of potential resident abuse, failure to meet professional standards, overall quality of care, inadequate nursing services, insufficient nursing staff and medication errors.
The eight other Iowa nursing homes currently deemed eligible for special-focus status, and the number of months they have been on that list, are:
Azria Health Park Place, Des Moines: Eight months.
Bishop Drumm Retirement Center, Johnston: Nine months.
Caring Acres Nursing and Rehab Center, Anita: Seven months.
Chapters Living, Council Bluffs: Four months.
Greater Southside Health and Rehabilitation Center, Des Moines: 45 months.
The Ivy, Davenport: 10 months.
Northgate Care Center, Waukon: Three months.
Royal Oaks Nursing and Rehabilitation Center, Urbandale: Two months.

title: Evers, DNR push finance committee to release $10 million in PFAS settlement funds
description: Gov. Tony Evers and the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources are asking the Legislature’s Republican-controlled Joint Committee on Finance to release $10 million the state received earlier this summer as part of a lawsuit settlement with Tyco Fire Products over PFAS contamination in the Marinette area.  In June, Tyco and the state reached the settlement[...]
text:
A sign warning people not to drink water contaminated with PFAS chemicals in Marinette. (2019 photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)Gov. Tony Evers and the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources are asking the Legislature’s Republican-controlled Joint Committee on Finance to release $10 million the state received earlier this summer as part of a lawsuit settlement with Tyco Fire Products over PFAS contamination in the Marinette area. 
In June, Tyco and the state reached the settlement agreement, marking one of the first efforts in the state to hold a polluter responsible for PFAS pollution. The Marinette area’s water has been affected by PFAS contamination for years. 
Under state law, money received by the state in lawsuit settlements is under the control of JFC — even though the settlement requires that the money be spent by the DNR for PFAS remediation. 
On Thursday, Evers and DNR Secretary Karen Hyun urged the committee to release the funds quickly so the money can get out to residents. Evers said that after the DNR held listening sessions with community members, the settlement funds would be directed to help people with private wells test for PFAS and replace contaminated wells. 
“Every Wisconsinite deserves to have clean, safe water to drink, and for the past seven-plus years, my administration and I have been working to fight these forever chemicals that are affecting the health and well-being of kids, families, farmers, livestock, crops, and communities all over Wisconsin,” Evers said in a statement. “I’m proud of our work to create the PFAS Trust Fund, which is available to help ensure the state can support Wisconsinites in getting contaminants like PFAS out of their water for good.”
The DNR collaborated with local leaders and held listening sessions to develop the plan for spending the settlement money “to ensure these funds are put to good use and address the urgent needs of the impacted communities,” Evers said.
“I urge lawmakers to act quickly and approve our request by releasing these funds as quickly as possible so we can continue this fight and ensure Wisconsinites have clean drinking water,” he added.
The money has been deposited in the state’s PFAS trust fund, which was created as part of the 2023-25 budget to help the state remediate PFAS pollution. Earlier this year, Evers signed into law a bill that creates a number of programs aimed at getting that money out the door.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Drought conditions worsen across New Mexico, West
description: Record-breaking July temperatures have left nearly 95% of New Mexico in some degree of drought, according to a new outlook from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and “isolated” monsoon rains failed to provide meaningful relief to water supply challenges across the West.
text:
The Elephant Butte Reservoir, pictured above on July 30, 2026, remains at 1.4% of its capacity, according to a new drought outlook from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. (Photo courtesy New Mexico Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Department) Record-breaking July temperatures have left nearly 95% of New Mexico in some degree of drought, according to a new outlook from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and “isolated” monsoon rains failed to provide meaningful relief to water supply challenges across the West. 
The outlook, released Thursday, monitored the status of major reservoirs across the Colorado River and Rio Grande basins, noting that many have reached historic lows, including Lake Mead and Lake Powell. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
New Mexico’s Elephant Butte Reservoir remains at 1.4% of its capacity, prompting state officials earlier this month to close the lake’s main boat ramp due to safety concerns. 
Conditions will improve through November, officials said Thursday. While an uptick in monsoon rains will not “fully eliminate drought and its impacts,” forecasters predict a 90% chance of a “very strong” event triggered by a strengthening El Niño, potentially creating wetter conditions across the Intermountain West this fall. 
NOAA’s previous outlook in early July was more optimistic about the potential for significant monsoon rains across the region this summer. But the forecast released Thursday noted that New Mexico instead experienced its second-warmest July on record, and the eastern part of the state “continued to dry out” without receiving any significant precipitation. 
The administration’s drought map shows that 3% of New Mexico is in “severe drought,” namely Albuquerque, Santa Fe and parts of the northeastern corner of the state. About one-third of the state, predominantly in northern New Mexico, is suffering from “extreme drought,” the map shows. 
The outlook notes that conditions are unlikely to improve over the next two weeks, with all but the northern and western edges of New Mexico facing 100% probabilities of above-average temperatures.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: ACLU queries Tennessee school districts on Ten Commandments
description: A group led by the American Civil Liberties Union is seeking information from five Tennessee school districts about their plans to post the Ten Commandments after a new state law allowed the Bible document to go up in school buildings’ “prominent” locations. The ACLU of Tennessee, ACLU, Americans United for Separation of Church and State […]
text:
A coalition including the American Civil Liberties Union of Tennessee and the Freedom From Religion Foundation is asking school districts about their plans to post the Ten Commandments in schools. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A group led by the American Civil Liberties Union is seeking information from five Tennessee school districts about their plans to post the Ten Commandments after a new state law allowed the Bible document to go up in school buildings’ “prominent” locations.
The ACLU of Tennessee, ACLU, Americans United for Separation of Church and State and the Freedom From Religion Foundation sent letters Thursday requesting public records from school districts that are planning to put the Ten Commandments in school buildings. The letters went to the Blount County School District, Rutherford County Schools, Washington County Schools, White County Schools and Wilson County Schools, whose school boards authorized the posting.
The letters request all school district emails and other communications, including school board documents, dealing with the display of the Ten Commandments, in addition to proposed or approved designs for the displays.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
The groups issued a statement saying, “Forcing biblical scripture on public-school children violates families’ religious freedom. Families and faith communities, not the government, get to decide what role religious doctrine and belief play in their lives. We are committed to protecting students’ and parents’ constitutional rights and are launching an investigation of every school district that foolishly accepts the state’s invitation to trample those rights. We urge families who will be affected by these religious displays to contact our organizations.”
The legislature passed House Bill 47 this year allowing schools to put the Ten Commandments in “prominent” locations such as a “school entryway, cafeteria, or common area where students are likely to see the display.” The displays must have text with a font size no smaller than 26 points and a “style and manner that is easy for students to see and read,” the groups said in a statement.
Initially, House Bill 47 would have given local school boards and public charter school governing bodies authority to allow schools to put the Tennessee Commandments, the Declaration of Independence, U.S. Constitution, Tennessee Constitution, Bill of Rights and other historical documents in “prominent” locations to educate students.
Republican Sen. Mark Pody of Lebanon tried to amend the bill to request districts to post the Ten Commandments. But the bill’s House sponsor, Rep. Michael Hale of Smithville, opted to give school districts a choice, making it easier for the bill to withstand a constitutional challenge.
